school-c8-science-b.title: Class 8 Science (part 2 of 2)
school-c8-science-b.description: Every chapter of Class 8 Science as its own course — clear explanations, worked examples, activities, safety notes, quizzes and chapter tests — plus Revision & Practice. Chapters follow the rationalised NCERT Class 8 textbooks (2023–24 editions onward). NCERT has been introducing new Class 8 books from 2025–26; if your school uses those, chapter names and order differ, but most topics here still apply. Independent material, not affiliated with NCERT or any board.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Force and Pressure
courses.summary: Force as a push or pull, interaction between objects, net force, the effects of force, contact and non-contact forces, pressure and its applications, pressure in liquids and gases, and atmospheric pressure.
outcomes: Learners can explain force as an interaction and find net force in a line
Learners can describe effects of force on speed, direction and shape
Learners can classify contact and non-contact forces
Learners can calculate pressure and explain pressure in liquids, gases and the atmosphere

lessons.title: Force: a push or a pull

scenes.text: Two teams pull a rope at sports day.
For a while the rope doesn't move at all.
Equal forces in opposite directions cancel — the net force is zero.

steps.title: What is a force?
steps.body: A **push or a pull** on an object is a **force**. At least **two objects** must interact for a force to come into play — force arises due to an **interaction**. Force has **magnitude (strength)** and **direction**. SI unit: **newton (N)**.

steps.title: Net force
steps.body:
- Forces in the **same direction** add up.
- Forces in **opposite directions** — net force is the **difference**, in the direction of the larger force.
- If equal and opposite, net force = 0 → no change in motion.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Two friends push a box to the right with 40 N and 30 N. Net force? → 70 N to the right.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Team A pulls left with 500 N, team B pulls right with 450 N. Net force? → 50 N towards team A (left); the rope moves left.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a force needs a visible push — gravity and magnetism act without touching.
- Adding forces that act in opposite directions.

activity.prompt: Rohan pushes a cart forward with 60 N; friction acts backward with 15 N. Net force?

quiz.why: A force is a push or a pull on an object.

quiz.q: Forces of 20 N and 20 N act on an object in opposite directions. Net force:
quiz.why: Two equal forces in opposite directions cancel each other. The net force is 20 − 20 = 0 N.
The SI unit of force is the newton (N).

quiz.q: For a force to act, there must be:
quiz.why: A force needs an interaction between at least two objects, such as a hand and a ball.

quiz.q: 10 N and 6 N in the same direction give net force:
quiz.why: Forces in the same direction add up: 10 N + 6 N = 16 N. Subtracting would only be right if they pulled in opposite directions, and multiplying has no meaning for net force.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Effects of force

scenes.text: Priya kicks a stationary football: it moves.
The goalkeeper stops it; another player's header changes its direction.
At home, her brother presses clay into a pot — the force changes its shape.

steps.title: What a force can do
steps.body:
- Make a stationary object **move**.
- **Change the speed** of a moving object (speed up or slow down).
- **Change the direction** of motion.
- **Change the shape** of an object (pressing a balloon, kneading dough).
- Or any combination.

The **state of motion** of an object is described by its **speed and direction**. A state of rest is zero speed. A force may change the state of motion.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A cricketer hits a ball back towards the bowler. Effects? → Changes the direction and speed of the ball.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Squeezing a toothpaste tube. Effect? → Change of shape (and the paste moves out).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'A force always moves an object' — pushing a wall applies force but it doesn't move.
- Forgetting that a change of direction alone is also a change in the state of motion.

activity.prompt: Main effect of the force?

quiz.q: Pressing a rubber ball changes its:
quiz.why: A force can change an object's shape. Pressing the ball squeezes it, so its shape changes (deformation), while its material, mass and colour stay the same.

quiz.q: State of motion is described by:
quiz.why: The state of motion of an object is described by its speed and its direction of movement. Colour, shape and temperature say nothing about how it is moving.
Brakes press on the wheel and produce a force that opposes the motion, so the cycle slows down. A force opposite to motion reduces speed; it cannot increase it.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an effect of force?
quiz.why: A force can change speed, direction and shape, but it cannot change an object's colour. Colour is a property of the material, not a result of pushing or pulling.

quiz.q: Pushing a wall that doesn't move shows that:
options: A force may not always cause motion
quiz.why: You apply a force on the wall, yet it does not move because the wall resists it. So a force does not always produce motion; it may balance with another force.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Contact and non-contact forces

scenes.text: Ali runs a plastic comb through dry hair and brings it near tiny paper bits.
The bits jump to the comb without being touched!
Like magnets and gravity, this force acts at a distance.

steps.title: Contact forces
steps.body:
- **Muscular force:** force from muscles — lifting a bag, animals pulling carts.
- **Friction:** force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact (a rolling ball slowly stops).

steps.title: Non-contact forces
steps.body:
- **Magnetic force:** magnets attract iron and attract/repel each other without touching (like poles repel, unlike attract).
- **Electrostatic force:** exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body (comb and paper bits).
- **Gravitational force (gravity):** every object in the universe attracts every other object; the Earth pulls everything towards itself — that's why things fall.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Classify: a bullock pulling a cart; an apple falling; a magnet pulling a pin. → Muscular (contact); gravity (non-contact); magnetic (non-contact).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why does a rolling ball stop on grass? → Friction between the ball and the grass opposes its motion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling friction non-contact — it requires surfaces in contact.
- Thinking gravity acts only on the Earth — every object attracts every other.

activity.prompt: Contact or non-contact force?

quiz.q: A charged comb attracting paper bits shows:
quiz.why: A comb rubbed on dry hair gets charged, and the charge attracts light paper bits without touching them. This force between charged objects is the electrostatic force.

quiz.q: Force due to which things fall to Earth:
quiz.why: Things fall to the ground because the Earth pulls them towards its centre. This pull is gravity, which acts without any contact.
Friction acts only when two surfaces touch and rub, so it is a contact force. Magnetic and electrostatic forces act at a distance.
Magnets follow the rule that like poles repel and unlike poles attract. So two like poles push each other away.
Lifting a bag uses the force of our muscles, called muscular force. A magnet, a falling apple and a charged comb use magnetic force, gravity and electrostatic force instead.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Pressure

scenes.text: Mum's blunt knife squashes tomatoes; the sharp one slices easily.
School bags have wide straps; nails have pointed tips.
Same force — different area — different pressure.

steps.title: Pressure
steps.body:
**Pressure = Force ÷ Area on which it acts** (force acting perpendicular to the surface — called *thrust*).

- SI unit: **N/m²**, called the **pascal (Pa)**.
- Smaller area → larger pressure for the same force.
- Larger area → smaller pressure.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A box weighing 500 N rests on 0.25 m². Pressure? → 500 ÷ 0.25 = 2000 Pa.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: The same 500 N box is turned to stand on a face of 0.05 m². Pressure? → 500 ÷ 0.05 = 10,000 Pa (5 times more).

steps.title: Applications
steps.body:
- Sharp knives, pointed nails and needles: small area → high pressure, cuts/pierces easily.
- Wide school-bag straps, wide tyres of trucks and tractors, broad feet of camels: large area → low pressure, comfort/no sinking.
- Porters place a round cloth on their heads to increase area and reduce pressure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a heavier object always exerts more pressure — area matters.
- Using cm² with N and calling the result Pa without converting (1 m² = 10,000 cm²).

activity.prompt: A force of 300 N acts on an area of 0.015 m². Pressure?

quiz.why: Pressure is the force acting on each unit of area, so Pressure = Force ÷ Area. Dividing area by force, or multiplying, does not give force per unit area.
Pressure is measured in pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Newton is the unit of force, watt of power and joule of energy.

quiz.q: School bags have wide straps to:
quiz.why: A wide strap spreads the same weight over a larger area. Since pressure = force ÷ area, a larger area means less pressure on the shoulders.
Pressure = Force ÷ Area = 100 N ÷ 2 m² = 50 Pa. Multiplying (200) or dividing the wrong way (0.02) would be mistakes.
A pointed tip has a very small area. The same force on a small area gives a large pressure, so the nail goes into the wood easily.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Pressure in liquids, gases and the atmosphere

scenes.text: Tara makes three holes at different heights in a water bottle.
Water from the lowest hole shoots out the farthest.
That's why dam walls are thicker at the bottom!

steps.title: Liquids
steps.body:
- Liquids exert pressure on the **bottom and walls** of their container.
- Pressure of a liquid **increases with depth**.
- At the same depth, liquid exerts equal pressure in all directions on the walls.
- Hence **dams** are made thicker at the base; water from lower taps of a tank flows out faster.

steps.title: Gases and the atmosphere
steps.body:
- Gases exert pressure on the walls of their container (a blown-up balloon stays inflated).
- The envelope of air around the Earth is the **atmosphere**; the pressure it exerts is **atmospheric pressure** — very large (about **1,00,000 Pa** at sea level; roughly the weight of a 10-tonne mass pressing on each square metre).
- We are not crushed because the pressure inside our bodies is about equal and balances it.

steps.title: Worked example 1 — rubber sucker
steps.body: Press a rubber sucker on a smooth surface: air is pushed out from below, so atmospheric pressure outside holds it firmly. It is hard to pull off.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why does a water tank tap at the bottom flow faster than one higher up? → Pressure increases with depth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Liquids push only downward' — they push sideways on walls too.
- 'Air has no weight or pressure' — atmospheric pressure is huge.

statements.s: Liquid pressure increases with depth.
Dams are thicker at the top.
statements.why: Thicker at the bottom, where pressure is greatest.

statements.s: Gases exert pressure on the walls of containers.
We are crushed by atmospheric pressure.
A rubber sucker sticks because of atmospheric pressure.

quiz.q: Water from the lowest hole of a bottle goes farthest because:
options: Pressure is greatest at the bottom
quiz.why: Liquid pressure grows with depth. The lowest hole has the most water above it, so the pressure is greatest there and the water is pushed out farthest.

quiz.q: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about:
quiz.why: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 10⁵ Pa, i.e. 1,00,000 Pa. The other values are far too small for the weight of the whole column of air above us.

options: Air inside exerts pressure on its walls
quiz.why: The air molecules inside keep hitting the balloon's walls and push them outwards. This gas pressure keeps the balloon inflated.

quiz.q: Dams are wider at the base because:
quiz.why: Water pressure increases with depth, so the lower part of a dam faces a bigger push. A wider base makes the dam strong enough to bear it.

quiz.q: At the same depth, liquid pressure on the walls is:
quiz.why: At a given depth, a liquid pushes equally in all directions - up, down and sideways. So pressure on the walls is the same as pressure on the bottom at that depth.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

questions.q: Force is a:
questions.why: A force is a push or a pull on an object. Speed and mass are different quantities, and energy is not the same thing as force.

questions.q: Which is a non-contact force?
questions.why: Magnetic force acts at a distance without touching. Muscular force, friction and pushing all need contact.

questions.q: Unit of pressure:
questions.why: Pressure is force per unit area, so its unit is N/m², called pascal. Newton is for force, metre for length and kilogram for mass.

questions.q: Forces of 8 N east and 3 N west. Net force:
questions.why: Opposite forces subtract: 8 N − 3 N = 5 N, and the net force acts in the direction of the larger force, which is east.

questions.q: A force can change all EXCEPT:
questions.why: A force can change speed, direction and shape, but pushing or pulling does not change the amount of matter in an object. So its mass stays the same.

questions.q: Pressure of 400 N on 0.2 m²:
questions.why: Pressure = Force ÷ Area = 400 N ÷ 0.2 m² = 2000 Pa. Dividing by a number smaller than 1 makes the answer bigger.

questions.q: Assertion: A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one. Reason: A sharp edge has a smaller area and so exerts more pressure.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true. A sharp edge has a small area, so the same force gives more pressure (P = F/A), and that is why it cuts better.

questions.q: Electrostatic force acts between:
questions.why: Electrostatic force acts between charged bodies, and a charged body can also attract an uncharged one. It is not limited to magnets or touching surfaces.

questions.q: Why does a camel walk easily on sand?
questions.why: A camel has broad feet, so its weight is spread over a large area. Less pressure on the sand means it does not sink in.

questions.q: Case: A tank of water has taps at heights 0.5 m, 1 m and 1.5 m from the bottom. Which tap's water comes out fastest?
questions.why: Liquid pressure increases with depth. The tap at 0.5 m from the bottom lies deepest below the surface, so water comes out of it with the greatest speed.

questions.q: A brick of weight 30 N measures 0.2 m × 0.1 m × 0.05 m. Maximum pressure it can exert:
questions.why: Pressure is greatest on the smallest face: 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.005 m². So P = 30 N ÷ 0.005 m² = 6000 Pa.

questions.q: Same brick, minimum pressure:
questions.why: Pressure is least on the largest face: 0.2 × 0.1 = 0.02 m². So P = 30 N ÷ 0.02 m² = 1500 Pa.

questions.q: We don't feel atmospheric pressure crushing us because:
options: Pressure inside our body balances it
questions.why: Air does press on us, but the pressure of the fluids inside our body is equal to it. The two balance, so we do not feel crushed.

questions.q: Assertion: Gravity acts only on objects near the Earth. Reason: Every object in the universe attracts every other object.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because gravity acts between all objects, not just near the Earth. The reason is true: every object attracts every other object, which is why gravity is universal.

questions.q: A pressure of 5000 Pa acts on 0.4 m². The force:
questions.why: Force = Pressure × Area = 5000 Pa × 0.4 m² = 2000 N. Do not just repeat the pressure value; the area must be multiplied.

questions.q: Why do tractors have very broad rear tyres?
options: To reduce pressure on soft soil and avoid sinking
questions.why: Broad tyres spread the heavy weight over a larger area. This lowers the pressure on soft soil, so the tractor does not sink.

questions.q: A rubber sucker pressed on a smooth wall sticks because:
options: Gravity pulls it to the wall
Air is pushed out below and atmospheric pressure holds it
questions.why: Pressing the sucker pushes the air out from under it. The outside atmospheric pressure is then greater than the pressure below, and it holds the sucker on the wall.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Friction
courses.summary: What friction is and why it arises, the factors it depends on, static, sliding and rolling friction, why friction is a necessary evil, ways to increase and reduce it, and fluid friction (drag) with streamlining.
outcomes: Learners can explain the cause of friction and what it depends on
Learners can compare static, sliding and rolling friction
Learners can give examples where friction helps and where it harms
Learners can describe methods of increasing/reducing friction and explain streamlining

lessons.title: What is friction? Why does it happen?

scenes.text: A freshly mopped floor makes Ravi slip.
A book pushed on a table stops after a short distance.
Both are about friction — the force that opposes motion between surfaces.

steps.title: Friction
steps.body: **Friction** is the force that **opposes relative motion** between two surfaces in contact. It acts along the surfaces, opposite to the direction of motion (or attempted motion).

steps.title: Cause
steps.body: Even surfaces that look smooth have tiny **irregularities** (bumps and hollows). When two surfaces touch, these irregularities **interlock**. To move one over the other, we must overcome this interlocking. Rough surfaces have more irregularities → more friction. Pressing surfaces harder makes them interlock more → more friction.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body:
- **Nature of the surfaces** (rough or smooth).
- **How hard the surfaces are pressed together** (weight/normal force).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A ball rolled on a carpet, a cement floor and a glass sheet. Where does it go farthest? → Glass (smoothest, least friction); carpet least far.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why is a heavy box harder to push than an empty box? → It presses harder on the floor, so friction is larger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Friction acts in the direction of motion' — it opposes motion.
- 'Polished surfaces have zero friction' — friction is reduced, never zero.

statements.s: Friction opposes relative motion.
Friction is caused by interlocking of irregularities.
Friction does not depend on the nature of surfaces.
Pressing surfaces harder increases friction.
A perfectly smooth surface exists in daily life.

options: Opposite to the direction of motion
quiz.why: Friction opposes the motion between two surfaces, so it acts opposite to the direction of motion. That is why moving objects slow down.
Surfaces look smooth but have tiny bumps and hollows. These irregularities interlock when surfaces touch, and that interlocking causes friction.
The rougher the surface, the more the irregularities interlock, so friction is greater. A rough carpet is much rougher than glass, polished marble or ice.

options: Nature of surfaces and how hard they press
quiz.why: Friction depends on how rough the two surfaces are and how hard they are pressed together. Colour, time and temperature are not the main factors.

quiz.q: A heavier box on the same floor experiences:
quiz.why: A heavier box presses harder on the floor, so more irregularities interlock. That gives more friction.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Static, sliding and rolling friction

scenes.text: Two workers struggle to start moving a heavy cupboard.
Once it starts sliding, it's a bit easier.
Then they put it on a trolley with wheels — now it rolls easily!

steps.title: Three types
steps.body:
- **Static friction:** acts when we try to move an object at rest.
- **Sliding friction:** acts when the object is sliding over another.
- **Rolling friction:** acts when one body rolls over another.

**Static > Sliding > Rolling.** Sliding friction is less than static because, once moving, the irregularities don't get time to lock fully. Rolling friction is the smallest — that's why wheels and **ball bearings** are used.

steps.title: Measuring friction
steps.body: Pull a brick tied to a **spring balance** across a table: the reading just before it starts moving gives static friction; the steady reading while it slides gives sliding friction.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why are suitcases fitted with wheels? → Rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction, so less force is needed.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A spring balance reads 12 N just before a block moves and 9 N while it slides steadily. Which is static friction? → 12 N; sliding friction 9 N.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sliding friction is greater than static.
- Thinking wheels remove friction — they replace sliding with rolling friction, which is smaller.

activity.prompt: Arrange from LARGEST to SMALLEST friction
items: Static friction
Sliding friction
Rolling friction

quiz.why: Rolling friction is the smallest of the types because a rolling wheel does not drag over the surface. Static friction is the largest and sliding is in between.
Ball bearings turn sliding into rolling, and rolling friction is much smaller. So they reduce friction between moving machine parts.

quiz.q: Friction just before an object starts moving:
quiz.why: The friction that acts on an object at rest, just before it starts to move, is called static friction. It is the force that has to be overcome to start motion.

quiz.q: Friction can be measured with a:
quiz.why: A spring balance measures force, so it can measure the pull needed to overcome friction. A thermometer, barometer and ruler measure temperature, air pressure and length.

quiz.q: Why is it easier to keep a box sliding than to start it moving?
quiz.why: Once the box is sliding, the irregularities get less time to lock, so sliding friction is smaller than static friction. That is why less force keeps it moving than started it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Friction: a necessary evil

scenes.text: Imagine writing — the pencil just slides without marking.
Imagine walking — your feet slip with every step.
Yet friction also wears out shoes and heats engines. Friend and foe!

steps.title: Where friction helps
steps.body:
- Walking without slipping; holding a glass; writing with a pen/pencil.
- Brakes stopping vehicles; nails and screws holding in wood; knots staying tied.
- Lighting a matchstick (friction produces heat).

steps.title: Where friction harms
steps.body:
- **Wear and tear** of shoe soles, tyres, machine parts, ball-bearings, steps of staircases.
- Produces **heat**: engines heat up, energy is wasted.
- Makes movement harder, so more fuel/energy is needed.

steps.title: Increasing friction
steps.body:
- Grooved/treaded soles and **treaded tyres** grip the ground.
- Brake pads press on the wheel rims/discs.
- Gymnasts apply a coarse powder on hands; kabaddi players rub their hands with soil for a better grip.
- Sand on slippery roads.

steps.title: Reducing friction
steps.body:
- **Lubricants** (oil, grease, graphite) form a thin layer between surfaces.
- Powder on a carrom board.
- **Wheels** and **ball bearings** (rolling instead of sliding).
- Polishing surfaces; air cushion between moving parts in some machines.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why do tyres of a new car have deep treads, and why are old smooth tyres dangerous? → Treads increase grip (friction) and push water out; worn tyres can skid, especially in rain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Friction is always bad' — we couldn't walk or brake without it.
- 'Oil increases friction' — lubricants reduce it.

activity.prompt: Does it increase or reduce friction?

items.text: Sprinkling sand on an icy road

quiz.why: Lubricants like oil and grease form a thin layer between surfaces. This fills the irregularities and reduces friction.

quiz.q: Kabaddi players rub hands with soil to:
quiz.why: Soil on the hands makes them rougher and absorbs sweat, so friction increases. This gives the players a better grip.

quiz.q: Which is an example where friction is helpful?
quiz.why: Walking is possible only because friction between shoes and ground gives grip. The other options are harmful effects of friction.

quiz.q: Shoe soles wear out due to:
quiz.why: Rubbing of the soles against the ground wears the material away over time. This wear and tear is caused by friction.

quiz.q: Friction is called a necessary evil because:
quiz.why: Friction helps us (walking, writing, brakes) but also causes wear and wasted energy. Since we need it yet it also harms, it is called a necessary evil.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Fluid friction and streamlining

scenes.text: A fish slips through water; a bird glides through air.
A jet's pointed nose and smooth body look similar.
Nature and engineers both fight 'drag'.

steps.title: Fluid friction (drag)
steps.body:
Liquids and gases are called **fluids**. Objects moving through fluids experience friction called **drag**. It depends on:

- the **speed** of the object relative to the fluid,
- the **shape** of the object,
- the **nature of the fluid**.

steps.title: Streamlining
steps.body: To reduce drag, objects are given **streamlined** shapes — pointed or rounded at the front, broader in the middle and tapering at the back. Birds and fish have such shapes naturally; aeroplanes, boats, racing cars and ships are designed like this. Swimmers wear smooth suits and caps.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why is a cyclist in a race bent forward with a pointed helmet? → To reduce air resistance (drag).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Two boats of the same weight: one with a pointed front, one with a flat front. Which needs less fuel? → The pointed (streamlined) one.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only solids experience friction.
- Saying drag doesn't depend on speed (it increases with speed).

activity.prompt: Match the example to the idea
pairs: Air resistance on a fast car
Depends on speed, shape and fluid

quiz.q: Friction exerted by fluids is called:
quiz.why: Liquids and gases are fluids, and the friction they apply on moving objects is called fluid friction or drag. Static and rolling friction are about solids.
A streamlined shape lets the fluid flow smoothly around the object. This reduces fluid friction, so the object moves more easily.
A fluid is anything that can flow, which means liquids and gases. Air is a gas, while iron, wood and glass are solids.

quiz.q: Drag on a car increases when it:
quiz.why: Drag depends on speed, and it increases as the speed of the object increases. A slower or stopped car meets less drag.

quiz.q: Which animal has a naturally streamlined body?
quiz.why: Fish live in water and have a naturally streamlined body. This shape reduces water drag so they swim easily.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

questions.q: Friction opposes:
questions.why: Friction acts between two touching surfaces and opposes their relative motion. It has nothing to do with light, gravity or heat as such.

questions.q: Smallest type of friction:
questions.why: Rolling friction is the smallest, because wheels roll instead of dragging. Static and sliding friction are larger.

questions.q: Oil in machine parts:
questions.why: Oil is a lubricant. It forms a thin film between machine parts and reduces friction, which also lowers wear.

questions.q: Friction depends on the:
questions.why: Friction depends on the nature of the surfaces, i.e. how rough or smooth they are. The shape of the room, colour and day do not matter.

questions.q: Which INCREASES friction?
questions.why: Treads (grooves) on tyres make the surface rougher and give better grip, so they increase friction. Lubricants, ball bearings and polishing all reduce friction.

questions.q: Assertion: Sliding friction is less than static friction. Reason: When sliding, irregularities do not get enough time to lock into each other.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. While sliding, the irregularities have no time to lock deeply, so sliding friction is less than static friction.

questions.q: Why do we fall on a wet marble floor?
questions.why: Water on smooth marble forms a thin film between the foot and the floor. This reduces friction, so there is less grip and we slip.

questions.q: Fluid friction depends on:
options: Speed, shape and nature of the fluid
questions.why: Fluid friction depends on the speed of the object, its shape and the nature of the fluid. It is certainly not independent of these factors.

questions.q: Heat produced when you rub your palms is due to:
questions.why: Rubbing the palms makes the surfaces move against each other, and work done against friction appears as heat. So the palms warm up.

questions.q: Case: A delivery worker finds pushing a fridge on the floor very hard. Best solution:
questions.why: Wheels replace sliding with rolling, and rolling friction is much smaller. So a trolley makes the fridge far easier to move.

questions.q: A spring balance shows 15 N just as a block starts moving, then 11 N steadily. The block's static friction:
questions.why: Static friction rises until the block just starts to move, and its maximum value is the pull at that instant, 15 N. The 11 N is the smaller sliding friction.

questions.q: Why do aeroplanes have pointed noses?
questions.why: A pointed nose gives a streamlined shape. Air slips past it easily, so air drag is reduced.

questions.q: Assertion: Friction is undesirable in all situations. Reason: Friction causes wear and tear.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because friction is also useful (walking, brakes, grip). The reason is true, as friction does cause wear and tear, but it does not make friction undesirable in all situations.

questions.q: Why is powder sprinkled on a carrom board?
options: To reduce friction so coins slide smoothly
questions.why: The powder makes the board smoother and acts like a lubricant. Less friction lets the coins slide easily.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Ball bearings use rolling instead of sliding, so they reduce friction through rolling friction. The other pairs state the opposite of the real effect.

questions.q: Case: On a rainy day, a car with worn-out smooth tyres skids while braking. Explanation:
options: Smooth tyres and water reduce friction between tyre and road
questions.why: Water on the road and smooth, worn tyres leave little grip. With less friction between tyre and road, the car skids when braking.

questions.q: Why are the soles of sports shoes grooved, while a skater's blades are smooth?
options: Runners need more friction for grip; skaters need less friction to glide
questions.why: Runners need more friction so they do not slip, hence grooved soles. Skaters need less friction to glide, hence smooth blades; the purpose decides what is needed.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Sound
courses.summary: How vibrations produce sound, the human voice box, why sound needs a medium, how we hear, amplitude, time period and frequency, loudness and pitch, audible range, and noise pollution with ways to reduce it.
outcomes: Learners can explain sound production by vibration and the role of the larynx
Learners can show that sound needs a medium and describe how the ear works
Learners can relate amplitude to loudness and frequency to pitch, and calculate frequency and time period
Learners can distinguish music and noise and suggest ways to reduce noise pollution

lessons.title: Sound from vibrations; the human voice

scenes.text: Ana touches the school bell just after it rings.
She feels it buzzing; when she holds it, the sound stops.
Sound is made by vibrating objects.

steps.title: Vibration
steps.body:
The **to-and-fro or back-and-forth** motion of an object is **vibration**. All sounds are produced by vibrating objects: a struck bell, a plucked guitar string, a stretched rubber band, the membrane of a tabla, the air column in a flute.

Musical instruments: stringed (sitar, violin, guitar — vibrating strings), wind (flute, shehnai — air column), percussion (tabla, dholak — membranes; manjira, ghatam — the body).

steps.title: The human voice
steps.body:
We speak using the **voice box (larynx)** at the upper end of the windpipe. Two **vocal cords** are stretched across it with a narrow slit between them. When air is forced through the slit by the lungs, the cords vibrate and produce sound. Muscles make the cords tighter or looser to change the type of sound.

Typical lengths: about **20 mm in men**, about **15 mm in women** (shorter), and very short in children — so men's voices are lower-pitched than women's and children's.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A rubber band is stretched between two pencils and plucked. What do you hear and see? → A twang; the band visibly vibrates. Stretching it tighter makes the sound higher in pitch.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Put your fingers lightly on your throat and hum. → You feel vibrations of the vocal cords.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Sound is made by air only' — any vibrating object can produce sound.
- Confusing larynx (voice box) with the windpipe or the food pipe.

activity.prompt: Match the instrument to its vibrating part

quiz.why: Sound is produced when objects vibrate. Light, heat alone or magnets do not make sound by themselves.

quiz.q: The human voice box is the:
quiz.why: The voice box is the larynx, at the top of the windpipe, and it holds the vocal cords. The pharynx is the throat and the eardrum is part of the ear.
Men's vocal cords are about 20 mm long, which is longer than women's. That is why men's voices are usually deeper.

quiz.q: In a flute, sound comes from vibrating:
quiz.why: A flute is a wind instrument, so the sound comes from the vibrating column of air inside it. Strings and membranes are in other instruments.

quiz.q: To-and-fro motion of an object is:
quiz.why: Vibration is the to-and-fro (back and forth) motion of an object. Rotation is turning, and translation is moving along a path.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Sound needs a medium; how we hear

scenes.text: Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, even when standing close.
In a jar emptied of air, a ringing bell becomes almost silent.
Sound needs a medium — solid, liquid or gas.

steps.title: Propagation
steps.body: Sound travels through **solids, liquids and gases**, but **cannot travel through a vacuum**. Example: place a ringing phone/bell in a glass jar and pump out the air — the sound becomes fainter and fainter. You can hear a scratch at one end of a long table by putting your ear at the other end (sound through a solid). Whales and dolphins communicate under water (liquid).

steps.title: The ear
steps.body:
- The **outer ear** (shaped like a funnel) collects sound and sends it down the **ear canal**.
- At the end is a thin stretched membrane, the **eardrum**. Sound makes it vibrate.
- The **middle ear** passes these vibrations (through tiny bones) to the **inner ear**.
- From there signals go to the **brain**, and we hear.

Never put sharp or hard objects (pins, sticks) in the ear — they can damage the eardrum.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Why can't sound travel from the Moon to the Earth? → Space between them is a vacuum — there's no medium.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A toy 'string telephone' (two cups joined by a tight thread) works because sound travels through the solid thread.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Sound travels in space' — no, light does; sound doesn't.
- 'The eardrum is a bone' — it's a membrane.

activity.prompt: Order the path of sound as we hear it
items: Sound waves reach the outer ear
They travel down the ear canal
The eardrum vibrates
Middle ear passes vibrations to the inner ear
Signals go to the brain

quiz.why: Sound needs a material medium such as air, water or iron to travel. A vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot pass through it.
The eardrum is a thin, stretched membrane in the ear. It vibrates when sound waves reach it.

quiz.q: Astronauts in space talk using radio because:
options: There's no air to carry sound
quiz.why: Space has no air, so sound cannot travel there. Astronauts therefore use radio, which does not need a medium.
Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases because each has particles that can pass on the vibration. It cannot travel through a vacuum.

quiz.q: Putting a pin in your ear is dangerous because:
quiz.why: The eardrum is thin and delicate, so a pin can tear or damage it and harm hearing. Never put sharp objects in your ear.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Amplitude, frequency, loudness and pitch

scenes.text: A big drum booms deep and loud; a whistle shrieks high.
Hit the drum harder: louder, same note.
Loudness and pitch depend on different things.

steps.title: Describing vibration
steps.body:
- **Oscillation:** one complete to-and-fro motion.
- **Frequency:** number of oscillations per second; unit **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second.
- **Time period:** time for one oscillation (seconds). **Time period = 1 ÷ frequency**.
- **Amplitude:** maximum displacement from the rest position.

steps.title: Loudness and pitch
steps.body:
- **Loudness** depends on **amplitude** (it is proportional to the square of the amplitude). Unit of loudness: **decibel (dB)**. Normal talking ≈ 60 dB; busy traffic ≈ 70 dB; noise above **80 dB is physically painful**.
- **Pitch (shrillness)** depends on **frequency**: higher frequency → higher pitch. A bird's chirp is high-pitched; a lion's roar is low-pitched but loud. Children's and women's voices usually have higher pitch.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A pendulum makes 40 oscillations in 4 s. Frequency and time period?

- f = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 Hz.
- T = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1 s.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A tuning fork vibrates 256 times in one second, and another 512 times. Frequencies? → 256 Hz and 512 Hz; the second has the higher pitch (twice the frequency).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Pitch and loudness are the same' — a soft sound can be high-pitched.
- Writing frequency in seconds — it's in Hz (per second).

activity.prompt: A string makes 1,200 vibrations in 3 seconds. Frequency?

quiz.why: Loudness depends on the amplitude of the vibration: bigger amplitude means louder sound. Frequency decides pitch instead.
Pitch depends on frequency: more vibrations per second give a higher pitch. Amplitude decides loudness.
Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Decibel is the unit of loudness.
Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/50 s = 0.02 s. Do not mix up frequency and time period.

quiz.q: Sound above about ___ is physically painful.
quiz.why: Sound louder than about 80 dB is physically painful and harmful to the ears, as per the NCERT figure. Lower values like 20 to 40 dB are quiet to ordinary sounds.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Audible range, noise and noise pollution

scenes.text: Loudspeakers blast music past midnight next to a hospital.
Patients can't sleep; Dadi's blood pressure rises.
Unpleasant, excessive sound is noise pollution.

steps.title: Audible and inaudible
steps.body:
Humans can hear frequencies from about **20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)** — the **audible range**.

- Below 20 Hz: **infrasonic** (infrasound).
- Above 20 kHz: **ultrasonic** (ultrasound). Some animals, like dogs, can hear sounds higher than 20 kHz. Ultrasound is used in medicine (scanning).

steps.title: Noise and music
steps.body: **Noise:** unpleasant sounds (traffic horns, construction). **Music:** pleasant sounds from instruments or voices. Even music becomes noise if too loud.

steps.title: Noise pollution
steps.body:
**Sources:** vehicles, explosions/firecrackers, machines, loudspeakers, TV/music at high volume, kitchen appliances, coolers and ACs.

**Effects:** lack of sleep, hypertension (high blood pressure), anxiety and many health disorders; prolonged exposure to loud sound can cause temporary or even permanent **hearing impairment**.

**Measures:** silencers in vehicles and machines; soundproofing; noisy activities and industries away from homes; limit horn use; keep TV/music at low volume; **plant trees along roads and around buildings** to cut down sound.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Classify 10 Hz, 1,000 Hz, 30,000 Hz. → Infrasonic, audible, ultrasonic.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Suggest two ways your school can reduce noise. → Plant trees along the boundary; avoid loudspeakers near classrooms; no honking zones near the gate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'If I can't hear it, it isn't sound' — infrasound and ultrasound are sounds outside our hearing range.
- 'Music can never harm hearing' — loud music through earphones can.

activity.prompt: Infrasonic, audible or ultrasonic?

quiz.why: Humans can hear sounds with frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below or above that range we cannot hear.
Sound with frequency above 20 kHz is above the human audible range, so it is ultrasonic. Infrasonic sound is below 20 Hz.

quiz.q: A way to reduce noise pollution:
quiz.why: Trees absorb and block sound, so planting them along roads reduces noise. Louder speakers, honking or removing silencers increase noise.

quiz.q: Long exposure to loud noise can cause:
quiz.why: Loud noise over a long time can damage the delicate parts of the ear. This can lead to hearing impairment.
Any sound that is unpleasant to the ear is called noise. Music is pleasant, and an echo is a reflected sound.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

questions.q: Sound is produced by:
questions.why: Sound is produced by vibrating objects. Light, gravity and magnetism do not by themselves produce sound.

questions.q: Sound cannot travel through:
questions.why: Sound needs a medium to travel through. Air, water and steel are media, but a vacuum has none.

questions.q: Unit of loudness:
questions.why: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Hertz measures frequency and pascal measures pressure.

questions.q: Pitch depends on:
questions.why: Pitch depends on frequency: the higher the frequency, the higher the pitch. Amplitude controls loudness, not pitch.

questions.q: Voice box is also called:
questions.why: The voice box is the larynx, which contains the vocal cords. The trachea is the windpipe and the cochlea is in the ear.

questions.q: Frequency of a pendulum making 30 oscillations in 6 s:
questions.why: Frequency = number of oscillations ÷ time = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 Hz. Multiplying by time would give a wrong value.

questions.q: Assertion: Women's voices are generally higher-pitched than men's. Reason: Women's vocal cords are shorter.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Shorter vocal cords vibrate at a higher frequency, which gives a higher pitch.

questions.q: Time period of a vibration of frequency 250 Hz:
questions.why: Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/250 = 0.004 s. A high frequency means a very short time for one vibration.

questions.q: Which is ultrasonic?
questions.why: Ultrasonic sound has a frequency above 20 kHz. Only 30 kHz is above that limit; 10 Hz, 200 Hz and 15 kHz are not ultrasonic.

questions.q: If the amplitude of a sound is doubled, loudness becomes about:
questions.why: Loudness is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude makes it 2² = 4 times louder.

questions.q: Case: A family lives next to a busy highway and can't sleep. Most effective long-term step:
options: Plant a thick row of trees and use soundproof windows
questions.why: Trees absorb sound and soundproof windows block it, which reduces noise over the long term. Louder music or open windows would make the problem worse.

questions.q: Why can we hear a knock through a wall?
questions.why: Sound can travel through solids, so the vibrations of the knock pass through the wall to your ear. Sound does not travel only in a vacuum, and light does not carry it.

questions.q: Assertion: A loud sound always has high pitch. Reason: Loudness depends on amplitude while pitch depends on frequency.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because loudness and pitch are independent. The reason is true: loudness depends on amplitude and pitch on frequency, so a loud sound can have a low pitch.

questions.q: A bat emits sound of 50,000 Hz. Humans cannot hear it because:
questions.why: The audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. 50,000 Hz is above it, so it is ultrasonic and humans cannot hear it.

questions.q: Time period of a vibration is 0.005 s. Its frequency:
questions.why: Frequency = 1 ÷ time period = 1 ÷ 0.005 = 200 Hz. A short time period means a high frequency.

questions.q: Which part of the ear vibrates first when sound enters?
questions.why: The thin eardrum membrane is the first part that vibrates when sound enters the ear. It then passes the vibrations on inwards.

questions.q: Case: A string under tension is tightened further. What happens to its sound?
questions.why: Tightening a string makes it vibrate faster, so its frequency rises. A higher frequency means a higher pitch.

courses.title: Ch 11 · Chemical Effects of Electric Current
courses.summary: Which liquids conduct electricity and how to test them, the chemical effects of current (gas bubbles, deposits, colour change), electrolysis of water, and electroplating with its everyday uses and environmental care.
outcomes: Learners can build and use a tester (bulb, LED or compass) to test liquids
Learners can explain why tap water conducts but distilled water hardly does
Learners can identify chemical effects of current
Learners can describe electroplating and its uses such as chromium, tin and zinc coatings

lessons.title: Do liquids conduct electricity?

scenes.text: Zara dips two wires from a battery-and-LED tester into lemon juice.
The LED glows!
In distilled water it barely glows; add a pinch of salt — it glows again.

steps.title: Conductors and insulators
steps.body: Materials that allow electric current to pass are **conductors**; those that don't are **insulators** (poor conductors). Most liquids that conduct electricity are solutions of **acids, bases and salts**: lemon juice, vinegar, salt solution, tap water.

steps.title: Testers
steps.body:
- Battery + bulb + wires: bulb glows if current flows. A weak current may not make the bulb glow even though current flows (the filament needs enough current).
- Use an **LED** instead: it glows even with a weak current. An LED has two leads — the longer connects to the positive terminal.
- Or use a **magnetic compass**: a wire carrying current deflects the needle, even for tiny currents.

steps.title: Water
steps.body: **Distilled water** is free of salts and is a **poor conductor**. **Tap water, pond water, rain water** contain dissolved salts and conduct. Under certain conditions most materials can conduct — e.g. air during lightning. **Never experiment with mains or household electricity** — it is dangerous.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Your bulb tester doesn't glow in a liquid. Does that prove it's an insulator? → No; the current may be too weak. Check with an LED or compass.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why is it dangerous to touch electrical appliances with wet hands? → Water with salts conducts electricity and can give a shock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Pure water conducts well' — distilled water is a poor conductor; it's the dissolved salts that conduct.
- Connecting the LED leads the wrong way round (it won't glow).

activity.prompt: Good conductor or poor conductor?

quiz.why: Distilled water has no dissolved salts, so it has no ions to carry current. This makes it a poor conductor, unlike tap water or salt solution.

quiz.q: An LED is preferred over a bulb in testers because:
options: It glows even with weak current
quiz.why: An LED glows even when only a very weak current flows. So it can show conduction in liquids where a bulb would stay dark.

quiz.q: Most conducting liquids are solutions of:
quiz.why: Most conducting liquids are solutions of acids, bases and salts, because they contain ions. Oils and sugar solutions do not give ions.

quiz.q: A compass needle deflects near a wire because:
quiz.why: An electric current produces a magnetic effect. The needle deflects because of the magnetic field around the wire.

quiz.q: Longer lead of an LED connects to:
quiz.why: An LED works in one direction only. Its longer lead must be connected to the positive terminal of the cell.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Chemical effects of electric current

scenes.text: Electrodes from a battery are dipped in water with a little salt.
Tiny bubbles form on both electrodes.
The current is causing a chemical reaction.

steps.title: What happens
steps.body:
Passing current through a conducting solution causes **chemical reactions**. We may observe:

- **Bubbles of gas** on the electrodes
- **Deposits of metal** on electrodes
- **Change in colour** of the solution

These are **chemical effects of electric current**.

steps.title: Electrolysis of water
steps.body: In 1800, the British chemist **William Nicholson** showed that passing current through water produces bubbles of **oxygen** at the electrode connected to the **positive** terminal and **hydrogen** at the electrode connected to the **negative** terminal.

steps.title: Worked example 1 — potato test
steps.body: Insert two copper wires from a battery into a cut potato for some time. A **greenish-blue spot** appears around the wire connected to the **positive** terminal. This can be used to identify the positive terminal of a hidden battery.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Two electrodes in a solution: one gets a reddish metal coating. What happened? → A metal (copper) was deposited by the current — a chemical effect.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up which gas forms where: hydrogen at negative, oxygen at positive.
- Thinking chemical effects happen in solids like wires — they happen in conducting liquids.

statements.s: Passing current through a solution can produce gas bubbles.
Hydrogen forms at the positive electrode in water.
statements.why: Hydrogen at negative; oxygen at positive.

statements.s: A colour change can be a chemical effect of current.
William Nicholson showed electrolysis of water in 1800.
The potato turns greenish-blue near the negative wire.

options: Gas bubbles, metal deposits, colour change
quiz.why: Chemical effects of current include gas bubbles at the electrodes, deposits of metal and a change in colour of the solution. Heat, light and sound are different effects.

quiz.q: In electrolysis of water, oxygen collects at:
quiz.why: In the electrolysis of water, oxygen collects at the positive electrode and hydrogen at the negative electrode.

quiz.q: Greenish-blue spot on a potato appears near the wire connected to:
quiz.why: A greenish-blue spot appears on a potato near the wire joined to the positive terminal. This can be used to identify the positive wire.
The chemical effect of current needs a conducting liquid (an electrolyte) in which ions can move. Heating of a filament and light from a bulb happen in solid wires.
Hydrogen bubbles form at the negative electrode (cathode) when water is electrolysed. Oxygen forms at the positive electrode.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Electroplating

scenes.text: A new bathroom tap gleams silver and doesn't rust.
Underneath is cheaper metal, coated with a thin layer of chromium.
That coating was put there using electricity.

steps.title: What is electroplating?
steps.body: Depositing a thin layer of a desired metal on another material by passing electric current through a solution is **electroplating**.

steps.title: Copper plating (classroom set-up)
steps.body:
- Solution: **copper sulphate** (with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid).
- Two cleaned copper plates as electrodes, connected to a battery.
- On passing current, **copper from the solution is deposited on the plate connected to the negative terminal**.
- An equal amount of copper **dissolves into the solution** from the plate connected to the positive terminal, so the solution's copper stays roughly constant.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Chromium plating:** shiny, doesn't corrode, resists scratches — car parts, bath taps, kitchen gas burners, bicycle handlebars, wheel rims. Chromium is expensive, so objects are made of cheaper metal and only coated.
- **Jewellery:** gold or silver plating on less expensive metals — looks like gold/silver at lower cost.
- **Tin cans** for food: **tin** is electroplated onto iron; tin is less reactive than iron, so food doesn't come into contact with iron and spoil.
- **Zinc coating on iron** (bridges, automobiles) protects iron from corrosion and rust.

steps.title: Environment
steps.body: Electroplating factories must dispose of used conducting solutions according to rules — they are polluting wastes.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: To silver-plate a copper key, where does the key go? → In a solution of a silver salt, connected to the **negative** terminal. The object to be plated always goes to the negative terminal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Connecting the object to be plated to the positive terminal (it would dissolve!).
- Thinking tin is coated on iron because it is stronger — it's because it is less reactive.

activity.prompt: Match the coating to its purpose
pairs: Looks like gold at lower cost

quiz.q: In copper electroplating, copper is deposited on the plate connected to:
quiz.why: The object to be plated is joined to the negative terminal. Copper ions from the solution move to it and are deposited there.
Food cans are coated with tin because tin is less reactive than iron. This protects the iron and keeps the food safe.

quiz.q: Chromium is used for plating because it:
quiz.why: Chromium has a bright, shiny finish and does not corrode. So it is used to plate things like taps and bicycle parts.
A zinc coating covers the iron and protects it from rusting. This is called galvanisation.
The solution must contain the plating metal's ions. Copper sulphate gives copper ions, which then deposit on the object.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Practice and safety: putting it together

scenes.text: Neel's stall tests liquids and shows a copper-plated coin.
Visitors ask tricky questions.
He answers with the ideas from this chapter.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Some liquids conduct (acids, bases, salts); distilled water is a poor conductor.
- Current through conducting liquids causes chemical effects.
- Electroplating deposits a thin metal layer; the object goes to the negative terminal.
- Never use mains electricity for experiments; use cells/batteries.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A tester bulb doesn't glow in a liquid but the compass deflects. Conclusion? → The liquid conducts, but weakly.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why should you not repair electrical appliances while standing on a wet floor? → Water with impurities conducts; you could get a shock through your body to the ground.

steps.title: Worked example 3
steps.body: After electroplating for an hour, the positive copper plate is thinner. Why? → Copper dissolves from it into the solution.

steps.title: Safety reminders
steps.body:
- Wear goggles/gloves with chemicals; work with a teacher.
- Don't taste or touch solutions.
- Dispose of solutions as instructed.

activity.prompt: Safe experiment checklist
items: Use only cells/batteries, never mains
Wear goggles and gloves
Keep the area dry
Clean electrodes with sandpaper before plating
Ask your teacher how to dispose of used solution

quiz.q: A compass deflects but bulb doesn't glow. The liquid:
quiz.why: The compass deflection shows that a current flows, but it is too small to make the bulb glow. So the liquid conducts weakly and is not a perfect insulator.

quiz.q: During copper plating, the positive plate:
quiz.why: The positive plate (copper) dissolves into the solution to replace the copper deposited on the object. So the positive plate gets thinner.
Cells or batteries give a low, safe voltage. Mains supply or lightning can cause fatal electric shocks, so they must never be used in such experiments.

quiz.q: Adding salt to distilled water makes it:
quiz.why: Salt dissolves in water to give ions, and ions carry the current. So salt makes distilled water conduct electricity.

options: Disposed of safely as per rules
quiz.why: Used solutions may contain harmful chemicals, so they should be disposed of safely as per rules. Pouring them in drains or rivers pollutes water.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

questions.q: Which liquid conducts electricity?
questions.why: Salt solution contains ions, so it conducts electricity. Distilled water, kerosene and vegetable oil have no free ions and are poor conductors.

questions.q: Depositing a metal layer using electricity is:
questions.why: Electroplating is coating a metal layer on an object using electric current. Distillation and fermentation are unrelated processes.

questions.q: Food cans are coated with tin because:
options: Tin is less reactive than iron
questions.why: Tin is less reactive than iron, so it does not react easily with food. That keeps the food in the can safe and protects the iron.

questions.q: LED testers are useful because:
questions.why: An LED glows even for a very weak current, so it can detect conduction that a bulb would miss. That makes it a sensitive tester.

questions.q: In water electrolysis, hydrogen forms at:
questions.why: During the electrolysis of water, hydrogen bubbles form at the negative electrode, and oxygen at the positive one.

questions.q: Assertion: Distilled water is a poor conductor. Reason: It lacks dissolved salts.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Conduction in a liquid needs ions, and distilled water has no dissolved salts to supply them.

questions.q: Object to be electroplated is connected to:
questions.why: The object to be plated is joined to the negative terminal, because positive metal ions move to the negative electrode and deposit there.

questions.q: Chromium plating is used on:
questions.why: Chromium plating is shiny and resists corrosion, so it is used on bath taps and bicycle parts. Food cans use tin instead.

questions.q: Which is NOT a chemical effect of current?
questions.why: A glowing bulb filament is the heating effect of current. Gas bubbles, colour change and metal deposits are chemical effects.

questions.q: Case: Paheli's tester bulb doesn't glow in a liquid. Boojho says the liquid is an insulator. Best reply:
options: Not necessarily — current may be too weak; test with an LED or compass
questions.why: A bulb may not glow even when a weak current passes. So the liquid is not necessarily an insulator, and a more sensitive test like an LED or a compass should be used.

questions.q: Zinc coating on iron protects it from:
questions.why: A zinc coating protects iron from corrosion and rust. This process is called galvanising.

questions.q: A greenish-blue spot on a potato appears near the wire from the:
questions.why: The greenish-blue spot appears near the wire connected to the positive terminal. This is a way to tell the terminals apart.

questions.q: Assertion: During copper plating, the copper concentration of the solution remains nearly constant. Reason: Copper dissolving from the positive plate replaces copper deposited on the negative plate.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Copper deposited on the negative plate is replaced by copper dissolving from the positive plate, so the concentration stays nearly constant.

questions.q: Why must we not touch switches with wet hands?
options: Impure water conducts and can cause shock
questions.why: Ordinary water has dissolved impurities, so it conducts electricity. Wet hands can therefore let current pass through the body and cause a shock.

questions.q: Gold-plated jewellery is made because:
options: It looks like gold at lower cost
questions.why: Gold plating puts a thin layer of gold on a cheaper metal. It looks like gold but costs much less.

questions.q: Case: A tester shows a liquid conducts. Which could it be?
questions.why: Only liquids with ions conduct, and vinegar is an acid solution, so it conducts. Coconut oil, distilled water and pure alcohol are poor conductors.

questions.q: If the positive and negative connections in a copper plating set-up are swapped, the original object to be plated will:
questions.why: If the connections are swapped, the original object becomes the positive plate. Copper then dissolves from it into the solution, so it loses copper.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Some Natural Phenomena
courses.summary: Charging by rubbing, two kinds of charges and their interactions, transfer of charge and the electroscope, earthing, how lightning forms and how to stay safe, lightning conductors, and earthquakes — causes, measurement, India's risk zones and protection.
outcomes: Learners can explain charging by rubbing, types of charge and the electroscope
Learners can describe how lightning forms and list lightning safety rules
Learners can explain the cause of earthquakes and how they are measured
Learners can follow earthquake safety steps at home, school and outdoors

lessons.title: Charging by rubbing; two kinds of charges

scenes.text: After rubbing a balloon on her hair, Ishita sticks it to the wall.
Two such balloons push each other away.
Rubbing gives objects electric charge — and charges push or pull.

steps.title: Charging by rubbing
steps.body: Rubbing some objects together makes them **electrically charged**. A plastic refill rubbed with polythene, a comb run through dry hair, or a balloon rubbed with wool can attract small paper bits. The charges produced this way are **static charges** — they don't move. When charges move, they make an **electric current**.

steps.title: Two kinds
steps.body:
There are two kinds of charges: **positive** and **negative**.

- **Like charges repel**; **unlike charges attract**.
- By convention, the charge on a **glass rod rubbed with silk** is called **positive**; the charge on a plastic straw rubbed with polythene is **negative**.
- When two objects are rubbed, one gets positive and the other negative charge (charges get transferred).

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Two balloons rubbed with wool are hung near each other. What happens? → They repel — both have the same kind of charge.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A charged straw is brought near a charged glass rod (rubbed with silk). → They attract: unlike charges (negative and positive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Attraction proves both are charged' — a charged object can also attract an *uncharged* object (paper bits). **Repulsion** is the sure test of charge.
- Thinking rubbing *creates* charge from nothing — charge is transferred.

statements.s: Like charges attract each other.
A glass rod rubbed with silk is positively charged (by convention).
Static charges flow continuously like current.
statements.why: Static charges don't move; moving charges are current.

statements.s: Repulsion is a sure test that an object is charged.
statements.why: Attraction can happen with uncharged objects too.

statements.s: Rubbing transfers charges between objects.

quiz.why: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. So two charges of the same kind push each other away.

quiz.q: A comb run through dry hair can attract:
quiz.why: A comb rubbed on dry hair becomes charged and attracts light things like small paper bits. It cannot attract heavy items like nails or bottles this way.

quiz.q: Charge on a glass rod rubbed with silk is called:
quiz.why: By convention, a glass rod rubbed with silk gets a positive charge. The silk gets the opposite (negative) charge.

quiz.q: Charges that do not move are:
quiz.why: Charges that stay at rest on an object are static charges. Current is made of moving charges.

quiz.q: The sure test of charge is:
quiz.why: Attraction can also occur between a charged and an uncharged object, so it is not a sure test. Only repulsion shows that both objects carry the same kind of charge.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Transfer of charge, electroscope and earthing

scenes.text: Ravi builds an electroscope with a jar, a paper clip and two foil strips.
He touches the clip with a charged refill — the strips spread apart.
He touches the clip with his finger — the strips fall back.

steps.title: Electroscope
steps.body: An **electroscope** detects whether an object is charged. Two thin **aluminium foil strips** hang from a metal clip in a jar. When a charged object touches the clip, charge is **transferred** to the strips through the metal; both strips get the same charge and **repel** — they diverge. Charge can be transferred from a charged object to another through a metal conductor.

steps.title: Earthing
steps.body: When you touch the clip with your hand, the strips collapse: charge flows through your body to the **earth**. Transferring charge from a charged object to the earth is **earthing**. Buildings have earthing wires to protect us from electric shocks due to leakage of current.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: The electroscope strips spread out wider when a more strongly charged object touches it. Why? → More charge, more repulsion.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why do household appliances have a third (earth) pin? → To carry leaking current safely to the earth so that people don't get shocks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The strips diverge because they attract' — they repel (same charge).
- Thinking earthing is only for lightning — it's also for appliances.

activity.prompt: Order what happens in an electroscope
items: A charged object touches the metal clip
Charge flows through the clip to the foil strips
Both strips get the same charge
The strips repel and spread apart
Touching the clip with a hand earths the charge and the strips collapse

quiz.why: An electroscope is a device that detects whether an object is charged. It does not detect magnetism, temperature or sound.

quiz.q: The foil strips diverge because they:
quiz.why: When a charged object touches the electroscope, both foil strips get the same kind of charge. Like charges repel, so the strips move apart.

quiz.q: Transferring charge to the earth is:
quiz.why: Transferring charge from an object to the earth is called earthing. Charging means giving charge to an object.
Earthing gives leaking charge an easy path into the ground. This protects people from electric shocks in buildings.
Charge flows easily through conductors such as metals. Plastic, rubber and dry wood are insulators.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Lightning and lightning safety

scenes.text: Black clouds roll in during cricket practice.
Coach blows the whistle: 'Everyone inside — NOW!'
Someone wants to shelter under the big tree alone in the field. Coach says no.

steps.title: How lightning forms
steps.body:
During a thunderstorm, air currents move upward while water droplets move downward. These vigorous movements **separate charges**: positive charges collect near the upper edges of clouds and negative charges near the lower edges; positive charges also accumulate near the ground. When the accumulated charge becomes very large, the air (normally a poor conductor) can no longer resist the flow; negative and positive charges meet, producing **streaks of bright light and sound** — **lightning** and **thunder**. This is an **electric discharge**. (Lightning between clouds also happens.)

Benjamin Franklin showed in the 18th century that lightning and the spark from your clothes are the same phenomenon.

steps.title: Safety (no open place is safe)
steps.body:
- When you hear thunder, rush to a safe place: a **house or building**, or a **car/bus with windows and doors closed**.
- **Outdoors:** avoid open fields, tall trees, poles, metal objects, and isolated sheds. **Do not** shelter under an isolated tall tree. Do not lie flat on the ground. **Squat low** on the ground with hands on knees and head between hands, making yourself the smallest target.
- **Indoors:** avoid landline phones with cords, running water (bathing, showers), and unplug electrical appliances such as computers and TVs. Electric lights can stay on.
- Wait some time after the last thunder before going out.

steps.title: Lightning conductor
steps.body: A metallic rod, taller than the building, installed in its walls during construction. One end is out in the air; the other is buried deep in the ground. It provides an easy route for the charge to reach the ground. Metal columns, wiring and water pipes in buildings also offer some protection — never touch them during a storm.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is a closed car safe during lightning? → The metal body conducts the charge around the outside and down to the ground (keep windows closed and don't touch metal parts).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sheltering under a tree — very dangerous.
- Using an umbrella in an open field — avoid; metal and height increase risk.
- Taking a shower during a thunderstorm.

a.text: You're on an open football field. Thunder rumbles and lightning flashes nearby. No building is close. What do you do?

choices.label: Run to the lone tall tree for cover
choices.feedback: Isolated tall trees attract lightning — dangerous.

choices.label: Squat low, feet together, hands on knees, head tucked
choices.feedback: Best option when no shelter is near.

t.text: Move away from the tree! Squat low in a dry spot away from tall objects.

choices.label: Squat low away from the tree

b.text: The storm passes; a bus arrives. Your friend wants to stand outside to watch the sky.

choices.label: Get in the bus and keep windows closed until thunder has stopped for a while
Stand outside holding the metal pole
choices.feedback: Metal and open spaces are risky.

p.text: Never hold metal poles in a storm. Get inside the bus.

e.text: Safe! In an emergency (someone struck by lightning), call 112 — it is safe to touch and help them; they don't carry charge.

quiz.why: Lightning is the sudden flow of charge between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. This flow is an electric discharge.

quiz.q: During a thunderstorm, a safe place is:
quiz.why: A closed car or building is the safest shelter in a thunderstorm. A lone tree, open field or rooftop make you the highest point and a target.

options: An easy path for charge to the ground
quiz.why: A lightning conductor gives the charge an easy path down to the ground. This protects the building from damage.
Water conducts electricity, so a bath or shower during lightning is unsafe. Reading, staying inside and sitting on a chair are fine.
In a thundercloud, negative charge collects near the lower edges and positive charge near the upper part. This separation of charge leads to lightning.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Earthquakes

scenes.text: Desks start shaking during a test; a fan swings.
The teacher calls 'Drop, cover, hold!' and everyone ducks under desks.
Later they learn: India has zones where earthquakes are more likely.

steps.title: What and why
steps.body:
An **earthquake** is a sudden shaking or trembling of the earth lasting a very short time, caused by a disturbance deep inside the earth's crust. The outermost layer of the earth is fragmented into **plates**, which are always moving. When plates brush past one another, or one goes under another (collision), they disturb the crust; this shows up as an earthquake on the surface. Earthquakes can also be caused by volcanic eruptions, a meteor hitting the earth, or underground nuclear explosions, but most are due to plate movements.

Earthquakes can cause floods, landslides and **tsunamis** (a major tsunami hit the Indian Ocean on 26 December 2004). They **cannot be predicted** precisely.

steps.title: Where in India
steps.body: Boundaries of plates are weak zones (seismic or fault zones). In India the most threatened areas include Kashmir, the western and central Himalayas, the whole of the North-East, the Rann of Kutch, Rajasthan and the Indo-Gangetic plain; some areas of South India are also at risk. Major Indian earthquakes include **Bhuj (Gujarat), 26 January 2001** and **Kashmir, 8 October 2005**.

steps.title: Measuring
steps.body: Tremors produce waves that are recorded by a **seismograph** (a vibrating rod or pendulum records on paper). Their destructive energy is expressed as a **magnitude** on the **Richter scale**. The scale is not linear: an earthquake of **magnitude 6** has about **a thousand times more energy** than one of magnitude 4. Earthquakes of magnitude 7 and above are very destructive.

steps.title: Protection
steps.body:
- **Buildings:** in seismic zones, follow earthquake-resistant designs; mud or timber is better than heavy construction; light roofs; fix cupboards and shelves to walls; keep heavy objects low.
- **At home/school:** **Drop, Cover, Hold** — take shelter under a sturdy table; stay away from tall, heavy objects and glass. In bed, don't get up — protect your head with a pillow.
- **Outdoors:** move to an open space away from buildings, trees and overhead power lines; drop to the ground.
- **In a vehicle:** don't come out; ask the driver to drive slowly to a clear spot and stay inside till the tremors stop.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running down stairs or using a lift during shaking.
- Standing near windows or tall cupboards.
- Believing earthquakes can be predicted exactly.

activity.prompt: Earthquake-ready checklist for your family
items: Know 'Drop, Cover, Hold'
Fix tall cupboards and shelves to walls
Keep heavy objects on low shelves
Agree on an open meeting place outside
Keep a torch, water, first-aid kit and 112 on the emergency list

quiz.why: Most earthquakes occur when the plates of the earth move and rub or collide. Rain, wind and tides are not the main cause.
A seismograph records the waves produced by an earthquake. An electroscope detects charge, a thermometer temperature and a barometer air pressure.

quiz.q: Magnitude of an earthquake is expressed on the:
quiz.why: The magnitude of an earthquake is measured on the Richter scale. Celsius is for temperature, decibel for loudness and Beaufort for wind.

quiz.q: During an earthquake indoors you should:
options: Drop, cover under a sturdy table and hold
quiz.why: Indoors during an earthquake, drop down, cover yourself under a sturdy table and hold on. Stairs, lifts and windows are unsafe.

quiz.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake compared with magnitude 4 has energy about:
quiz.why: The Richter scale is non-linear: each step of 1 releases about 32 times more energy, so 2 steps give about 32 × 32 ≈ 1000 times. A magnitude 6 quake is thus far stronger than 4.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)
NDMA (earthquake safety guidance)

questions.q: Like charges:
questions.why: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. This is the basic rule of electric charges.

questions.q: Instrument to detect charge:
questions.why: An electroscope, with its foil strips that spread apart, is used to detect charge. A thermometer and barometer measure other things, and a seismograph records earthquakes.

questions.q: Instrument recording earthquakes:
questions.why: A seismograph records the waves from an earthquake. A hygrometer measures humidity and an ammeter measures current.

questions.q: Safest place during lightning outdoors with no building near:
options: Squatting low away from tall objects
questions.why: Outdoors with no shelter, crouch low away from tall objects so you are not the highest point. A lone tree or hill top attracts lightning, and an umbrella does not protect you.

questions.q: Transfer of charge to earth is:
questions.why: Passing charge from an object to the earth is called earthing. Plating and rubbing are different processes.

questions.q: Assertion: A charged balloon sticks to a wall. Reason: A charged object can attract an uncharged object.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. The charged balloon attracts the uncharged wall, so it sticks.

questions.q: Which area of India is highly earthquake-prone?
questions.why: North-East India lies near the boundary of the earth's plates, so it is highly earthquake-prone. The other options are not as exposed.

questions.q: Lightning conductors work by:
options: Providing a path for charge to the ground
questions.why: A lightning conductor gives the charge an easy path to the ground. It does not produce charge, stop clouds or store lightning.

questions.q: During a thunderstorm, which is unsafe indoors?
questions.why: Water conducts electricity, so taking a shower during a thunderstorm is unsafe. Reading, sitting away from windows and keeping lights on are fine.

questions.q: Case: Two charged straws repel; a third object is attracted by one of them. What can you conclude about the third object?
options: It may be oppositely charged or uncharged
questions.why: The two straws repel, so they carry the same charge. Attraction by one of them does not prove the third is charged, because a charged object also attracts an uncharged one.

questions.q: A tsunami can be triggered by:
questions.why: An earthquake under the sea moves the seabed and can push huge amounts of water, which causes a tsunami. Lightning, rainbows and static charge cannot do this.

questions.q: Bhuj earthquake occurred in:
questions.why: The Bhuj earthquake in Gujarat took place on 26 January 2001.

questions.q: Assertion: Earthquakes can be predicted exactly in advance. Reason: Seismographs record earthquake waves.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because earthquakes cannot be predicted exactly. The reason is true, since seismographs record earthquake waves, but they only record and do not predict them.

questions.q: Why do the foil strips of an electroscope collapse when touched by hand?
options: Charge flows through the body to earth
questions.why: Your body conducts the charge from the electroscope into the earth, so it gets discharged. The strips then have no like charges to repel each other and collapse.

questions.q: In a moving car during an earthquake, you should:
