options: Stay inside; driver should stop slowly in a clear spot
questions.why: Stay inside the car, which gives protection, and the driver should stop slowly in a clear spot. Avoid bridges and tall buildings that can fall.

questions.q: Case: During a storm, a student says 'lights are on, so we must switch everything off and stand under a tree outside'. What is correct?
options: Stay indoors; unplug sensitive appliances; lights can stay on
questions.why: Staying indoors is safest in a storm. Sensitive appliances should be unplugged, but standing under a tree, bathing or using a corded phone are unsafe.

questions.q: Separation of charges in a thundercloud happens because:
options: Rising air currents and falling droplets move vigorously
questions.why: Strong rising air currents and falling water droplets rub and separate charges inside the cloud. This builds up the charge that causes lightning.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Light
courses.summary: Laws of reflection, regular and diffused reflection, reflection of reflected light (periscope, kaleidoscope, multiple images), dispersion of sunlight, the human eye and its care, and how visually impaired people read and write using Braille.
outcomes: Learners can state and apply the laws of reflection
Learners can distinguish regular and diffused reflection and luminous and illuminated objects
Learners can find the number of images formed by two inclined mirrors
Learners can label the parts of the eye, explain persistence of vision and care for their eyes

lessons.title: Laws of reflection

scenes.text: Ayesha shines a torch on a mirror in a dark room.
The beam bounces off and lands on the wall.
Tilt the mirror and the spot moves — at an equal angle.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Incident ray:** ray falling on the mirror.
- **Reflected ray:** ray coming back from the mirror.
- **Normal:** line drawn at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray strikes.
- **Angle of incidence (∠i):** between incident ray and normal.
- **Angle of reflection (∠r):** between reflected ray and normal.

steps.title: Laws of reflection
steps.body:
- **∠i = ∠r** (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection).
- The incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the **same plane**.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: A ray strikes a mirror making 30° with the mirror surface. Angle of reflection? → Angle with normal = 90° − 30° = 60°, so ∠r = 60°.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: A ray falls along the normal (∠i = 0°). → It reflects back along the same path (∠r = 0°).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring angles from the mirror instead of the normal.
- Thinking the laws fail for rough surfaces — they hold at every point.

activity.prompt: A ray makes 25° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection (from the normal)?

quiz.q: Angle of incidence = 40°. Angle of reflection:
quiz.why: By the first law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. So it is 40°.
Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, the line at 90° to the mirror at the point of incidence, and not from the mirror surface.

quiz.q: A ray along the normal reflects:
quiz.why: A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°. The angle of reflection is also 0°, so it retraces its own path.

quiz.q: The incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie:
quiz.why: The second law of reflection says that the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.

quiz.q: A ray makes 50° with the mirror. ∠i =
quiz.why: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is 90° to the mirror. So ∠i = 90° − 50° = 40°.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Regular and diffused reflection; reflecting reflected light

story.title: Why does the wall not shine?

scenes.text: A mirror gives a clear image; a painted wall doesn't.
Both reflect light — so what's different?
And how does a submarine crew look above water?

steps.title: Regular vs diffused
steps.body:
- **Regular reflection:** from smooth, polished surfaces (mirror, still water); parallel rays reflect parallel → clear image.
- **Diffused (irregular) reflection:** from rough surfaces (paper, wall, cardboard); parallel rays reflect in different directions → no clear image. It is NOT due to failure of the laws; each tiny part of the surface obeys them, but the normals point in different directions.

steps.title: Luminous and illuminated
steps.body:
- **Luminous:** emit their own light — Sun, a burning candle, an electric bulb.
- **Illuminated:** visible because they reflect light falling on them — the Moon, a book, your face. We see objects only when light from them enters our eyes.

steps.title: Reflected light can be reflected again
steps.body:
- In a barber's shop, mirrors in front and behind let you see the back of your head.
- **Periscope:** two plane mirrors at 45° in a tube; used in submarines, tanks and bunkers to see over obstacles.
- **Two mirrors at an angle θ** form multiple images: number of images **n = (360°/θ) − 1** (when 360/θ is a whole number). At 90° → 3 images; 60° → 5; 45° → 7. **Parallel mirrors** give infinitely many images in theory.
- **Kaleidoscope:** three mirror strips forming a prism with coloured glass pieces; makes beautiful repeating patterns — used by designers.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: Number of images of a coin between two mirrors at 60°? → 360/60 − 1 = 5.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Is the Moon luminous? → No; it is illuminated by sunlight.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Diffused reflection breaks the laws of reflection' — false.
- Using 360/θ without subtracting 1.

activity.prompt: Regular or diffused reflection?

quiz.q: Images formed by two mirrors at 90°:
quiz.why: Number of images = 360° ÷ angle − 1 = 360/90 − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3.
A luminous object gives out its own light. The Sun does, while the Moon, a mirror and a book only reflect light.
Rough surfaces send reflected rays in many directions, which is diffused reflection. Smooth mirrors and still water give regular reflection.
A periscope uses two plane mirrors fixed at 45° to bend light so we can see over obstacles. It does not need a lens or prism.
Number of images = 360/45 − 1 = 8 − 1 = 7.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Sunlight: white or coloured?

scenes.text: After an evening shower, a rainbow arcs across the sky.
In the lab, a glass prism splits a beam of sunlight into the same colours.
White light is a mixture of colours.

steps.title: Dispersion
steps.body: Sunlight (white light) consists of **seven colours**: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (**VIBGYOR**). Splitting of light into its colours is **dispersion**. A **rainbow** is a natural phenomenon showing dispersion: sunlight is split by raindrops; you see it with your back to the Sun.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body: You can see a rainbow by spraying water with your back to the morning Sun. → Water droplets disperse sunlight.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Put a plane mirror in a bowl of water facing sunlight at an angle; colours appear on a white wall. → The water–mirror combination acts like a prism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the prism 'adds' colour to white light — it separates colours already present.
- Getting the order wrong — remember VIBGYOR.

activity.prompt: Arrange the colours of the spectrum in order (VIBGYOR)
items: Violet
Indigo
Blue
Green
Yellow
Orange
Red

quiz.q: Splitting of white light into colours:
quiz.why: The splitting of white light into its colours is called dispersion. Reflection and diffusion do not split the light.
Sunlight has seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, remembered as VIBGYOR.

quiz.q: A rainbow is seen with the Sun:
quiz.why: A rainbow is seen when the Sun is behind you and raindrops are in front of you. The drops disperse sunlight toward your eyes.

quiz.q: Which colour is at the top of VIBGYOR order (first)?
quiz.why: In the word VIBGYOR the first letter V stands for violet. So violet comes first and red is last.

options: Separates colours already in white light
quiz.why: White light already contains all the colours. A prism only separates them (dispersion); it does not make or add colours.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: The human eye and its care

scenes.text: A free eye-camp comes to Neha's school.
The doctor shows a model: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina.
'Eat carrots and greens, and don't rub your eyes!'

steps.title: Parts of the eye
steps.body:
- **Cornea:** transparent front part of the eye.
- **Iris:** dark muscular structure behind the cornea; gives the eye its colour; controls the size of the **pupil**.
- **Pupil:** opening through which light enters; it becomes small in bright light and large in dim light.
- **Lens:** behind the pupil; focuses light on the retina.
- **Retina:** the screen at the back with nerve cells — **cones** (sensitive to bright light and colour) and **rods** (sensitive to dim light). Signals go to the brain through the **optic nerve**.
- **Blind spot:** the point where the optic nerve leaves the eye; no sensory cells, so no vision there.

steps.title: Persistence of vision
steps.body: The impression of an image persists on the retina for about **1/16th of a second**. If still images are shown faster than 16 per second, we see motion — that's how cinema works (usually 24 pictures per second).

steps.title: Care of the eyes
steps.body:
- Get eyes checked regularly; use spectacles if advised.
- Don't read in too little or too much (glare) light; reading distance about **25 cm** is best for normal vision.
- Never look directly at the Sun or a powerful light.
- Don't rub your eyes; if dust enters, wash with clean water; see a doctor if it continues.
- Eat foods with **vitamin A** (carrots, broccoli, green leafy vegetables, cod-liver oil, eggs, milk, curd, cheese, butter, papaya, mango). Lack of vitamin A can cause **night blindness**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why does it take time to see clearly when you enter a dark cinema hall from sunlight? → The pupil needs time to widen to let in more light; rods take time to adjust.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The iris is the opening' — the pupil is the opening; the iris controls it.
- 'We see in the dark because of cones' — rods work in dim light.

activity.prompt: Match the part of the eye with its job
pairs: Controls size of pupil; gives eye colour

quiz.why: Rods in the retina respond to dim light, while cones respond to bright light and colour.
The image stays on the retina for about 1/16 of a second after the object is gone. This is persistence of vision, and it makes films look continuous.

quiz.q: Vitamin whose lack causes night blindness:
quiz.why: Lack of vitamin A causes night blindness, because it is needed for a healthy retina. Eating carrots, milk and green vegetables helps.

quiz.q: Comfortable reading distance for normal eyes:
quiz.why: A normal eye can read comfortably at about 25 cm. Too close (5 cm) strains the eyes, and a much larger distance makes the print look smaller.

quiz.q: The part that gives the eye its colour:
quiz.why: The iris is the coloured part of the eye, and its pigment gives the eye its colour. The pupil is the opening in the middle of it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

lessons.title: Helping the visually impaired: Braille and eye donation

scenes.text: Aman, who is visually impaired, reads a storybook by running his fingertips over raised dots.
Each pattern of dots is a letter.
His friend's family has pledged to donate their eyes after death.

steps.title: Visually challenged people
steps.body: Some people cannot see from birth, and some lose sight due to disease or injury. Such persons try to identify things by touching and listening; they develop their other senses more sharply. Resources include **non-optical aids** (Braille writer slate and stylus, recordings, talking books) and **optical aids** (bifocal lenses, contact lenses, tinted lenses, magnifiers, telescopic aids).

steps.title: Braille
steps.body: The most popular resource is **Braille**, developed by **Louis Braille**, who himself became visually challenged after an accident in childhood. The present system was presented in **1821**. Braille uses **63 dot patterns (characters)**, each representing a letter, a combination of letters, a common word or a grammatical sign. Dots are arranged in cells of **two vertical rows of three dots** each. Patterns are read by touch; Braille texts can be produced by hand or by machine; typewriters and printers for Braille are available.

steps.title: Eye donation
steps.body: Corneal blindness can be cured by replacing the defective cornea with that of a donated eye. Eyes can be donated **after death** by anyone (even people who wore glasses or had cataract surgery). Eyes must be removed within **4–6 hours** after death, at home or hospital. The donor's identity is kept confidential. Donated eyes are used by eye banks.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How many dots can a single Braille cell have? → 6 (two columns of three).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'People who wear spectacles can't donate eyes' — they can.
- 'Braille is a language' — it is a writing system that can represent many languages.

activity.prompt: Questions people often ask about vision and blindness

items.q: Can someone with diabetes or high blood pressure donate eyes?
items.a: Many people with these conditions can pledge; the eye bank's doctors decide what is usable at the time.

items.q: Does donating eyes disfigure the face?
items.a: No. Removal is done carefully and the face is not disfigured.

items.q: How do visually challenged students take exams?
items.a: With Braille, screen readers, scribes or extra time as per rules — many excel in every field.

items.q: How can I be a good friend to a visually challenged classmate?
items.a: Introduce yourself when you approach, ask before helping, describe surroundings clearly and treat them as you'd treat anyone.

quiz.why: Louis Braille developed the Braille system for visually impaired people, in 1821. Edison, Raman and Helen Keller are not credited with it.

quiz.q: Number of dot patterns in Braille:
quiz.why: As given in NCERT, the Braille system has 63 dot patterns or characters. That is more than the 26 letters, so it also covers numbers and signs.

quiz.q: A Braille cell has dots arranged in:
quiz.why: A Braille character is made of six dots arranged in two vertical rows of three. Different combinations of raised dots give different characters.

quiz.q: Eyes must be removed after death within about:
quiz.why: Eyes must be removed within about 4-6 hours after death for the cornea to be usable. After that time they cannot be used.

quiz.q: Which can be replaced through eye donation to cure blindness?
quiz.why: In eye donation the transparent cornea of a donor replaces a damaged one. The brain, optic nerve and iris colour cannot be replaced in this way.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Science (topic)

questions.q: Angle of incidence is 35°. Angle of reflection:
questions.why: By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = angle of incidence. So it is 35°.

questions.q: Which is luminous?
questions.why: A burning candle gives out its own light, so it is luminous. The Moon, a book and a mirror only reflect light.

questions.q: Splitting of white light into seven colours:
questions.why: The splitting of white light into its seven colours is called dispersion. Reflection and absorption do not separate the colours.

questions.q: Images formed by two mirrors at 60°:
questions.why: Number of images = 360/60 − 1 = 6 − 1 = 5. A smaller angle between the mirrors gives more images.

questions.q: Part of the eye that controls the pupil size:
questions.why: The iris is a muscular ring that widens or narrows the pupil. This controls how much light enters the eye.

questions.q: Assertion: Diffused reflection happens from rough surfaces. Reason: The laws of reflection fail on rough surfaces.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is true: rough surfaces cause diffused reflection. The reason is false, because the laws of reflection still hold at every point; the normals simply point in different directions.

questions.q: Night blindness is caused by lack of:
questions.why: A lack of vitamin A affects the retina and leads to night blindness. Vitamin C, iron and vitamin B12 are linked with other deficiencies.

questions.q: Cones are sensitive to:
questions.why: Cones respond to bright light and let us see colours. Rods respond to dim light.

questions.q: A ray makes 60° with the mirror surface. Angle of reflection:
questions.why: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal: 90° − 60° = 30°. The angle of reflection equals it, so it is 30°.

questions.q: Persistence of vision is about:
questions.why: Persistence of vision is about 1/16 of a second. This is why still pictures shown quickly in cinema look like movement.

questions.q: Case: A boy places a candle between two mirrors and counts 7 images. The angle between the mirrors is:
questions.why: Number of images = 360/θ − 1. For 7 images, 360/θ = 8, so θ = 360/8 = 45°.

questions.q: A periscope is useful in a:
questions.why: A periscope uses two mirrors to see over obstacles, so it is used in a submarine. A microscope or a camera flash does not work that way.

questions.q: The blind spot has:
questions.why: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye. It has no rods or cones, so no image is detected there.

questions.q: Assertion: We see a book in a lit room. Reason: The book reflects light into our eyes.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. The book does not give its own light; it reflects light into our eyes, so we see it.

questions.q: Two mirrors are placed parallel facing each other with a candle between. Number of images (ideal):
questions.why: Parallel mirrors keep reflecting the image of each other again and again. Ideally this gives an infinite number of images (360/0 − 1 is unbounded).

questions.q: When moving from bright sunlight into a dark room, the pupil:
questions.why: In a dark room the iris relaxes and the pupil becomes larger. A larger pupil lets in more light so we can see better.

questions.q: If angle between two mirrors is decreased from 90° to 30°, number of images changes from:
questions.why: Images = 360/90 − 1 = 3 at 90°, and 360/30 − 1 = 11 at 30°. So the number rises from 3 to 11 as the angle decreases.

questions.q: Which statement about eye donation is correct?
options: People who wore spectacles can donate eyes
questions.why: Eyes are donated after death, and people who wore spectacles can also donate. Only a healthy cornea matters, not age or glasses.

courses.title: Class 8 Science · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Key facts, definitions and formulas from every Class 8 Science chapter on one sheet, two mixed mock papers with explanations, and tips for answering diagram, reasoning and case-based questions.
outcomes: Learners can recall the key facts of all chapters quickly
Learners can answer mixed MCQ, assertion–reason and case-based questions
Learners can plan revision and write clear science answers

lessons.title: Fact sheet: biology chapters

scenes.text: Kabir makes a one-page sheet for Crops, Microbes, Conservation, Reproduction and Adolescence.
He covers each line and recalls it.
Active recall beats re-reading.

steps.title: Crops & microbes
steps.body:
- Kharif (monsoon): paddy, maize, soybean, groundnut, cotton · Rabi (winter): wheat, gram, pea, mustard, linseed.
- Practices: soil prep → sowing → manure/fertiliser → irrigation → weeding → harvesting → storage.
- Rhizobium (legume roots) fixes N; manure adds humus; drip irrigation saves water.
- Microbes: bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae (+ viruses inside hosts). Lactobacillus → curd; yeast → bread/alcohol; Fleming → penicillin; Jenner → smallpox vaccine.
- Malaria: Plasmodium via female Anopheles; cholera/typhoid: bacteria via water; pasteurisation ≈ 70 °C for 15–30 s then chill.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body:
- Deforestation → less rain, soil erosion, desertification, floods, global warming.
- Biosphere reserve (biodiversity + culture) > national park (ecosystem) > sanctuary (animals protected).
- Pachmarhi BR: Satpura NP + Bori and Pachmarhi WLS. Endemic: found only there. Red Data Book: endangered species. ~17 trees per tonne of paper; paper recyclable 5–7 times.

steps.title: Reproduction & adolescence
steps.body:
- Testes → sperms; ovaries → eggs; fertilisation in oviduct → zygote → embryo → foetus (in uterus).
- External fertilisation: frog, fish. Viviparous: humans, cows. Oviparous: hen, frog. Hydra: budding; Amoeba: binary fission. Dolly (1996): first cloned mammal.
- Adolescence 11–19 y; testosterone/estrogen controlled by pituitary; thyroxine (iodine), insulin (pancreas), adrenalin (adrenal).
- Menstrual cycle ~28–30 days; menarche ~10–12 y, menopause ~45–50 y. XX girl, XY boy — father's sperm decides.

steps.title: Answer-writing tip
steps.body: For 'Give reasons' questions, write the cause and the effect in one sentence: 'Fertilisers are not used in excess *because* they reduce soil fertility and pollute water.'

steps.title: Classic slips
steps.body:
- Mosquito *causes* malaria ✘ (it carries Plasmodium).
- Mother decides baby's sex ✘.
- Manure is a chemical ✘.

cards.back: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules
Heat milk ~70 °C for 15–30 s, then chill
Found only in a particular area
Cell formed by fusion of sperm and egg

quiz.why: Mustard is sown in winter and harvested in spring, so it is a rabi crop. Maize, cotton and soybean are kharif crops.
Yeast respires and releases carbon dioxide. The gas forms bubbles in the dough, so the bread rises.
Oviparous animals lay eggs, and a frog does. Dogs, humans and cows give birth to young ones (viviparous).
The thyroid gland needs iodine to make thyroxine. Insulin, adrenalin and oestrogen do not need iodine.
Satpura National Park is in Madhya Pradesh and lies within the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve. Sundarbans, Kaziranga and Gir are elsewhere.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

lessons.title: Fact sheet: chemistry and physics chapters

scenes.text: Sana lists P = F/A, f = 1/T and VIBGYOR on one card.
She revises it on the bus every morning.
By exam day, it's automatic.

steps.title: Coal, petroleum, combustion
steps.body:
- Exhaustible: coal, petroleum, natural gas, minerals, forests. Inexhaustible: sunlight, air.
- Coal → coke (steel), coal tar (dyes, drugs, naphthalene), coal gas. Carbonisation = plants → coal.
- Petroleum (marine origin) → LPG, petrol, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax, bitumen. CNG is cleaner.
- Combustion: fuel + O₂ + ignition temperature. CO₂ extinguisher for electrical/oil fires. Flame: outer blue (hottest), middle yellow (luminous), inner dark (unburnt vapour).
- Calorific value (kJ/kg): hydrogen ~150,000 highest; LPG ~55,000; CO from incomplete burning is poisonous; SO₂/NOx → acid rain.

steps.title: Force, pressure, friction, sound
steps.body:
- Force = push/pull (N). Contact: muscular, friction; non-contact: magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational.
- **Pressure = Force ÷ Area** (Pa). Liquid pressure increases with depth; atmospheric pressure ≈ 1,00,000 Pa.
- Friction: static > sliding > rolling; reduce with lubricants, ball bearings; drag depends on speed, shape, fluid; streamlining.
- Sound: vibration; needs a medium; f (Hz) = oscillations/second; **T = 1/f**; loudness ∝ amplitude² (dB); pitch ∝ frequency; audible 20 Hz–20 kHz; > 80 dB painful.

steps.title: Electricity, natural phenomena, light
steps.body:
- Acids/bases/salt solutions conduct; distilled water is poor. Water electrolysis: O₂ at +, H₂ at −. Electroplating: object at −; Cr on taps, Sn on cans, Zn on iron.
- Like charges repel; electroscope; earthing; lightning = discharge; squat low outdoors, avoid trees/showers. Earthquakes: plates; seismograph; Richter (M6 ≈ 1000 × energy of M4); Drop–Cover–Hold.
- ∠i = ∠r; regular vs diffused; images between mirrors = 360/θ − 1; VIBGYOR; rods (dim) & cones (colour); persistence ~1/16 s; Braille 63 patterns (1821).

steps.title: Worked numerical
steps.body: A 600 N person stands on one foot of area 0.02 m². Pressure? → 600/0.02 = 30,000 Pa. On two feet (0.04 m²) → 15,000 Pa.

steps.title: Classic slips
steps.body:
- Water on an oil fire ✘.
- Pitch depends on amplitude ✘.
- Hydrogen at positive electrode ✘.

activity.prompt: Match the quantity to its unit

quiz.why: The outer blue zone of a flame is hottest, because there combustion is complete with plenty of air. The dark zone near the wick is the coolest.
Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/25 = 0.04 s.
Rolling friction is the smallest, since a wheel rolls rather than slides. Static and sliding friction, and drag, are larger.
Number of images = 360/30 − 1 = 12 − 1 = 11.

quiz.q: Tin is coated on iron cans because tin is:
quiz.why: Tin is less reactive than iron, so it does not react with the food. That is why iron cans are coated with it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

lessons.title: Mock paper A

scenes.text: Timer on. No notes.
Eight mixed questions.
Score 7+ and you're on track.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: Attempt all questions in the quiz. Afterwards read each explanation and write one line on what you learned from any mistake.

steps.title: Model long answer
steps.body: *Why is CNG considered a better fuel than petrol for city transport?* → CNG burns more completely, producing far less smoke and fewer harmful gases; it reduces air pollution in crowded cities; it is also easier to supply by pipeline.

steps.title: Model reasoning answer
steps.body: *Why are dam walls thicker at the bottom?* → Liquid pressure increases with depth, so the base must withstand the greatest pressure.

activity.prompt: Which three facts did you get wrong or forget in Mock A? Write them in your own words.
activity.hint: Rewriting in your own words helps memory far more than re-reading.

quiz.q: A1. Seed drill is used for:
quiz.why: A seed drill is a farm tool used for sowing seeds evenly and at the right depth. Harvesting, threshing and irrigation use other tools.

quiz.q: A2. Disease caused by a protozoan:
quiz.why: Malaria is caused by a protozoan called Plasmodium. Cholera is caused by bacteria, and measles and polio by viruses.
Paraffin wax is a product obtained from petroleum and is used to make candles. Diesel is a fuel and bitumen is used for roads.

quiz.q: A4. Which is a non-contact force?
quiz.why: Gravity acts at a distance without contact, so it is a non-contact force. Friction, pushing and muscular force need contact.

quiz.q: A5. Force 80 N on 0.4 m² gives pressure:
quiz.why: Pressure = Force ÷ Area = 80 N ÷ 0.4 m² = 200 Pa.
Sound needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. It does travel through water, wood and air.

quiz.q: A7. In electroplating, metal is deposited on the electrode connected to:
quiz.why: The metal is deposited on the object connected to the negative terminal, because the positive metal ions move toward it.

quiz.q: A8. Assertion: The Moon is luminous. Reason: The Moon reflects sunlight.
options: A and R true; R explains A
quiz.why: The assertion is false because the Moon does not produce light of its own; it is illuminated. The reason is true, as the Moon reflects sunlight, which is why we see it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

lessons.title: Mock paper B

scenes.text: Next day, Kabir tries Mock B.
More case-based questions this time.
He reads each case slowly before choosing.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: Case-based questions describe a situation. Underline the key science words in the case, then match them to the concept.

steps.title: Model case answer
steps.body: *A farmer's well water is falling every year and his fields are sandy and uneven. What would you advise?* → Use sprinkler (or drip for orchards) irrigation to save water; add manure to improve water-holding capacity; plant trees around fields to reduce runoff.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body: Step 1: Is A true? Step 2: Is R true? Step 3: Does R correctly explain A? Only then choose.

activity.prompt: Exam-week plan
items: Day 1: Biology fact sheet + Mock A
Day 2: Physics & chemistry sheet + Mock B
Day 3: Redo every wrong answer
Day 4: Draw and label eye, flame, ear diagrams
Day 5: Rest, light revision, sleep 8+ hours

quiz.q: B1. Which fertility method uses legumes?
quiz.why: Growing legumes in rotation with other crops puts nitrogen back into the soil, thanks to Rhizobium bacteria in their roots. This is crop rotation.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1929, the first antibiotic. The smallpox vaccine was developed by Edward Jenner.

quiz.q: B3. Case: A pan of oil catches fire. Best immediate step:
options: Cover with a lid to cut off air
quiz.why: Burning oil should be smothered by covering the pan with a lid, which cuts off the air. Water would spread the burning oil and can make it dangerous.

options: Found only in a specific area
quiz.why: Endemic species are found only in one specific area and nowhere else. Species found everywhere are widespread, and migratory ones move between places.
Hydra reproduces asexually by budding: a small bud grows on the parent's body and then separates as a new Hydra. Binary fission is seen in amoeba.

quiz.q: B6. Case: A tadpole tank lacks iodine; tadpoles don't become frogs. Hormone affected:
quiz.why: Thyroxine needs iodine to be made, and it controls the change from tadpole to frog (metamorphosis). Without iodine the tadpoles cannot develop into frogs.

quiz.q: B7. A 200 Hz sound compared with 100 Hz is:
quiz.why: Pitch depends on frequency, and 200 Hz is higher than 100 Hz, so it is higher pitched. Loudness depends on amplitude, so it is not necessarily louder.
A closed car works like a shelter and lets the charge pass around it to the ground. An open field, a lone tree and water are all dangerous in lightning.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

lessons.title: Diagram and answer-writing skills

scenes.text: Riya loses marks for unlabelled diagrams.
Her teacher shows: pencil, label lines straight, title at the bottom.
Next test, full marks.

steps.title: Diagrams to practise
steps.body:
- Candle flame zones
- Human eye (cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, blind spot)
- Ear path (outer ear, eardrum, middle ear, inner ear)
- Electroscope
- Electroplating set-up (copper sulphate, plates, battery terminals)
- Life cycle of a frog
- Laws of reflection (normal, ∠i, ∠r)

steps.title: Diagram rules
steps.body:
- Use a pencil; label on one side; draw label lines with a ruler; no arrowheads touching wrong parts.
- Give a title.
- Keep it large enough to read.

steps.title: Example answer structure
steps.body: Q: *Explain how lightning conductors protect buildings.* → (1) Definition: metal rod taller than the building, earthed. (2) Working: provides an easy path for charge to flow to the ground. (3) Result: charge doesn't pass through the building, preventing damage.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- One-word answers for 3-mark questions.
- Missing units in numericals.

activity.label: Calm breathing before you start writing

quiz.why: Diagrams are drawn in pencil so they stay neat and mistakes can be corrected. Crayons, glitter pens and red ink make them messy.
Label lines should be straight and drawn with a ruler so each label clearly points to the right part. Wavy or random lines cause confusion.
A 3-mark answer needs a few points: a definition, an explanation and an example or result. One word or only a diagram is not enough.
A numerical answer is incomplete without units such as Pa, Hz or N. The unit tells what the number measures.
Active recall and practising questions make you retrieve what you know and show your weak points. Reading once, only highlighting or skipping weak chapters is less effective.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

questions.q: Kharif crops are sown in:
questions.why: Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon rains in the rainy season, like paddy and maize. Winter-sown crops are rabi crops.

questions.q: Yeast is a:
questions.why: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It is not a virus, a bacterium or a protozoan.

questions.q: Coke is almost pure:
questions.why: Coke is a product of coal and is almost pure carbon. It is a fuel used in industry.

questions.q: Unit of pressure:
questions.why: Pressure is force per unit area, so its unit is pascal (N/m²). Decibel measures loudness, newton force and hertz frequency.

questions.q: Fertilisation in frogs is:
questions.why: In frogs the eggs and sperms meet outside the female's body, in water, so fertilisation is external. Internal fertilisation happens inside the body, as in humans.

questions.q: Adam's apple is the:
questions.why: The Adam's apple is the enlarged larynx (voice box), which sticks out in the neck of boys at adolescence. It is not the thyroid, pituitary or collarbone.

questions.q: Pitch depends on:
questions.why: Pitch depends on the frequency of vibration: higher frequency means higher pitch. Amplitude decides loudness.

questions.q: Assertion: Oil fires should not be put out with water. Reason: Oil floats on water and continues to burn.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Oil is lighter than water and floats, so water spreads the burning oil and the fire grows.

questions.q: Number of images between mirrors at 72°:
questions.why: Number of images = 360/72 − 1 = 5 − 1 = 4.

questions.q: Calorific value of a fuel releasing 2,25,000 kJ from 5 kg:
questions.why: Calorific value = heat released ÷ mass = 2,25,000 kJ ÷ 5 kg = 45,000 kJ/kg.

questions.q: Case: A town notices more floods and dry wells after nearby forests were cleared. Best explanation:
options: Less water soaks into soil and runoff increases
questions.why: Trees and roots let rainwater soak into the soil. After clearing forests, less water enters the ground and more runs off, causing floods and falling groundwater, which dries up wells.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: Typhoid is caused by bacteria, not a virus, so that pair is wrong. Malaria (protozoa), cholera (bacteria) and measles (virus) are correct.

questions.q: Time period of a sound with frequency 400 Hz:
questions.why: Time period = 1 ÷ frequency = 1/400 = 0.0025 s.

questions.q: A brick of 24 N has faces 0.02 m², 0.01 m² and 0.005 m². Maximum pressure:
questions.why: Pressure is greatest on the smallest face: 24 N ÷ 0.005 m² = 4800 Pa. The larger faces would give lower pressure.

questions.q: Assertion: The sex of a child is determined by the father. Reason: Sperms carry either X or Y chromosome.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Eggs always carry X, while a sperm carries X (girl) or Y (boy), so the father decides the sex of the child.

questions.q: Why is a seed drill better than broadcasting?
options: Uniform depth and spacing; seeds covered from birds
questions.why: A seed drill places seeds at a uniform depth and spacing and covers them with soil, so birds cannot eat them. Broadcasting scatters seeds unevenly and wastes them.

questions.q: Case: A student's tester bulb doesn't glow in lemon juice but a compass needle deflects. Correct conclusion:
options: Lemon juice conducts; current is weak
questions.why: A compass needle deflects only if a current flows, so lemon juice does conduct. The current is too weak to light the bulb.

questions.q: An earthquake of magnitude 7 compared with magnitude 5 releases energy about:
questions.why: Each step on the Richter scale means about 32 times more energy, so two steps mean about 32 × 32 ≈ 1000 times. The scale is not linear.

questions.q: Which combination stops combustion fastest for a small paper fire?
options: Water (cools below ignition temperature and cuts air)
questions.why: Water cools the paper below its ignition temperature and also cuts off air, so combustion stops. Fanning, oxygen or dry leaves would feed the fire.

questions.q: The pupil becomes smaller in bright light because:
options: The iris contracts it to reduce light entering
questions.why: In bright light, the muscles of the iris contract and make the pupil smaller. This reduces the light entering the eye and protects the retina.

school-c8-social-a.title: Class 8 Social Science — History, Geography, Civics (part 1 of 2)
school-c8-social-a.description: Class 8 History (Our Pasts III), Geography (Resources and Development) and Civics (Social and Political Life III), chapter by chapter, with timelines, case studies, quizzes and tests — plus Revision & Practice. Chapters follow the rationalised NCERT Class 8 textbooks (2023–24 editions onward). NCERT has been introducing new Class 8 books from 2025–26; if your school uses those, chapter names and order differ, but most topics here still apply. Independent material, not affiliated with NCERT or any board.

courses.title: History Ch 1 · How, When and Where
courses.summary: Why dates matter (and when they don't), how historians divide the past into periods and the problems with James Mill's scheme, how the British used surveys and official records, and what other sources tell us.
outcomes: Learners can explain why history is more than a list of dates
Learners can critique the Hindu–Muslim–British periodisation
Learners can describe how colonial rulers recorded information (surveys, census, archives)
Learners can name sources beyond official records and their value

lessons.title: Dates and what they hide

scenes.text: Rohan memorises '1757 — Plassey' but can't explain what changed.
His teacher asks: 'Who lived through it? What did ordinary people feel?'
History is about processes, not just dates.

steps.title: Are dates important?
steps.body: Earlier, history meant battles, kings and dates — when a ruler was crowned, married, died. Dates still help us place events in order. But many important changes — how people farmed, traded, dressed, learned — happened slowly over decades; you can't pin them to one date. Historians today ask **how** and **why** changes happened and **who** they affected.

steps.title: Which dates?
steps.body: The dates we choose reflect the story we tell. British historians in India focused on Governors-General (Warren Hastings was the first, from 1773) and their policies, as if Indian history were a list of British officials. Telling a different story (about peasants, women, tribals) needs different dates and sources.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why can't we date 'the spread of tea drinking in India' precisely? → It happened gradually across regions and classes over many years; it was a process.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking history = memorising dates.
- Assuming the British story of India is the whole story.

statements.s: History is only about kings and battles.
statements.why: It is also about everyday life and slow changes.

statements.s: Some changes cannot be given a single date.
Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General.
The dates we choose depend on the story we tell.

options: They are always exact for processes
quiz.why: Dates help us put events in order and understand what came before and after. They do not replace evidence or explain everything.
Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal, from 1773. Clive was earlier and Dalhousie and Curzon came later.

quiz.q: Which is a 'process' rather than an event?
quiz.why: A process happens gradually over a long time, such as the spread of new farming methods. A battle, a treaty signing and a coronation are single events with a date.
British-written histories centred on Governors-General and their policies, i.e. on rulers. They gave little attention to peasants, women or folk songs.

options: How and why changes happened and who they affected
quiz.why: Modern historians ask how and why changes happened and whom they affected. They look beyond dates and kings.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Dividing the past into periods

scenes.text: In 1817 James Mill split Indian history into 'Hindu', 'Muslim' and 'British' boxes.
Was everyone in the 'Muslim period' Muslim? Were all rulers before that Hindu?
Historians found the boxes misleading.

steps.title: James Mill's periodisation
steps.body: The Scottish economist and political philosopher **James Mill** wrote *A History of British India* (three volumes, **1817**). He divided Indian history into **Hindu, Muslim and British** periods. He thought all Asian societies were at a lower level of civilisation than Europe and that British rule could 'civilise' India — so he wanted English laws, institutions and ideas introduced.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body:
- Rulers' religion was not the only thing that mattered; many faiths co-existed in every period.
- It ignored the rich diversity of India's past.
- It assumed Britain was superior and the bringer of progress.

Many historians use **ancient, medieval and modern** instead, but this too is borrowed from European history and can imply that 'modern' = progress brought by British rule.

steps.title: The colonial period
steps.body: When one country subjugates another and brings political, economic, social and cultural changes, we call it **colonisation**. Historians call the time of British rule the **colonial period** and study how it affected Indians — not all were affected the same way.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is calling c. 1200–1700 the 'Muslim period' misleading? → Most people were not Muslim, many rulers of the time were not Muslim, and many cultures and faiths flourished.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking periodisation is neutral — it carries assumptions.
- Confusing James Mill with John Stuart Mill (his son).

activity.prompt: Match the idea to its description
pairs: Wrote A History of British India (1817)
Subjugation of one country by another with deep changes
Era of British rule in India

quiz.q: James Mill's history was published in:
quiz.why: James Mill published A History of British India in three volumes in 1817. 1757 was Plassey and 1857 the Revolt.
Mill thought Indian society was backward and that British rule would civilise India. This shows his bias.

quiz.q: A problem with Mill's periods is that they:
options: Use rulers' religion as the main marker
quiz.why: Mill divided Indian history by the religion of the rulers, which is too simple. It ignores the variety of Indian society in each period.

options: Political, economic, social and cultural changes imposed by a ruling power
quiz.why: Colonisation is when one power rules another, bringing political, economic, social and cultural changes. It is more than travel, art or trade.

options: That British rule alone brought progress
quiz.why: The word 'modern' can wrongly suggest that British rule alone brought progress. It also ignores the earlier history of India.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Surveys, census and official records

scenes.text: In the 1870s and 1880s, officials go house to house counting people, castes and occupations.
Others map land, forests, plants and ancient ruins.
All of it goes into files that we can still read in archives.

steps.title: Administration produces records
steps.body: The British believed writing things down was important: every instruction, plan, policy decision, agreement and investigation was recorded. They set up **record rooms** and specialised institutions like **archives** and **museums** to preserve documents. Letters and memos moved from one department to another; **calligraphists** (expert hand-writers) copied documents before printing became widespread.

steps.title: Surveys
steps.body: The British thought a country had to be known properly to be administered effectively. By the early 19th century detailed **surveys** mapped the country; revenue surveys recorded topography, soil, flora, fauna, local histories and crops. From the end of the 19th century, a **census** was held every ten years, recording castes, religions and occupations. There were also botanical, zoological, archaeological, anthropological and forest surveys. Early maps of Bengal were made by **James Rennel** for Robert Clive.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did the British want so much information? → To control and tax the land effectively, plan administration, and understand (and govern) the people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking official records give the whole truth — they show what officials thought and wanted.
- Thinking the census began in 1947 — it was held every ten years from the end of the 19th century.

activity.prompt: Find these record-types in your own life (talk to family)
items: An old photo or letter in your family
A land or house record
A ration or Aadhaar-type identity document
A school report card from a grandparent
A newspaper clipping your family saved

quiz.why: Archives are the places where government documents and records are preserved. Markets and gymnasiums are not for keeping records.
The census was held every ten years, as a decadal count of the population. It was not annual.
Calligraphists were expert hand-writers who copied documents in beautiful writing before printing was common.

quiz.q: James Rennel made early maps for:
quiz.why: James Rennel made early maps of Bengal for Robert Clive. The Company needed maps to understand and control the land.
Official records show what officials thought and wanted, so they give only one viewpoint. They do not show peasants' feelings or private lives.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Other sources: what official records can't tell

scenes.text: Neha finds her great-grandmother's diary from the 1940s.
Beside it, old newspapers describe protests the official files call 'disturbances'.
Together they tell a fuller story.

steps.title: Limits of official records
steps.body:
Official records don't always tell us what people of the country felt, or what lay behind their actions. For that we look to:

- **Diaries** of people, **autobiographies**, accounts of pilgrims and travellers.
- **Popular books** sold in local bazaars.
- **Newspapers** (with printing, they spread ideas and debates).
- Writings of leaders and reformers; poets and novelists.

These too reflect the views of those who wrote them — and many people (peasants, tribals) could not write. Historians read every source critically.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A file says 'peasants were rebellious and lazy'. How should a historian treat it? → As the official's view; compare with peasants' songs, petitions, newspapers and other sources.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why do we know less about poor peasants than about Governors-General? → Peasants rarely left written records; officials and the educated left more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating any one source as the full truth.
- Ignoring oral traditions and songs as sources.

activity.prompt: Official or non-official source?

quiz.q: Which is NOT an official record?
quiz.why: A personal diary is a private record and not an official one. Census reports, survey maps and government memos are all kept by the government.

quiz.q: Why do historians use multiple sources?
options: Each source has its own viewpoint
quiz.why: Every source has its own viewpoint and may leave things out. Using many sources and comparing them gives a fuller, more balanced picture.

quiz.q: Newspapers became an important source because of:
quiz.why: Newspapers became an important source in the nineteenth century because printing made them widely available. Radio, television and the internet came later.

quiz.q: Many peasants' views are hard to find because:
quiz.why: Many peasants could not read or write, so they left few records. Their views are thus hard to find.
Popular books and prints were sold in local bazaars, so ordinary people could read them. They are a useful source on public opinion.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

questions.q: Who wrote A History of British India?
questions.why: James Mill wrote A History of British India in 1817. Macaulay is known for his Minute on education.

questions.q: Mill's periods were:
questions.why: Mill divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods, based on the rulers' religion. This is criticised as too simple.

questions.q: The first Governor-General:
questions.why: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General, from 1773. Wellesley, Canning and Cornwallis came as later or other officials.

questions.q: Where are government documents preserved?
questions.why: Government documents are kept in archives, special record rooms. Bazaars, forts and farms are not used for this.

questions.q: A census was conducted every:
questions.why: A census was conducted every ten years, a decade. It counted the people and gathered information about them.

questions.q: Assertion: Mill's periodisation is criticised. Reason: It defined periods by rulers' religion and ignored diversity.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Mill defined periods by rulers' religion and ignored the diversity of Indian society, which is why historians criticise him.

questions.q: Colonisation means:
options: Subjugation of one country by another causing major changes
questions.why: Colonisation means one country subjugates another and causes major political, economic and social changes. Tourism, migration and free trade do not involve such control.

questions.q: Which survey studied ancient remains?
questions.why: An archaeological survey studies ancient remains such as old buildings and monuments. Forest, zoological and botanical surveys study other things.

questions.q: Calligraphists:
questions.why: Calligraphists were skilled at beautiful handwriting and copied documents by hand. They did not print newspapers, draw maps or conduct the census.

questions.q: Why might a historian find a newspaper more useful than a government file?
options: It may show public opinion and debates
questions.why: A newspaper can show public opinion and debates of the time, which government files may not show. It is not always neutral or free of bias.

questions.q: Case: A 1880s official report calls a protest 'a riot by ignorant villagers'. What is the best historical approach?
options: Compare with other sources like petitions, songs and newspapers
questions.why: An official report shows only the officials' view. A historian should compare it with other sources such as petitions, songs and newspapers before judging.

questions.q: The British believed that to administer a country effectively they must:
options: Know it through surveys and records
questions.why: The British believed that to rule a country well they had to know it. So they made surveys, maps and records, as knowledge gave control.

questions.q: Assertion: The 'modern' period label is also problematic. Reason: It may imply that British rule alone brought progress.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Calling a period 'modern' may suggest that British rule alone brought progress.

questions.q: Which is a limitation of official records?
options: They may not show how ordinary people felt
questions.why: Official records mainly reflect the officials' view. They may not show how ordinary people felt, but they do have dates and were kept.

questions.q: Why is it hard to give a single date for many historical changes?
options: They happen gradually over long periods
questions.why: Many historical changes, like new farming methods, happen slowly over long periods. So no single date marks them.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
options: James Rennel — maps for Robert Clive
questions.why: James Rennel made maps for Robert Clive, so that pair is correct. Plassey was Clive's battle, the census had nothing to do with Mill, and calligraphists were not soldiers.

courses.title: History Ch 2 · From Trade to Territory: The Company Establishes Power
courses.summary: How the English East India Company came to India as traders, fought rivals, won Plassey and Buxar, gained the Diwani of Bengal, and expanded through wars, subsidiary alliances, paramountcy and the Doctrine of Lapse, building a new administration.
outcomes: Learners can trace the Company's journey from trade to rule
Learners can explain Plassey (1757), Buxar (1764) and the Diwani (1765)
Learners can describe Mysore and Maratha resistance and Company expansion policies
Learners can explain the Company's new administration and army

lessons.title: The Company arrives and fights for trade

scenes.text: In 1600 Queen Elizabeth I gives the English East India Company a charter.
Its ships sail to India for cotton, silk, pepper, cloves and indigo.
Portuguese, Dutch and French traders are there too — competition turns violent.

steps.title: From charter to factory
steps.body:
In **1600**, the East India Company got a charter from **Queen Elizabeth I** granting it the sole right (monopoly) to trade with the East — no other English company could compete. But other Europeans were already there: the **Portuguese** (Vasco da Gama reached India in **1498**; they had a base in Goa), the **Dutch** and soon the **French**.

The first English **factory** (a warehouse where traders worked) was set up on the banks of the **Hugli in 1651**. Merchants and traders settled around it. Later the Company built a fort and bought rights to villages; this grew into Calcutta.

steps.title: Trade and conflict in Bengal
steps.body: The Company persuaded the Mughal emperor **Aurangzeb** to issue a **farman** granting it the right to trade duty-free. The Company's officials misused it for private trade without paying duties, causing huge revenue loss to Bengal. After Aurangzeb's death (**1707**) Bengal's nawabs — **Murshid Quli Khan**, **Alivardi Khan**, **Sirajuddaulah** — asserted their power, refused concessions and demanded tributes.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did European companies fight each other in India? → They wanted to buy the same goods; competition raised prices and reduced profits; eliminating rivals meant more profit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Company came as a government — it came as a trading company.
- Saying the farman allowed private trade by officials — they misused it.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order

events.text: East India Company gets royal charter
First English factory on the Hugli

quiz.q: The East India Company got its charter from:
quiz.why: The East India Company got its charter from Queen Elizabeth I in 1600. Akbar and Aurangzeb were Mughal emperors, and Napoleon was French.
A factory then meant a warehouse where the Company's traders and goods were kept, not a place for making things. It was a trading post.

quiz.q: First English factory was on the banks of:
quiz.why: The first English factory in the east was set up on the banks of the Hugli river, in 1651. This led to the growth of Calcutta.

quiz.q: Duty-free trade right came through a farman of:
quiz.why: The Company got duty-free trade through a farman of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Later the Company misused this right.
Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer who reached India by sea in 1498. He was not French, Dutch or English.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Plassey, Buxar and the Diwani

scenes.text: June 1757: Sirajuddaulah's army faces Robert Clive at Plassey.
Mir Jafar, one of the nawab's commanders, has secretly struck a deal with Clive.
His troops never fight. The Company wins — and changes Indian history.

steps.title: Battle of Plassey (1757)
steps.body:
Conflicts grew between the Company and **Sirajuddaulah** over fortifications and trade. In **1757** **Robert Clive** led the Company's army against him at **Plassey**. The nawab lost mainly because **Mir Jafar**, one of his commanders, did not fight — Clive had promised to make him nawab. Plassey was the Company's **first major victory** in India.

Mir Jafar became nawab but was a puppet; when he protested he was replaced by **Mir Qasim**; when Mir Qasim complained, he was defeated at the **Battle of Buxar (1764)** and Mir Jafar was reinstated.

steps.title: The Diwani (1765)
steps.body: After Mir Jafar's death, in **1765**, the Mughal emperor appointed the Company as **Diwan** of the provinces of Bengal (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa). The Diwani gave the Company the right to use the vast **revenue** of Bengal. This solved its old problem: it no longer needed to bring gold and silver from Britain to buy Indian goods — Bengal's revenue paid for them, for its army and for its forts.

steps.title: 'Nabobs'
steps.body: Company officials became very rich through private trade and gifts. Robert Clive himself amassed a fortune. Returning officials were mocked in England as **'nabobs'** (an anglicised form of nawab). Clive was later questioned by Parliament about his wealth.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was the Diwani more important than Plassey for the Company's finances? → It gave permanent control over Bengal's revenue, funding trade, army and expansion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Plassey (1757, Sirajuddaulah) with Buxar (1764, Mir Qasim and allies).
- Thinking the Company immediately ruled all India after Plassey.

activity.prompt: Order the Company's rise in Bengal

quiz.why: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757 between Robert Clive and Sirajuddaulah. 1857 was the Revolt and 1764-65 are Buxar and the Diwani.
Mir Jafar, Sirajuddaulah's commander, did not fight at Plassey because Clive promised to make him nawab. Mir Qasim came later.

quiz.q: The Diwani gave the Company the right to:
quiz.why: The Diwani gave the Company the right to collect revenue in Bengal. It did not allow it to mint English coins or appoint Mughal emperors.

quiz.q: Battle of Buxar (1764) followed a conflict with:
quiz.why: The Battle of Buxar in 1764 followed the Company's conflict with Mir Qasim, whom it had made nawab. He was later removed after disputes over trade.
Nabobs were rich Company officials who returned to England with great wealth from India. They were mocked there for it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Expansion: alliances, Mysore and the Marathas

scenes.text: Tipu Sultan's toy shows a tiger mauling a British soldier.
His armies use iron-cased rockets that alarm the British.
In 1799 the British storm Seringapatam; Tipu dies defending his capital.

steps.title: Subsidiary alliance
steps.body: Introduced by **Lord Wellesley** (Governor-General 1798–1805). Indian rulers had to disband their own armed forces; the Company would protect them, but rulers had to **pay for the subsidiary forces**; if they failed, part of their territory was taken as penalty. Awadh and Hyderabad lost territories this way.

steps.title: Mysore
steps.body: Under **Haidar Ali** (1761–1782) and **Tipu Sultan** (1782–1799), Mysore became powerful and controlled the Malabar coast trade. Tipu stopped exports of sandalwood, pepper and cardamom through his ports and forged ties with the French, modernising his army. Four **Anglo-Mysore wars** were fought (1767–69, 1780–84, 1790–92, 1799). In the last, at **Seringapatam (1799)**, Tipu was killed defending his capital. Mysore was placed under the former Wodeyar dynasty with a subsidiary alliance.

steps.title: Marathas and paramountcy
steps.body: After their defeat at the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**, the Marathas split into states under chiefs (Sindhia, Holkar, Gaikwad, Bhonsle) under a Peshwa. A series of wars ended with the **Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19)**, which crushed Maratha power; the Peshwa was pensioned off. Under **Lord Hastings** (Governor-General 1813–1823) the Company claimed **paramountcy** — its authority was supreme, and it could annex any Indian kingdom. **Rani Channamma of Kittur** (Karnataka) led an armed resistance against the British (she was arrested in 1824 and died in prison in 1829).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did Indian rulers lose power under the subsidiary alliance? → They could not keep their own armies and paid heavily for Company troops, losing territory when they couldn't pay.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Wellesley introduced the Doctrine of Lapse (that was Dalhousie).
- Saying Tipu signed a subsidiary alliance — Mysore was given one after his death.

activity.prompt: Match the person to the role
pairs: Ruler of Mysore killed at Seringapatam (1799)

quiz.why: Lord Wellesley devised the subsidiary alliance, used between 1798 and 1805. Clive, Hastings and Dalhousie are linked to other policies.
Tipu Sultan was killed in 1799 defending Seringapatam against the Company. Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764) were earlier.
The Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19) crushed Maratha power. 1761 was the Third Battle of Panipat and 1857 the Revolt.
Paramountcy meant the Company claimed supreme authority over Indian states, which were to be subordinate to it. It was not equal status.
Rani Channamma was the queen of Kittur in Karnataka, who rose against the British. Jhansi's queen was Lakshmibai.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Doctrine of Lapse and the new administration

scenes.text: When the ruler of Jhansi died without a natural son, his adopted son was refused the throne.
Lord Dalhousie's policy: such kingdoms 'lapse' to the Company.
One after another, kingdoms were annexed.

steps.title: Doctrine of Lapse
steps.body: **Lord Dalhousie** (Governor-General 1848–1856) declared that if an Indian ruler died **without a male heir**, his kingdom would 'lapse' — become part of Company territory. Annexed this way: **Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1850), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853), Jhansi (1854)**. In **1856** **Awadh** was annexed, on the claim of 'misgovernment' — angering many.

steps.title: New administration
steps.body:
- **Warren Hastings** (Governor-General 1773–1785) organised administration and justice.
- British territories were divided into **Presidencies**: Bengal, Madras, Bombay, each ruled by a Governor; the supreme head was the **Governor-General**.
- **Districts** became the main administrative unit, under a **Collector** who collected revenue and taxes and maintained law and order.
- From 1772 a new justice system: each district had a criminal and a civil court; Maulvis and Hindu pandits interpreted Indian laws for European judges.
- **Regulating Act of 1773** set up a **Supreme Court** and a court of appeal (Sadar Nizamat Adalat) at Calcutta.

steps.title: The Company army
steps.body: The army recruited peasants as **sepoys** (from sipahi, soldier), trained in European style with muskets and matchlocks. In the early 19th century the Company created a uniform military culture; soldiers had to obey new rules — which clashed with caste and community feelings, as later in 1857.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did the annexation of Awadh anger people? → It was justified as 'misgovernment' but seen as unjust; nawab's officers, soldiers and families lost livelihoods; many sepoys came from Awadh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Jhansi was annexed in 1857 (it was 1854).
- Confusing Collector (district) with Governor (presidency).

activity.prompt: Order Dalhousie's annexations

quiz.q: Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by:
quiz.why: Lord Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse (1848-56). It said a kingdom would be annexed if a ruler died without a natural male heir.
Jhansi was annexed in 1854 under the Doctrine of Lapse after the ruler died without a natural heir.

quiz.q: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of:
quiz.why: Awadh was annexed in 1856, not for lapse but because the British claimed it was misgoverned. The Doctrine of Lapse was used for other states.

quiz.q: Main administrative unit under Company rule:
quiz.why: Under Company rule, the district was the main unit of administration, headed by a Collector. The Collector looked after revenue and order.

quiz.q: The Regulating Act of 1773 set up a:
quiz.why: The Regulating Act of 1773 set up a Supreme Court in Calcutta, along with the Governor-General's office. It created no parliament in Delhi or railways.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

questions.q: The East India Company was granted its charter in:
questions.why: The East India Company received its charter from Queen Elizabeth I in 1600. 1757 was Plassey and 1651 the first factory on the Hugli.

questions.q: Battle of Plassey was won by:
questions.why: Robert Clive won the Battle of Plassey in 1757 against Sirajuddaulah. Mir Jafar's betrayal helped him win.

questions.q: Subsidiary alliance was introduced by:
questions.why: Lord Wellesley introduced the subsidiary alliance. Dalhousie, Canning and Curzon belong to other policies and periods.

questions.q: Doctrine of Lapse was devised by:
questions.why: Lord Dalhousie devised the Doctrine of Lapse (1848-56). The other names are linked to different policies.

questions.q: Company became Diwan of Bengal in:
questions.why: The Company became Diwan of Bengal in 1765 and got the right to collect revenue. 1757 is Plassey and 1764 is Buxar.

questions.q: Tipu Sultan ruled:
questions.why: Tipu Sultan was the ruler of Mysore from 1782 until his death in 1799. He was not the ruler of Awadh, Bengal or Jhansi.

questions.q: Assertion: The Diwani benefited the Company. Reason: It gave the Company control over Bengal's revenues.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. By giving control over Bengal's revenues, the Diwani gave the Company a large income.

questions.q: Third Battle of Panipat (1761) weakened the:
questions.why: The Maratha defeat at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 weakened the Marathas. It did not affect Mysore, the Sikhs or the Mughals of Bengal in the same way.

questions.q: Which kingdom was NOT annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.why: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of misgovernment, not under the Doctrine of Lapse. Nagpur, Jhansi and Satara were annexed by lapse.

questions.q: The head of a district in Company administration:
questions.why: The Collector headed a district in Company administration and was in charge of revenue and law and order. A Peshwa, Nawab or Governor is a different post.

questions.q: Case: A ruler signs a treaty agreeing to disband his army, keep British troops and pay for them. He later can't pay and loses territory. This describes:
questions.why: A treaty where a ruler disbands his army, keeps British troops and pays for them is the subsidiary alliance of Wellesley. Failure to pay led to loss of territory.

questions.q: Why did the Company want to defeat Tipu Sultan?
options: He controlled Malabar trade and allied with the French
questions.why: Tipu Sultan controlled the Malabar trade and allied with the French, which threatened the Company. So the Company wanted to defeat him.

questions.q: Assertion: Mir Jafar did not fight at Plassey. Reason: Clive had promised to make him nawab.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Clive had promised to make Mir Jafar nawab, so Mir Jafar stayed out of the fighting.

questions.q: Which order is correct?
questions.why: The dates are Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764, Diwani 1765 and Seringapatam 1799, which gives the correct order. The other orders break this sequence.

questions.q: Paramountcy was claimed under:
questions.why: Paramountcy was claimed under Lord Hastings (Governor-General 1813-23). It said the Company's authority was above that of Indian rulers.

questions.q: Why was the Diwani a turning point for Company trade with India?
options: It made the Company Mughal emperor
Bengal's revenue replaced gold and silver imports from Britain for buying goods
questions.why: After the Diwani, the Company used Bengal's revenue to buy Indian goods, so it no longer needed to import gold and silver from Britain. Trade became self-financing.

questions.q: Case: A historian studying the Company's justice system after 1772 finds Maulvis and pandits working with European judges. Their role was to:
options: Interpret Indian laws for the courts
questions.why: Maulvis and pandits helped European judges by interpreting Indian laws, such as Hindu and Muslim personal laws. They did not write newspapers or collect revenue.

courses.title: History Ch 3 · Ruling the Countryside
courses.summary: How the Company became the Diwan and organised land revenue — the Permanent Settlement, Mahalwari and Ryotwari systems — and how it forced the cultivation of crops for Europe like indigo, leading to the Blue Rebellion and Champaran.
outcomes: Learners can explain the Company's revenue needs after the Diwani
Learners can compare Permanent Settlement, Mahalwari and Ryotwari systems
Learners can describe nij and ryoti indigo cultivation and its hardships
Learners can explain the Blue Rebellion (1859) and its aftermath

lessons.title: The Company becomes the Diwan

scenes.text: Five years after the Diwani, a terrible famine strikes Bengal.
About ten million people — one-third of the population — die.
Yet the Company keeps pushing for more revenue.

steps.title: Revenue first
steps.body: On **12 August 1765** the Mughal emperor appointed the East India Company as the **Diwan of Bengal**. The Company now had to administer the land and its revenue — but it was still mainly a trader. It wanted to buy fine cotton and silk cloth cheaply and increase revenue as much as possible.

steps.title: The crisis
steps.body: Within five years, the value of goods bought in Bengal doubled — paid for from Bengal's own revenue. Artisans deserted villages because they were forced to sell goods at low prices; peasants couldn't pay dues. Agricultural production declined. Then, in **1770**, a **famine** killed about **ten million people** in Bengal — about **one-third** of the population.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did artisans leave their villages? → They were forced to sell goods to the Company at low prices and could not earn a living.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Company invested in improving land — at first it focused only on collecting revenue.
- Confusing the 1770 famine with 1857.

activity.prompt: Order the events

quiz.q: Company became Diwan of Bengal on:
quiz.why: The Company became Diwan of Bengal on 12 August 1765, which gave it the right to collect revenue. The other dates relate to other events.

quiz.q: The 1770 famine in Bengal killed about:
quiz.why: The Bengal famine of 1770 killed about ten million people, around one-third of the population. A far smaller number would not be a famine of that size.

quiz.q: The Company's main aim was to:
options: Increase revenue and buy goods cheaply
quiz.why: The Company wanted to raise its revenue and buy goods cheaply, to make profit. It did not aim to help peasants or build schools.

options: They had to sell goods cheaply to the Company
quiz.why: The Company forced weavers and artisans to sell goods cheaply, so they could not earn a living. Many left their villages.
After the Diwani, high revenue demands and the Company's policies caused a crisis and farm output fell. It was not doubled or unaffected.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Revenue systems: Permanent, Mahalwari, Ryotwari

scenes.text: In 1793 Lord Cornwallis fixes the revenue that zamindars must pay — permanently.
But many zamindars can't pay, and their estates are auctioned.
Peasants still pay high rents. Who benefited?

steps.title: Permanent Settlement (1793)
steps.body:
Introduced under **Lord Cornwallis** in **Bengal**. Rajas and taluqdars were recognised as **zamindars**; they collected rent from peasants and paid **fixed revenue** to the Company, which would **never be increased**. The Company hoped for a regular income and that zamindars would invest in land.

**Problems:** revenue was set very high; zamindars who failed to pay lost their zamindari (estates **auctioned**). By the early 19th century, prices rose and cultivation expanded, so zamindars' income rose but the Company could not increase its fixed demand. Zamindars rarely invested in land; cultivators found the system oppressive — rents were high, rights insecure, and they often took loans from moneylenders.

steps.title: Mahalwari (1822)
steps.body: Devised by **Holt Mackenzie** for the North Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency. Revenue was fixed for each village (**mahal**), estimated by assessing each plot; it would be **revised periodically**, not fixed permanently. The village headman collected revenue.

steps.title: Ryotwari (Munro system)
steps.body: Tried by **Captain Alexander Read** and developed by **Thomas Munro** in South India (Madras Presidency), later in Bombay. Revenue settled directly with the **cultivators (ryots)**, whose fields were surveyed. Revenue was often set **too high**; peasants fled villages. The officials' hope to make peasants rich, enterprising farmers did not come true.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why could the Company not gain from rising prices in Bengal after 1793? → Its revenue demand was permanently fixed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing Mahalwari (village/mahal) with Ryotwari (individual ryot).
- Thinking Permanent Settlement helped peasants.

activity.prompt: Match the revenue system to its feature
pairs: Fixed revenue paid by zamindars; Cornwallis, 1793
Revenue fixed for a village (mahal), revised periodically

quiz.why: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis. 1765 was the Diwani and 1857 the Revolt.

quiz.q: Under Permanent Settlement, revenue was paid by:
quiz.why: Under the Permanent Settlement the rajas and taluqdars were made zamindars, and they paid a fixed revenue to the Company. Ryots did not pay it directly.
The Mahalwari system was devised by Holt Mackenzie in 1822. Thomas Munro devised ryotwari, and Cornwallis the Permanent Settlement.
In the ryotwari system, the settlement was made directly with the cultivators (ryots). It was not made with zamindars or rajas.

options: Revenue was often set too high
quiz.why: Under ryotwari, revenue was often fixed too high. Peasants could not pay and many fled their villages.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Crops for Europe: the indigo story

scenes.text: European cloth-makers want the rich blue dye from Indian indigo.
Planters force Bengal peasants to grow it on their best land.
Peasants say: 'It eats our rice fields and leaves us in debt.'

steps.title: Why indigo?
steps.body: By the late 18th century the Company also wanted to expand cultivation of crops for export: **jute** in Bengal, **tea** in Assam, **sugarcane** in the United Provinces, **wheat** in Punjab, **cotton** in Maharashtra and Punjab, **rice** in Madras. Indian indigo produced a rich blue colour preferred by European cloth makers over **woad** (a plant from temperate zones). Indigo from the West Indies and America declined (e.g. after a revolution in St Domingue in 1791), so demand for Indian indigo rose. Cloth printers like **William Morris** in Britain used Indian indigo.

steps.title: Two systems
steps.body:
- **Nij cultivation:** the planter produced indigo on land he controlled directly, with hired labourers. Problems: hard to get large fertile compact lands, labour needed at the same time as rice cultivation, and ploughs and bullocks were costly. So nij was less than 25% of land under indigo.
- **Ryoti system:** planters forced ryots to sign a contract (**satta**); ryots received cash advances at low interest and had to grow indigo on at least 25% of their land. The planter gave seed and drill; ryots did the rest. After harvest the price paid was very low, and the cycle of loans never ended. Indigo also exhausted the soil quickly.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did ryots hate the advance system? → Low prices, endless debt, and indigo took their best land and exhausted the soil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up nij (planter's own land) and ryoti (peasants' land under contract).
- Thinking indigo was a food crop.

activity.prompt: Nij or ryoti system?

items.text: Planter grows indigo on land he controls directly
Peasant must use 25% of land for indigo

quiz.why: Indigo was valued for its rich blue dye, used for colouring cloth. It was not a food, oil or fibre.
Ryots signed a contract called a satta with planters, taking an advance to grow indigo. The Diwani and farman are different documents.

options: A European plant giving a duller blue dye
quiz.why: Woad was a European plant that gave a duller blue dye. Indigo gave a richer blue, so woad was its competitor.

quiz.q: Under the ryoti system, at least ___ of land was for indigo.
quiz.why: Under the ryoti system, ryots had to grow indigo on at least 25 per cent of their land. This was written in the contract.

options: British artist and designer who used indigo
quiz.why: William Morris was a British designer who used indigo dye in his textiles. He was not a planter or a Governor-General.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: The Blue Rebellion and after

scenes.text: In March 1859, thousands of ryots in Bengal refuse to grow indigo.
Village headmen and even some zamindars support them; drums call meetings.
The government sets up an Indigo Commission.

steps.title: The rebellion (1859)
steps.body: In **March 1859** thousands of ryots in Bengal refused to grow indigo. They refused to pay rents, attacked indigo factories armed with swords, spears, bows and arrows; women fought with pots and pans. Those who worked for planters were socially boycotted; **gomasthas** (agents of planters) were beaten. Ryots felt they had support: Queen Victoria's proclamation after 1857 had raised hopes; some zamindars and village headmen (mandals) supported them. In Barasat, a magistrate issued a notice that ryots would not be compelled to accept indigo contracts — which spread as the news that 'the Queen had declared indigo need not be sown'.

steps.title: Indigo Commission (1860)
steps.body: Worried after 1857, the government set up the **Indigo Commission**. It held planters guilty of coercion and declared indigo production **not profitable** for ryots. Ryots were asked to fulfil existing contracts but could refuse future ones. Indigo production collapsed in Bengal; planters shifted to **Bihar**.

steps.title: Champaran (1917)
steps.body: In **1917** a peasant from Bihar persuaded **Mahatma Gandhi** to visit **Champaran** to see the plight of indigo cultivators. Gandhi's visit marked the beginning of the **Champaran movement** against indigo planters — an early milestone in his Indian campaigns.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did the government respond quickly in 1859–60? → It feared another rebellion soon after 1857.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating the Blue Rebellion to 1857.
