- Thinking the Indigo Commission favoured planters.

activity.prompt: Order the indigo story

quiz.why: The Blue Rebellion began in March 1859 in Bengal, when ryots refused to grow indigo. 1857 was the Revolt and 1917 Champaran.
Gomasthas were agents of indigo planters, who worked for them in the villages. They were not peasant leaders, judges or zamindars.

quiz.q: The Indigo Commission said indigo production was:
quiz.why: The Indigo Commission found that indigo production was not profitable for ryots. It told the ryots they need not accept contracts.
After the 1860 revolt, planters shifted indigo production to Bihar. Bengal's indigo trade then declined.
Gandhi started the 1917 indigo campaign in Champaran, Bihar. Dandi was linked to the salt march.

questions.q: Permanent Settlement was introduced by:
questions.why: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793. Munro and Mackenzie are linked to ryotwari and mahalwari.

questions.q: Ryot means:
questions.why: A ryot is a peasant or cultivator. A landlord is a zamindar and a merchant is a trader.

questions.q: Mahal means:
questions.why: Mahal means a village or an estate, the unit for which revenue was settled in the Mahalwari system. It is not a palace.

questions.q: The 1770 famine struck:
questions.why: The terrible famine of 1770 struck Bengal and killed about a third of its people. It did not strike Madras, Punjab or Gujarat.

questions.q: Ryotwari system was developed by:
questions.why: Thomas Munro developed the ryotwari system, first used in South India. Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement.

questions.q: Assertion: The Company could not increase its income in Bengal after 1793 despite rising prices. Reason: Revenue was permanently fixed.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. After 1793 the revenue was permanently fixed, so the Company could not claim more even when prices and incomes rose.

questions.q: Indigo was in demand in Europe because:
options: It gave a rich blue colour
questions.why: Indigo was in demand in Europe because it gave a rich blue dye. It was not food, medicine or fuel.

questions.q: Under nij cultivation:
options: Planters cultivated land they directly controlled
questions.why: In nij cultivation, planters grew indigo on land they directly controlled, using hired labour. In the ryoti system, ryots signed sattas.

questions.q: Blue Rebellion took place in:
questions.why: The Blue Rebellion took place in Bengal in 1859, when ryots refused to grow indigo. The 1857 revolt was a different event.

questions.q: The Indigo Commission was set up because:
options: The government feared another rebellion after 1857
questions.why: The Indigo Commission was set up because the government feared another rebellion like that of 1857. It was not asked for by planters.

questions.q: Case: A village's total revenue is assessed field by field, fixed for the village, and revised after some years; the headman collects it. Which system?
questions.why: In the Mahalwari system, revenue was assessed for the village (mahal) and the headman collected it, with revisions after some years. Permanent Settlement had a fixed amount and ryotwari was with the cultivator.

questions.q: Why did zamindars rarely invest in land under the Permanent Settlement?
options: Revenue was high and they risked losing estates; leasing out was easier
questions.why: Under the Permanent Settlement, revenue was high and zamindars who failed to pay lost their estates. So they preferred to lease out land rather than invest in it.

questions.q: Assertion: Ryots were happy with the advance system of indigo. Reason: They got cash loans at low interest.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because ryots were not happy with the advance system. The reason is true, as cash loans came at low interest at first, but they trapped ryots in debt and forced them to grow indigo.

questions.q: Which crop–region pair was promoted by the colonial state?
questions.why: The colonial state promoted tea in Assam as an export crop. The other pairs do not match the crop to its region.

questions.q: Why was nij cultivation limited to under 25% of indigo land?
options: Hard to get large compact fertile lands and labour, high cost of ploughs/bullocks
questions.why: Nij cultivation needed large, compact, fertile land and many labourers, and it was costly to keep ploughs and bullocks. So it stayed below 25 per cent of the indigo area.

questions.q: Case: A peasant in 1859 hears 'the Queen has declared indigo need not be sown'. This rumour arose from:
options: A Barasat magistrate's notice that ryots need not accept contracts
questions.why: A magistrate at Barasat told ryots they need not accept indigo contracts. News spread that the Queen had said so, which helped fuel the rebellion.

courses.title: History Ch 4 · Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age
courses.summary: How tribal groups lived (jhum cultivation, hunting–gathering, herding, settled farming), how colonial rule changed their lives through forest laws, trade and work, and the movement led by Birsa Munda.
outcomes: Learners can describe the different ways tribal groups lived
Learners can explain how colonial forest laws and trade affected tribal life
Learners can explain who the 'dikus' were and why tribals resented them
Learners can narrate Birsa Munda's movement and its significance

lessons.title: How tribal groups lived

scenes.text: In the North-East, families clear small forest patches and burn vegetation for jhum.
In Orissa, the Khonds hunt and gather forest produce.
In the hills, Gaddis drive sheep from pasture to pasture.

steps.title: Jhum (shifting) cultivation
steps.body: Practised on small patches, mostly in forests. Cultivators cut tree tops to let sunlight in and **burnt the vegetation** to clear land; the ash (containing potash) fertilised the soil. They used axes and hoes, scattered seeds rather than ploughing. After harvest they **moved to another field**; the old field was left fallow to recover. Common in the hilly and forested tracts of **north-east and central India**.

steps.title: Hunters, gatherers, herders, settled farmers
steps.body:
- **Hunter-gatherers:** e.g. **Khonds** of Orissa hunted collectively and gathered fruits and roots; they used forest shrubs and herbs for medicine and sold forest produce in local markets. They exchanged goods for rice and other items with local weavers and potters.
- **Herders:** **Van Gujjars** (Punjab hills) and **Labadis** (Andhra Pradesh) — cattle; **Gaddis** (Kulu) — sheep; **Bakarwals** (Kashmir) — goats. They moved with seasons.
- **Settled cultivators:** some, like the **Mundas** of Chottanagpur, settled and ploughed land; land belonged to the clan as a whole. Over time, chiefs became landlords and differences grew within society.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did jhum cultivators move from field to field? → To let used soil regain fertility; they burnt new patches for ash-rich soil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all tribal people lived the same way.
- Thinking jhum used ploughs.

activity.prompt: Match the group to its way of life
pairs: Cattle herders of the Punjab hills

quiz.why: Jhum is also called shifting cultivation, because the fields are moved to new patches. Terrace and irrigated farming stay on fixed fields.
The ash from burnt vegetation adds potash to the soil, which makes it fertile for the crop. It does not add plastic or salt in useful amounts.
The Bakarwals of Kashmir herded goats, moving with them between pastures. Cattle, camels and elephants are not their animals.
The Khonds lived in the forests of Orissa and were hunters and gatherers. They were not from Kashmir, Kerala or Punjab.

quiz.q: Among Mundas, land originally belonged to:
quiz.why: Among the Mundas, land originally belonged to the clan as a whole. It was not owned by a king, temples or the British.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Colonial rule and tribal life

scenes.text: New laws declare forests state property.
Jhum is banned; tribals can't cut trees or graze freely.
'The forest was ours. Now we need permission to enter it?'

steps.title: Chiefs and settlement
steps.body: Under British rule, tribal chiefs lost much of their administrative power and had to follow British laws and pay tribute. The British wanted tribals to **settle** as peasant cultivators — easier to control and tax. This was hard: in areas with little water and dry soil, settled ploughing was not productive; jhum cultivators resisted. Eventually the British allowed jhum in small patches.

steps.title: Forest laws
steps.body: The British declared forests **state property**. Some were **Reserved Forests** producing timber; people could not move freely, practise jhum, collect fruits or hunt. Forced to move, many became workers. To get labour for the forest department, the British set up **forest villages** where jhum cultivators could live if they worked for the department for free (cutting trees, preventing fires). Many groups rebelled — e.g. the **Songram Sangma (1906)** in Assam and the **forest satyagraha** of the 1930s in the Central Provinces.

steps.title: Trade and work
steps.body: Traders and moneylenders came more often to forests, offering cash loans and wanting forest produce. Example: **silk** — the Company encouraged silk production in **Hazaribagh** (Jharkhand), where **Santhals** reared cocoons; traders bought cocoons cheaply and made huge profits (the growers got a tiny share). Many tribals were recruited to work in **tea plantations of Assam** and in **coal mines** of Jharkhand, on very low wages, and were often not allowed to return home.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did the British want tribals to settle? → Settled peasants were easier to control and administer and provided regular revenue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking forest villages offered free land with no conditions — residents had to work free for the forest department.
- Thinking tribals benefited from silk trade profits — middlemen took most.

statements.s: British forest laws declared forests state property.
Jhum cultivators were happy to become settled ploughmen everywhere.
Forest villages required people to work for the forest department.
Santhal cocoon-rearers got most of the silk profits.
Tribals were recruited to work in Assam's tea plantations.

options: Jhum, hunting and collection of produce
quiz.why: Reserved forests restricted jhum cultivation, hunting and the collection of forest produce. This hurt the tribals' way of life.

quiz.q: Forest villages were set up to:
options: Get labour for the forest department
quiz.why: Forest villages were set up to give the forest department a regular supply of labour. The villagers had to work for it.

quiz.q: Silk cocoons were reared by Santhals in:
quiz.why: Santhals reared silk cocoons in Hazaribagh, in present Jharkhand. The traders paid them very little for them.

quiz.q: A tribal revolt in Assam in 1906:
quiz.why: The 1906 revolt in Assam against forest laws was led by Songram Sangma. The Blue Rebellion was in Bengal and Ulgulan was Birsa's.

quiz.q: Why did the British want settled cultivators?
quiz.why: Settled cultivators are easier to control and tax than people who keep moving. This is why the British wanted tribals to settle.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Dikus and tribal revolts

scenes.text: Moneylenders charge huge interest; traders buy forest goods cheaply.
Missionaries criticise tribal customs; British officers impose laws.
Tribals call these outsiders 'dikus' — and blame them for their misery.

steps.title: Who were the dikus?
steps.body: **Dikus** were **outsiders** — traders, moneylenders, missionaries, Hindu landlords and the British — whom tribal people saw as the cause of their misery and loss of land and freedom.

steps.title: A chain of revolts
steps.body: Tribal groups in different parts of the country rebelled against changes in laws, restrictions, new taxes and exploitation by traders and moneylenders: the **Kols (1831–32)**, the **Santhals (1855)**, the **Bastar rebellion in central India (1910)**, and the **Warli revolt in Maharashtra (1940)**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did tribals see missionaries as dikus? → Missionaries criticised their traditional culture and beliefs, even though some offered education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'diku' meant only the British.
- Mixing the Santhal (1855) and Kol (1831–32) revolts.

activity.prompt: Order the tribal revolts

quiz.why: Dikus were outsiders, such as moneylenders and traders, whom tribals saw as exploiters. They were not gods or tribal chiefs.
The Santhal rebellion was in 1855, against moneylenders and the British. 1831 was the Kol revolt and 1940 the Warli revolt.
The Bastar rebellion took place in Central India in 1910, over forest rules. Assam 1906 was the Songram Sangma revolt.
The Warli revolt of 1940 took place in Maharashtra. It was against the exploitation of tribals by moneylenders and landlords.
A moneylender from outside was seen as a diku, an exploiter of tribals. A tribal elder, a jhum field and a forest are not outsiders.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Birsa Munda and the vision of a golden age

scenes.text: Born in the mid-1870s, Birsa grows up among Munda families in Chottanagpur.
Thousands gather to hear him speak of a golden age when Mundas lived free and the land was theirs.
The British arrest him; he dies in jail in 1900. His memory lives on.

steps.title: Birsa's life
steps.body: **Birsa Munda** was born in the **mid-1870s** into a poor family. He grew up hearing songs and stories of Munda uprisings. He went to a missionary school and spent time with a Vaishnav preacher. Around **1895**, he urged Mundas to give up drinking liquor, clean their villages and stop believing in witchcraft and sorcery. He also opposed missionaries and Hindu landlords.

steps.title: The movement
steps.body: Birsa spoke of a **golden age (satyug)** in the past when Mundas lived a good life, built embankments, tapped natural springs, planted trees and orchards and practised cultivation — and did not kill their brethren. He wanted to drive out the missionaries, moneylenders, Hindu landlords and the government, and set up a **Munda Raj** with Birsa at its head. The British were alarmed and arrested him in **1895**, convicting him on charges of rioting; he was jailed for two years. Released in **1897**, he toured villages; his followers attacked symbols of diku and European power (police stations, churches, property of moneylenders and zamindars), raising white flags. In **1900** Birsa died of cholera in jail and the movement faded.

steps.title: Significance
steps.body:
- It forced the colonial government to introduce laws so that tribals' land **could not easily be taken over by dikus** (the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act, 1908**).
- It showed that tribal people could protest against injustice and express anger against colonial rule in their own way.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did Birsa's idea of a golden age attract people? → It promised the return of land rights and dignity lost to dikus and colonial laws.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Birsa died in battle (he died of cholera in jail, 1900).
- Thinking the movement achieved nothing — it led to tenancy laws.

activity.prompt: Order Birsa Munda's story
items: Born in the mid-1870s in a Munda family
Studies at a missionary school; meets a Vaishnav preacher
Around 1895 starts preaching reform and a golden age
Arrested in 1895 and jailed
Released in 1897; movement grows
Dies of cholera in jail in 1900
Chotanagpur Tenancy Act passed in 1908

quiz.why: Birsa Munda died in 1900 in jail, of cholera. 1895 was when he started his movement and 1947 is independence.

options: Give up liquor and superstitions; clean villages
quiz.why: Birsa asked the Mundas to give up liquor, stop believing in superstitions and keep their villages clean. He aimed to reform their society.

options: White flags as a symbol of Birsa Raj
quiz.why: Birsa's followers raised a white flag, a symbol of Birsa Raj. It showed their wish to rule themselves.
The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908 was a result of the Munda movement, as it protected tribal land. The other options are unrelated.

options: Missionaries, moneylenders, Hindu landlords and the government
quiz.why: Birsa wanted to drive out missionaries, moneylenders, Hindu landlords and the government. He saw them as dikus who took tribal land.

questions.q: Jhum cultivation is:
questions.why: Jhum is shifting cultivation: fields are burnt and sown, then moved to new patches. It is not terrace, irrigated or plantation farming.

questions.q: Birsa Munda belonged to the:
questions.why: Birsa Munda belonged to the Munda tribe of the Chottanagpur region. The Khonds, Santhals and Gaddis are other communities.

questions.q: Dikus were:
questions.why: Dikus were outsiders who exploited the tribals, such as moneylenders and landlords. They were not crops or tribal priests.

questions.q: Gaddis were:
questions.why: The Gaddis were shepherds of Kulu in the Himalaya, who grazed sheep. They were not farmers of Bengal or hunters of Orissa.

questions.q: Birsa Munda died in:
questions.why: Birsa died in jail in 1900. 1895 was when his movement began, and 1908 the Tenancy Act.

questions.q: Assertion: Tribals resented colonial forest laws. Reason: The laws stopped them from practising jhum and collecting forest produce.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Forest laws banned jhum and the collection of produce, so tribals lost their living and resented them.

questions.q: Santhals reared silk cocoons in:
questions.why: Santhals reared silk cocoons in Hazaribagh, now in Jharkhand. Kulu, Madras and Kashmir are not linked to this.

questions.q: Which revolt is correctly dated?
questions.why: The Santhal rebellion is correctly dated 1855. Bastar was 1910, Kol 1831 and Warli 1940, so the other pairs have wrong dates.

questions.q: Forest villages were:
options: Settlements where people had to work free for the forest department
questions.why: Forest villages were settlements where people were made to work for the forest department, often without pay, in return for a little land.

questions.q: Why did traders profit from Santhal silk?
options: They bought cocoons cheaply and sold silk at high prices
questions.why: Traders bought silk cocoons from Santhals at low prices and sold silk at high prices, keeping the profit. The Santhals got very little.

questions.q: Case: A group clears a forest patch, burns it, sows seeds in the ash without ploughing, and moves after harvest. Which practice?
questions.why: Clearing a patch, burning it and sowing in the ash without ploughing, then moving on, is jhum (shifting) cultivation. Nij and ryotwari relate to indigo and revenue.

questions.q: The Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) aimed to:
options: Protect tribal land from being taken over by dikus
questions.why: The Act aimed to protect the land of tribals from being taken over by dikus. It followed Birsa's movement.

questions.q: Assertion: Birsa's movement had no impact. Reason: It forced the government to pass laws to protect tribal land.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because Birsa's movement did matter. The reason is true: it pushed the government to pass laws like the Tenancy Act to protect tribal land.

questions.q: Why did the British find it hard to make jhum cultivators settle?
options: Lack of water and dry soil made ploughing unproductive, and tribals resisted
questions.why: Jhum cultivators lived where ploughing was unproductive because of dry soil and lack of water, and they resisted settling. So the British found it hard to make them settle.

questions.q: Birsa's 'golden age' referred to:
options: A past when Mundas lived free and well on their land
questions.why: Birsa's golden age (Satyug) was a past in which the Mundas lived freely and well on their land, without dikus. It was not a future British India.

questions.q: Case: Tribal workers recruited for Assam tea gardens were often not allowed to return home and got very low wages. This shows:
options: Exploitation of tribal labour under colonial rule
questions.why: Workers taken to Assam tea gardens were poorly paid and often not allowed to go home. This shows exploitation of tribal labour under colonial rule.

courses.title: History Ch 5 · When People Rebel: 1857 and After
courses.summary: Why nawabs, peasants and sepoys grew discontented with Company rule, how the 1857 rebellion began at Meerut and spread, its leaders, how the British suppressed it, and the major changes after 1858.
outcomes: Learners can explain the political, economic, social and military causes of 1857
Learners can narrate how the revolt began and spread and name its leaders
Learners can describe how the British regained control
Learners can list the changes introduced after 1858

lessons.title: Causes: nawabs, peasants and sepoys

story.title: A Mughal name removed from coins

scenes.text: From 1835 the Company's coins no longer carry the Mughal emperor's name.
In 1856 Governor-General Canning announces Bahadur Shah Zafar will be the last Mughal king.
Nawabs, peasants and sepoys all feel their world is being taken away.

steps.title: Nawabs and rulers lose power
steps.body:
From the mid-18th century, nawabs and rajas lost authority and honour. Residents were stationed at their courts; their armies were disbanded; revenues and territories were taken. Many kingdoms were annexed (Doctrine of Lapse; **Awadh 1856**). Rulers such as **Rani Lakshmibai** of Jhansi (who wanted her adopted son recognised) and **Nana Saheb** (adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, who pleaded for his father's pension) were refused.

The Company also planned to end the Mughal dynasty: the emperor's name was removed from coins (1835), and in 1849 Dalhousie announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar's death the family would be moved out of the Red Fort. In **1856** **Lord Canning** decided Bahadur Shah Zafar would be the **last Mughal king**.

steps.title: Peasants and sepoys
steps.body:
- **Peasants and zamindars:** high taxes and rigid collection; many lost lands to moneylenders when they couldn't repay loans.
- **Sepoys:** unhappy about pay, allowances and conditions; some rules violated their religious sensibilities. In **1824** sepoys refused to go to Burma by sea (crossing the sea was believed by many to mean loss of caste). In **1856** a new law said every new recruit must agree to serve **overseas** if required. Sepoys were also affected by peasants' hardship — most came from peasant families.

steps.title: Responses to reforms
steps.body: The British passed laws to stop **sati** (1829) and encourage **widow remarriage** (1856); English education was promoted. After **1830** Christian missionaries could function freely and own land and property. In **1850** a new law made conversion to Christianity easier — an Indian who converted could inherit ancestral property. Many Indians began to feel the British were destroying their religion, social customs and traditional way of life.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did annexation of Awadh especially anger sepoys? → Many sepoys came from Awadh; their families lost status and livelihoods.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the greased cartridges were the only cause — they were the spark, not the whole fire.
- Confusing Canning (1856 decision) with Dalhousie (annexations).

activity.prompt: Political or social/religious cause?

quiz.q: Bahadur Shah Zafar was declared the last Mughal king by:
quiz.why: Lord Canning declared in 1856 that Bahadur Shah Zafar would be the last Mughal king, and the family would move out of the Red Fort. This angered many.

quiz.q: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of:
quiz.why: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II. The Company refused to give him the Peshwa's pension.

options: They had to agree to serve overseas
quiz.why: In 1856 a law said that new sepoys had to agree to serve overseas if needed. Many believed crossing the sea meant loss of caste.
Awadh was annexed in 1856, on the claim of misgovernment. The revolt began only in 1857.

quiz.q: The 1850 law made it easier to:
options: Convert to Christianity and still inherit property
quiz.why: The 1850 law allowed an Indian who converted to Christianity to still inherit ancestral property. This increased fears about conversion.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: From Meerut to Delhi: the revolt spreads

scenes.text: Rumours spread that the new Enfield rifle cartridges are greased with fat of cows and pigs.
On 29 March 1857, Mangal Pandey attacks his officers at Barrackpore; he is hanged.
On 10 May, sepoys at Meerut rise, free their comrades and ride to Delhi.

steps.title: The spark
steps.body: Sepoys were ordered to bite off cartridges of the new **Enfield rifles**, rumoured to be coated with **fat of cows and pigs** — offensive to both Hindus and Muslims. On **29 March 1857**, young soldier **Mangal Pandey** was hanged for attacking his officers at **Barrackpore**. Some sepoys at **Meerut** refused to do army drill with the new cartridges; 85 were dismissed and jailed for ten years.

steps.title: Meerut to Delhi
steps.body: On **10 May 1857** soldiers at Meerut marched to the jail and released the imprisoned sepoys, attacked and killed British officers, captured guns and ammunition, and set fire to buildings. They rode to **Delhi** through the night and reached it on **11 May**, asking **Bahadur Shah Zafar** to become their leader. He agreed, and wrote letters to chiefs and rulers of the country to come forward and organise a confederacy of Indian states to fight the British.

steps.title: The rebellion spreads
steps.body: Regiment after regiment mutinied and joined other troops at Delhi, Kanpur and Lucknow. People of towns and villages also rose. Leaders: **Nana Saheb** (Kanpur) proclaimed himself Peshwa; in Lucknow, **Birjis Qadr**, son of the deposed nawab **Wajid Ali Shah**, was proclaimed nawab, and his mother **Begum Hazrat Mahal** took an active part; **Rani Lakshmibai** joined the rebel sepoys and fought with **Tantia Tope**, Nana Saheb's general; in Mandla (MP), **Rani Avantibai Lodhi** of Ramgarh raised an army; **Ahmadullah Shah**, a maulvi from Faizabad, prophesied the end of British rule; **Bakht Khan**, a soldier from Bareilly, led fighters to Delhi; **Kunwar Singh**, an old zamindar of Bihar, joined the rebels and fought for many months.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was Bahadur Shah Zafar's support important? → It gave the rebellion a symbol of legitimacy that could unite people across regions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating Meerut uprising to 29 March (that was Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore).
- Thinking only sepoys joined — peasants, zamindars and town people did too.

activity.prompt: Order the events of 1857

events.text: Rebels reach Delhi; Bahadur Shah accepts leadership

quiz.q: The revolt at Meerut began on:
quiz.why: The revolt at Meerut began on 10 May 1857, when sepoys rose and marched to Delhi. 29 March was the Mangal Pandey incident.

quiz.q: Mangal Pandey was hanged for an attack at:
quiz.why: Mangal Pandey attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was hanged. This was before the revolt at Meerut.
Nana Saheb led the rebels at Kanpur, as the adopted son of the last Peshwa. Kunwar Singh was in Bihar and Bakht Khan in Delhi.

quiz.q: Begum Hazrat Mahal was active in:
quiz.why: Begum Hazrat Mahal was active in Lucknow, in Awadh, and took charge of the rebellion there. Jhansi was Lakshmibai's.
Kunwar Singh was an old zamindar from Bihar, who fought against the British. He was not from Mysore, Faizabad or Bareilly.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: The Company fights back

scenes.text: The Company brings reinforcements from England and new laws to convict rebels.
After months of fighting, Delhi is recaptured in September 1857.
Bahadur Shah is tried and exiled to Rangoon.

steps.title: Suppression
steps.body:
The Company used all its power. Reinforcements came from England; new laws were passed so rebels could be convicted easily. Forces moved into the heart of the revolt.

- **Delhi** was recaptured in **September 1857** after months of fighting. **Bahadur Shah Zafar** was tried in court and sentenced to life imprisonment; his sons were shot before his eyes. He and his wife **Begum Zinat Mahal** were sent to prison in **Rangoon** in October 1858, where he died in **November 1862**.
- **Lucknow** was taken in **March 1858**.
- **Rani Lakshmibai** was defeated and killed in **June 1858**.
- **Tantia Tope** escaped to the jungles of central India and continued guerrilla war with tribal and peasant support; he was captured, tried and killed in **April 1859**.

steps.title: Why it didn't succeed everywhere
steps.body: The British had large resources, better communication (telegraph) and fresh troops; many rulers stayed loyal to the British; the rebellion lacked a single coordinated plan across India. Yet it took the British two years to suppress it, showing its strength. The British also tried to win back loyalty by giving rewards to loyal landholders.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why were rewards given to loyal landholders? → To win back the support of landed elites and divide the rebels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Bahadur Shah died in Delhi (he died in Rangoon, 1862).
- Thinking the revolt ended in 1857 itself.

activity.prompt: Order the suppression

events.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar dies in Rangoon

quiz.q: Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to:
quiz.why: Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon in Burma and died there in 1862. He was not sent to Kabul or London.
The British recaptured Delhi in September 1857, after a long fight. May 1857 was when the rebels took it.
Rani Lakshmibai died fighting in June 1858. She was killed in battle, not in 1862 or 1857.

quiz.q: Tantia Tope fought a guerrilla war in:
quiz.why: Tantia Tope carried on a guerrilla war in the jungles of Central India, helped by tribal and local people. This was far from the Himalayas or Bengal delta.

options: Rebels had no leaders at all
quiz.why: The British had greater resources and fresh reinforcements, so they could keep up the fight. The rebels did not have more guns.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Aftermath: changes after 1858

scenes.text: On 1 November 1858, a proclamation in Queen Victoria's name is read across India.
Power passes from the Company to the British Crown.
The British promise to respect customs — but also reorganise the army to prevent another revolt.

steps.title: Major changes
steps.body:
- **Government of India Act, 1858:** powers of the East India Company transferred to the **British Crown**. A member of the British Cabinet became the **Secretary of State for India**, assisted by a council (India Council).
- The Governor-General was given the title **Viceroy** — a personal representative of the Crown.
- **Ruling chiefs** were assured their territory would never be annexed in future; they could pass on kingdoms to heirs, including **adopted sons** — but they had to acknowledge the British Queen as their Sovereign Paramount.
- **Army:** the proportion of Indian soldiers would be reduced and European soldiers increased; more soldiers would be recruited from among Gurkhas, Sikhs and Pathans.
- **Land and property of Muslims** were confiscated on a large scale; they were treated with suspicion and hostility, as the British believed they were responsible for the rebellion.
- The British decided to **respect the customary religious and social practices** of the people.
- Policies were made to protect **landlords and zamindars** and give them security of rights over their lands.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why recruit more Gurkhas, Sikhs and Pathans after 1857? → The British considered them loyal and wanted fewer soldiers from regions (like Awadh) that had rebelled strongly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Company continued to rule after 1858.
- Confusing the Secretary of State (in Britain) with the Viceroy (in India).

activity.prompt: Match the post-1858 change to its meaning
pairs: Crown takes over from the Company
Cabinet member in Britain responsible for India
More European soldiers; recruitment from Gurkhas, Sikhs, Pathans

quiz.q: After 1858 India was governed directly by:
quiz.why: After 1858 the British Crown governed India directly, after the Act of 1858 ended Company rule. The Mughals and Marathas had no power then.
The Governor-General was given the title Viceroy, meaning the personal representative of the Crown. Diwan, Peshwa and Nawab are Indian titles.

quiz.q: Ruling chiefs could now pass their kingdoms to:
quiz.why: After 1858 the British assured Indian rulers that their kingdoms would not be annexed and that adopted sons could succeed them. This ended the Doctrine of Lapse.

quiz.q: The proportion of Indian soldiers in the army was:
quiz.why: After 1857 the British reduced the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army and raised that of Europeans. They no longer trusted the sepoys fully.

quiz.q: Queen Victoria's proclamation was announced on:
quiz.why: Queen Victoria's proclamation was announced on 1 November 1858. 15 August 1947 is independence and 10 May 1857 the Meerut revolt.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

questions.q: The 1857 revolt began at:
questions.why: The revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May, when sepoys rebelled. They then marched to Delhi.

questions.q: Rebels proclaimed as their leader:
questions.why: The rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar, the Mughal emperor, as their leader. He gave the revolt a symbolic leader.

questions.q: Rani Lakshmibai ruled:
questions.why: Rani Lakshmibai was the queen of Jhansi. Kittur's queen was Channamma.

questions.q: After 1858, India was ruled by:
questions.why: After 1858 the British Crown took over the rule of India from the Company. The Peshwa and Mughals had lost power.

questions.q: Mangal Pandey was hanged in 1857 for an incident at:
questions.why: Mangal Pandey attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 and was hanged. Meerut and Kanpur saw the later revolt.

questions.q: Rumours about Enfield cartridges claimed they were greased with:
questions.why: The rumour said the Enfield rifle cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs. Cow fat offended Hindus and pig fat offended Muslims.

questions.q: Assertion: Many sepoys were angered by the 1856 rule on overseas service. Reason: Crossing the sea was believed by many to mean loss of caste.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Many Indians believed that crossing the sea meant loss of caste, so the rule on overseas service angered sepoys.

questions.q: Who led the rebels at Lucknow along with Birjis Qadr?
questions.why: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the rebels at Lucknow, along with her son Birjis Qadr. The others were not leaders there.

questions.q: Tantia Tope was a general of:
questions.why: Tantia Tope was a general of Nana Saheb at Kanpur. He later continued the fight in Central India.

questions.q: Which was NOT a change after 1858?
questions.why: After 1858 the Doctrine of Lapse was ended, not strengthened, and adopted heirs were allowed. The Viceroy title and a Secretary of State for India were new.

questions.q: Case: An old zamindar from Bihar who fought the British for months in 1857–58. Who?
questions.why: Kunwar Singh was an old zamindar from Bihar who fought the British for months. Nana Saheb was from Kanpur and Bakht Khan from Delhi.

questions.q: Order of events:
questions.why: The correct order is Barrackpore (29 March) → Meerut (10 May) → Delhi (May) → Delhi recaptured (September 1857). The others reverse this order.

questions.q: Why did the British treat Muslims with suspicion after 1857?
options: They believed Muslims were largely responsible for the rebellion
questions.why: After 1857 the British saw Muslims as largely responsible for the rebellion, so they regarded them with suspicion and distrust.

questions.q: Assertion: The 1857 revolt was only a mutiny of soldiers. Reason: Peasants, zamindars, rulers and townspeople also joined in many regions.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because the revolt was far more than a soldiers' mutiny. The reason is true: peasants, zamindars, rulers and townspeople joined in many regions, making it a wider rebellion.

questions.q: Bahadur Shah Zafar died in:
questions.why: Bahadur Shah Zafar died in 1862 in Rangoon, in exile. He was not killed in Delhi or London.

questions.q: Why was Bahadur Shah's letter to rulers significant?
options: It called for a confederacy of Indian states against the British
questions.why: Bahadur Shah's letter called on rulers to form a confederacy of Indian states to fight the British. This showed the revolt's wider unity.

questions.q: Case: After 1858 a ruler without a biological son adopts an heir. Unlike before, the kingdom:
options: Can pass to the adopted son, but the ruler must accept the Queen as Sovereign Paramount
questions.why: After 1858 the kingdom could pass to an adopted son, as the Doctrine of Lapse was ended. The ruler had to accept the Queen as the Sovereign Paramount.

courses.title: History · Civilising the "Native", Educating the Nation
courses.summary: How the British debated what Indians should learn — Orientalists versus Anglicists, Macaulay's Minute and Wood's Despatch — what happened to local pathshalas, and how Indians like Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore imagined a national education.
outcomes: Learners can compare Orientalist and Anglicist views of education
Learners can explain Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Wood's Despatch (1854)
Learners can describe the pathshala system and how it changed after 1854
Learners can compare Gandhi's and Tagore's ideas of education

lessons.title: Orientalists: learning from the East

scenes.text: William Jones, a judge, arrives in Calcutta in 1783.
He studies Sanskrit and translates ancient texts.
In 1784 he helps found the Asiatic Society of Bengal.

steps.title: William Jones and the Orientalists
steps.body: **William Jones** came to Calcutta in **1783** as a junior judge of the Supreme Court set up by the Company. A linguist, he knew Greek, Latin, French, English, Arabic and Persian, and learned Sanskrit. With **Henry Thomas Colebrooke** and **Nathaniel Halhed** he set up the **Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784)** and started the journal *Asiatick Researches*. They shared a deep respect for ancient Indian culture — they were **Orientalists** (scholars with knowledge of the language and culture of Asia).

steps.title: Their ideas and institutions
steps.body: Orientalists believed British rulers should promote Indian rather than Western learning, to win Indians' hearts and to understand the laws and customs of the land. Institutions: the **madrasa in Calcutta (1781)** to promote Arabic, Persian and Islamic law; the **Hindu College in Benaras (1791)** to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts useful for administration.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did some British officials support Indian learning? → They believed it would help them understand the people they ruled and make Indians respect their rulers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Orientalists were Indian scholars (they were mostly British).
- Mixing up Calcutta Madrasa (1781) and Benaras Hindu College (1791).

activity.prompt: Order the Orientalist milestones

events.text: Hindu College set up in Benaras

quiz.q: William Jones arrived in Calcutta in:
quiz.why: William Jones arrived in Calcutta in 1783 as a judge at the Supreme Court. He was fond of the study of ancient Indian culture.

quiz.q: Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in:
quiz.why: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 by William Jones, Henry Colebrooke and Nathaniel Halhed. It studied Indian languages and texts.
Orientalists respected ancient Indian and Asian learning and wanted to promote it. Anglicists favoured Western knowledge.
The Calcutta madrasa was set up in 1781 to promote the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law. Physics and English literature were not its aim.

quiz.q: Hindu College in Benaras was set up in:
quiz.why: The Hindu College in Benaras was set up in 1791 to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts. 1857 and 1916 are far from this date.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Anglicists: Macaulay and Wood's Despatch

story.title: 'One shelf of a good European library…'

scenes.text: In 1835, Thomas Babington Macaulay dismisses Eastern learning in his Minute.
The English Education Act makes English the medium for higher education.
In 1854 Wood's Despatch links English education to jobs and trade.

steps.title: Criticism of Orientalism
steps.body: From the early 19th century many officials criticised Orientalist ideas. **James Mill** attacked them, arguing education should be practical and teach Western science. **Thomas Babington Macaulay** saw India as uncivilised and argued in his **Minute (1835)** that knowledge of English would allow Indians to read some of the finest literature the world had produced and to understand Western science and philosophy.

steps.title: English Education Act (1835)
steps.body: Following Macaulay's minute, the **English Education Act of 1835** was introduced: English became the medium of instruction for higher education, and support to Oriental institutions like the Calcutta Madrasa and Benaras Sanskrit College was stopped (they were seen as 'temples of darkness'). English textbooks began to be produced for schools.

steps.title: Wood's Despatch (1854)
steps.body: In **1854**, the Court of Directors of the Company in London sent an educational despatch, issued by **Charles Wood**, President of the Board of Control. It emphasised the **practical benefits of European learning**: it would make Indians appreciate British goods (expanding trade), improve their moral character (making them truthful and honest), and supply civil servants. Results: education departments were set up; steps were taken to set up a system of university education — **universities in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (1857)**; changes in school education. Missionaries also set up schools; after 1857 the British were cautious about direct religious teaching.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did Wood's Despatch link education to trade? → Educated Indians would develop tastes for British goods and increase demand for them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Macaulay's Minute (1835) with Wood's Despatch (1854).
- Thinking Anglicists wanted to promote Sanskrit.

activity.prompt: Match the person/document to its idea
pairs: English to be taught; Eastern learning dismissed
English the medium for higher education
Universities in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay
Education should be practical and teach Western science

quiz.why: Macaulay wrote his Minute on Indian education in 1835, urging English education. 1854 is Wood's Despatch and 1857 the Revolt.
Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854 by Charles Wood of the Company's Board of Control. It favoured European learning.

quiz.q: Universities were set up in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay in:
quiz.why: Following Wood's Despatch, the universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay were set up in 1857. 1835 was Macaulay's Minute.
Anglicists wanted English education and Western knowledge taught in India. Orientalists wanted Sanskrit and Persian learning.

quiz.q: Wood's Despatch claimed European learning would:
options: Improve moral character and expand trade
quiz.why: Wood's Despatch said European learning would improve people's moral character and also expand trade, as Indians would want British goods. It did not aim to end British rule.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: Pathshalas and the local school system

scenes.text: In the 1830s, William Adam visits villages of Bengal and Bihar.
He finds over 1 lakh pathshalas with more than 20 lakh children.
Classes meet under trees, in a guru's home or temple corner.

steps.title: William Adam's report
steps.body: In the 1830s **William Adam**, a Scottish missionary, toured districts of **Bengal and Bihar** at the Company's request to report on vernacular schools. He found **over 1 lakh pathshalas** with **more than 20 lakh children**. They were small, set up by wealthy people or the community, or started by a guru. The system was **flexible**: no fixed fees, no printed books, no separate building, no benches or chairs, no blackboards, no separate classes or attendance registers, no annual exams or regular timetable. Classes were held under a banyan tree, in a corner of a shop or temple, or at the guru's home. Fees depended on parents' income. Teaching was oral; the guru decided what to teach according to each student's needs. Classes were not held during harvest time, when rural children worked in fields.

steps.title: Changes after 1854
steps.body: The Company decided to improve vernacular education by introducing order and rules. It appointed **government pandits** to visit pathshalas and improve teaching; each guru had to submit periodic reports and teach according to a regular timetable; teaching was based on **textbooks**, and learning was tested through annual examinations. Students had to pay regular fees, attend regularly, sit on fixed seats and obey rules of discipline. Pathshalas that accepted the new rules got government grants; those that wished to stay independent got none.

steps.title: Effect on the poor
steps.body: The new rules — regular attendance even during harvest — hurt poor peasant children. Inability to attend was seen as indiscipline. Many of them could no longer study.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was the old pathshala better suited to poor families? → Flexible fees and timings, holidays at harvest time — children could work and study.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking pathshalas had printed textbooks and exams before 1854.
- Thinking the new system helped all children equally.

activity.prompt: Old pathshala or after 1854?

quiz.why: William Adam toured the schools of Bengal and Bihar in the 1830s and reported on them. He did not tour Madras, Punjab or Bombay.
Adam found over one lakh pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar, which showed how widespread local schools were. They were not just a hundred or so.

quiz.q: In old pathshalas, teaching was mostly:
quiz.why: In the old pathshalas, teaching was mostly oral, as the guru taught without printed textbooks. He decided what to teach.

quiz.q: After 1854 pathshalas that accepted rules received:
quiz.why: After 1854 the Company gave grants to pathshalas that accepted its rules and kept to a timetable. Those that did not were left without it.

quiz.q: New rules hurt poor children because:
options: Regular attendance was required even during harvest
quiz.why: The new rules required regular attendance, even at harvest time when poor children had to work in the fields. So many could not keep up.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

lessons.title: National education: Gandhi and Tagore

scenes.text: In 1901 Rabindranath Tagore starts a school in a rural setting at Santiniketan.
Mahatma Gandhi argues schools should teach crafts and build self-respect.
Both want education to free Indian minds.

steps.title: The agenda for national education
steps.body: By the mid-19th century, many Indians felt Western education would help modernise India. Others reacted against it. They argued that colonial education created a sense of inferiority, made Indians see Western civilisation as superior and destroyed pride in their own culture.

steps.title: Mahatma Gandhi
steps.body: Gandhi argued that colonial education **enslaved** Indians and made them admire British rule. He wanted an education that could help Indians **recover their sense of dignity and self-respect**. During the national movement he urged students to leave British institutions. He believed education should be in **Indian languages**, and that it should develop a person's mind and soul — not just literacy. He emphasised learning through **hands-on work and crafts**, which would develop mind and the capacity to understand.

steps.title: Rabindranath Tagore
steps.body: Tagore started the **Santiniketan** school in **1901**. As a child he hated school, which he found oppressive. He felt childhood should be a time of **self-learning**, outside a rigid, restricting discipline; teachers had to be imaginative, understand the child and help develop curiosity. Santiniketan was set in a rural setting, in harmony with **nature**, where children could cultivate natural creativity. Unlike Gandhi, Tagore wanted to combine elements of modern Western civilisation (science and technology) with what was best in Indian tradition, and emphasised art, music and dance as well.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How did Gandhi and Tagore differ? → Gandhi was highly critical of Western civilisation and its worship of machines; Tagore wanted to combine the best of Western science with Indian tradition. Both rejected rote, colonial-style schooling.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Tagore founded Santiniketan in 1857.
- Thinking Gandhi wanted English as the main medium.

activity.prompt: Gandhi's idea, Tagore's idea, or both?

items.text: Learning through crafts and hands-on work
School in harmony with nature at Santiniketan
Combine Western science with Indian tradition
Colonial education created a sense of inferiority

quiz.why: Rabindranath Tagore started Santiniketan in 1901. It was set up as an alternative to colonial schools.
Gandhi believed colonial education enslaved Indians and created a sense of inferiority. He did not think it was perfect.

quiz.q: Tagore felt childhood should be a time of:
quiz.why: Tagore believed childhood should be a time of self-learning, creativity and freedom. He opposed rigid, strict schooling.
Gandhi emphasised learning through crafts and hands-on work, which develops mind and soul. He did not rely on books or English alone.

quiz.q: Who wanted to combine Western science with Indian tradition?
quiz.why: Tagore wanted to combine what was best in Western science with Indian tradition. Macaulay, Wood and Mill favoured Western ideas.

sources: NCERT Class 8 History — Our Pasts III (topic)

questions.q: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in:
questions.why: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 by William Jones. 1835 is Macaulay's Minute and 1854 Wood's Despatch.

questions.q: Macaulay's Minute was in:
questions.why: Macaulay's Minute, favouring English education, was written in 1835. 1854 is Wood's Despatch.

questions.q: Santiniketan was founded by:
questions.why: Rabindranath Tagore founded Santiniketan in 1901. Macaulay and Jones lived in other times, and Gandhi's ideas were different.

questions.q: William Adam reported on schools in:
questions.why: William Adam reported on the schools of Bengal and Bihar in the 1830s. His report described the many local pathshalas.

questions.q: Wood's Despatch was issued in:
questions.why: Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854 by Charles Wood. 1835 was Macaulay's Minute.

questions.q: Assertion: Orientalists supported Indian learning. Reason: They believed it would help understand Indian laws and win Indians' respect.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Orientalists thought knowing Indian learning would help them understand Indian laws and win the respect of Indians.

questions.q: Which was an Orientalist institution?
questions.why: The Hindu College at Benaras (1791) was an Orientalist institution that promoted Sanskrit learning. The English Education Act and Wood's Despatch were Anglicist, and Bombay University is Western.

questions.q: Anglicists argued that:
options: English and Western sciences should be taught
questions.why: Anglicists argued that English and Western sciences should be taught in India. Orientalists supported Sanskrit and Persian.

questions.q: Old pathshalas had:
options: Flexible fees and no fixed timetable
questions.why: Old pathshalas were flexible, with fees according to means and no fixed timetable. There were no printed textbooks, benches or annual exams.

questions.q: Case: A guru in 1860 must follow a timetable, use textbooks and submit reports to get a grant. This reflects:
questions.why: A guru who had to keep a timetable, use textbooks and submit reports to get a grant was following the reforms after Wood's Despatch of 1854. Earlier pathshalas were far more flexible.

questions.q: Why did Wood's Despatch favour European learning?
options: It would expand trade and supply honest civil servants
It wanted to end British rule
questions.why: Wood's Despatch said European learning would expand trade and give the Company honest, trained civil servants. It did not aim to end British rule or promote Sanskrit.

questions.q: Assertion: Gandhi wanted education only to teach reading and writing. Reason: Gandhi believed education should develop mind and soul through crafts and work.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false, because Gandhi wanted much more than reading and writing. The reason is true: he wanted education to develop mind and soul through crafts and work.

questions.q: Which statement about Tagore is correct?
options: He valued art, music and nature in education
questions.why: Tagore valued art, music, dance and nature in education, and set up Santiniketan this way. He opposed strict discipline.

questions.q: Why did poor peasant children suffer under the new pathshala rules?
options: Attendance was required even at harvest time when they worked
questions.why: The new rules required regular attendance, even at harvest time, when peasant children worked in the fields. So poor children found it hard to keep up.

questions.q: Correct chronological order:
options: Calcutta Madrasa → Asiatic Society → Macaulay's Minute → Wood's Despatch → Santiniketan
questions.why: The dates are Calcutta Madrasa 1781, Asiatic Society 1784, Macaulay 1835, Wood's Despatch 1854 and Santiniketan 1901. This gives the right order.

questions.q: Case: A writer in 1910 argues that colonial schooling makes Indians ashamed of their own culture. Whose view does this match most closely?
questions.why: Gandhi argued that colonial education made Indians think their own culture was inferior. Macaulay, Mill and Wood supported Western learning.

courses.title: History · Women, Caste and Reform
courses.summary: Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century movements to change the lives of women (sati, widow remarriage, girls' education, child marriage) and to challenge caste inequality — Rammohun Roy, Vidyasagar, the Phules, Pandita Ramabai, Begum Rokeya, Sri Narayana Guru, Periyar, Ambedkar and others.
outcomes: Learners can explain reforms against sati and for widow remarriage and girls' education
Learners can name women who wrote and worked for women's rights
Learners can describe challenges to caste by reformers like Phule, Narayana Guru, Ambedkar and Periyar
Learners can identify major reform organisations and their aims

lessons.title: Working towards change: sati and widow remarriage

scenes.text: In early-19th-century Bengal, some widows are pressured to die on their husbands' funeral pyres.
Rammohun Roy argues ancient texts do not require it.
In 1829 sati is banned.

steps.title: The context
steps.body: Two hundred years ago things were very different: most children were married off at an early age; women in many communities were expected to stay at home and had little education; widows were often expected to live without remarriage; in some areas, **sati** — widows being praised for choosing death on their husbands' funeral pyre — occurred. With new forms of communication (books, newspapers, pamphlets), people could debate these practices.

steps.title: Rammohun Roy
steps.body: **Raja Rammohun Roy** (1772–1833) founded a reform association known as the **Brahmo Sabha** (later **Brahmo Samaj**) in Calcutta. He wanted to spread Western education and bring greater freedom and equality for women. He argued, with quotes from ancient sacred texts, that the practice of widow burning had no sanction there. British officials, influenced by such arguments, banned **sati in 1829**.

steps.title: Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar and widow remarriage
steps.body: **Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar** used ancient texts to argue that widows could remarry. The British officials adopted his suggestion and passed a law in **1856** permitting **widow remarriage**. **Veerasalingam Pantulu** formed an association for widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency; **Swami Dayanand Saraswati**, who founded the **Arya Samaj** (1875), also supported widow remarriage. Still, the number of widows who actually remarried remained low; those who did were not easily accepted.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How did reformers like Rammohun Roy and Vidyasagar make their arguments persuasive? → They quoted ancient sacred texts, showing the practices they opposed had no religious sanction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying sati was banned in 1856 (that was the widow remarriage law; sati banned 1829).
- Thinking laws instantly changed society — social acceptance was slow.

activity.prompt: Order the reforms

quiz.why: Rammohun Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in Calcutta in 1828, to reform Hindu society. Vidyasagar, Phule and Dayanand worked on other movements.
Sati was banned in 1829, after Rammohun Roy campaigned against it. 1856 was the Widow Remarriage Act.

quiz.q: Widow remarriage law was passed in:
quiz.why: The Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, mainly due to the efforts of Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar. 1829 was the year sati was banned.
Swami Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875. Rammohun Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha, and Periyar and Narayana Guru worked in the south.

quiz.q: Veerasalingam Pantulu worked for widow remarriage in:
quiz.why: Veerasalingam Pantulu worked for widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency. He is not linked to Bengal, Punjab or Kashmir.

lessons.title: Girls begin going to school; women write

scenes.text: In Pune, around 1848, Savitribai Phule walks to teach girls at a school she and Jyotirao run.
People throw mud and stones at her.
She carries a spare sari and keeps teaching.

steps.title: Girls' education
steps.body: Many reformers felt education for girls was necessary to improve women's condition. Vidyasagar and others set up schools for girls in Calcutta; in the Bombay Presidency many schools were set up. Many people feared that schools would take girls away from home and prevent domestic duties, or that travelling through public places would corrupt them, so many girls were taught at home by liberal fathers or husbands. **Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule** started schools for girls in **Pune** (around **1848**). In **Muslim** households, the **Begums of Bhopal** played a notable role, founding a primary school for girls at Aligarh. **Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain** started schools for Muslim girls in **Patna and Calcutta**.

steps.title: Women write
steps.body:
By the end of the 19th century, women themselves worked for reform, wrote books, edited magazines, founded schools and training centres and set up women's associations.

- **Pandita Ramabai**, a great scholar of Sanskrit, wrote about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women; she founded a **widows' home at Poona** where widows could get vocational training.
- **Tarabai Shinde**, educated at home in Poona, published *Stripurushtulna* (A Comparison between Women and Men), criticising social differences.
- Begum Rokeya wrote *Sultana's Dream*, a satirical fantasy of a land where women ruled.

steps.title: Child marriage
steps.body: In **1929**, the **Child Marriage Restraint Act** was passed (setting minimum ages of marriage across British India for the first time; the limits were raised in later decades). Later laws raised the ages; today in India the legal minimum age of marriage is 18 for women and 21 for men, and child marriage is a punishable offence.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did many families resist sending girls to school in the 19th century? → Fear of girls leaving home, travelling in public places and neglecting domestic duties.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking women were only passive recipients of reform — many led it.
- Mixing Pandita Ramabai (widows' home, Poona) with Begum Rokeya (schools in Patna, Calcutta).

activity.prompt: Match the reformer to the contribution
pairs: Schools for Muslim girls in Patna and Calcutta; Sultana's Dream
Primary school for girls at Aligarh

quiz.why: Tarabai Shinde wrote Stripurushtulna, which compared the condition of women and men. Rokeya, Ramabai and Savitribai are known for other work.
Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain started schools for Muslim girls in Patna and Calcutta. Phule's schools were in Pune.

quiz.q: Pandita Ramabai founded a widows' home at:
quiz.why: Pandita Ramabai set up a widows' home at Poona (Pune), where widows learned skills to earn a living. It was not in Madras, Calcutta or Lucknow.

quiz.q: Child Marriage Restraint Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Child Marriage Restraint Act (Sarda Act) was passed in 1929. 1829 was the sati ban and 1856 the widow remarriage law.
Begum Rokeya wrote Sultana's Dream, a satire in which women rule and men stay indoors. It points to the unfairness women faced.

lessons.title: Caste and social reform

scenes.text: In some villages, 'untouchable' communities are not allowed to use the common tank.
In 1927, B.R. Ambedkar leads a movement asserting equal rights.
Across India, reformers challenge caste inequality.

steps.title: Caste inequality
steps.body: Society was divided along caste lines. Brahmans and Kshatriyas were considered 'upper castes'; then traders and moneylenders (Vaishyas); then peasants and artisans (Shudras); at the lowest rung were those who laboured to keep cities and villages clean or did work considered polluting — they were classed as **'untouchables'**, not allowed to enter temples, draw water from wells used by upper castes, or bathe in ponds where upper castes bathed.

steps.title: Early reformers
steps.body: Some reformers within upper castes (e.g. the **Paramhansa Mandali** in Bombay, 1840) worked against caste and untouchability. Christian missionaries set up schools for tribal groups and 'lower' castes. As cities grew and new jobs appeared (factories, municipalities, army — the Mahar community found jobs in the Mahar Regiment), some low-caste people found new opportunities, though they were often exploited (e.g. indentured labour on plantations in Mauritius, Trinidad and Indonesia).

steps.title: Demands for equality and justice
steps.body:
- **Haridas Thakur**'s Matua sect in Bengal (among Chandala cultivators) questioned Brahmanical texts that supported caste.
- **Sri Narayana Guru** (Kerala, from the Ezhava caste) proclaimed the ideal of unity: 'oneness of humankind… one caste, one religion, one god for humankind'.
- **Jyotirao Phule** (born 1827) attacked Brahmans' claim to superiority, saying Aryans were outsiders; he formed the **Satyashodhak Samaj** (1873) and wrote **Gulamgiri** (1873), linking the conditions of 'lower' castes in India and Black slaves in America.
- **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** (born into a Mahar family) led a **temple entry movement in 1927**, joined by Mahar caste followers, and fought for dignity and rights; later he became chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constitution.
- **E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)** founded the **Self-Respect Movement**, criticised Hindu scriptures that upheld caste and the subordination of women.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did Phule dedicate Gulamgiri to Americans who fought slavery? → He saw a link between the oppression of 'lower' castes in India and the enslavement of Black people in America.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Periyar founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (that was Phule).
- Thinking caste reformers were all from upper castes.

activity.prompt: Match the reformer to the movement or idea

quiz.why: Jyotirao Phule wrote Gulamgiri in 1873, linking the condition of lower castes in India to slavery in America. Ambedkar and Periyar did not write it.
Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker) founded the Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu to fight caste inequality. Vivekananda and Rammohun Roy led other movements.
Sri Narayana Guru came from Kerala, from the Ezhava community, and fought caste discrimination. He was not from Punjab, Bengal or Maharashtra.

quiz.q: Ambedkar led a temple entry movement in:
quiz.why: Ambedkar led a temple entry movement in 1927, to claim the right of all castes to enter temples. 1947 is independence and 1885 the Congress.

quiz.q: Paramhansa Mandali was founded in Bombay in:
quiz.why: The Paramhansa Mandali was founded in Bombay in 1840 to work against caste. 1873 was the Satyashodhak Samaj.

lessons.title: Reform organisations: Brahmo, Arya, Aligarh, Singh Sabha and more

scenes.text: By the late 19th century, newspapers print debates of Brahmo Samajists, Arya Samajists, Aligarh reformers and Singh Sabhas.
Each sets up schools and colleges.
Different paths — a shared desire to reform society.

steps.title: Organisations
steps.body:
- **Brahmo Samaj** (1830): prohibited idolatry and sacrifice, believed in the Upanishads; forbade members from following practices not in line with these.
- **Derozio and Young Bengal**: **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio**, a teacher at **Hindu College, Calcutta** in the 1820s, encouraged students to question tradition; the Young Bengal Movement attacked tradition, demanded education for women.
- **Ramakrishna Mission**: named after Ramakrishna Paramhansa, founded by **Swami Vivekananda**; stressed social service and selfless action for salvation.
- **Prarthana Samaj** (Bombay, 1867): sought to remove caste restrictions, abolish child marriage, encourage women's education, end the ban on widow remarriage.
- **Veda Samaj** (Madras, 1864): worked to abolish caste distinctions and promote widow remarriage and women's education.
- **Aligarh Movement**: **Sayyid Ahmed Khan** founded the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College** at Aligarh (1875), later the Aligarh Muslim University; offered modern education including Western science.
- **Singh Sabha Movement**: first Singh Sabhas formed at **Amritsar (1873)** and **Lahore (1879)**; sought to rid Sikhism of superstitions, caste distinctions and practices seen as non-Sikh; promoted education among Sikhs.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: What did most reform organisations share? → They used schools, books and newspapers to change social practices and promote education, including women's education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing Prarthana Samaj (Bombay) with Veda Samaj (Madras).
- Saying Vivekananda founded the Brahmo Samaj.

activity.prompt: Which region was each organisation founded in?

quiz.q: Young Bengal Movement was inspired by:
quiz.why: The Young Bengal Movement was inspired by Henry Derozio, a teacher at the Hindu College, Calcutta. He encouraged students to question old ideas.

quiz.q: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College was founded by:
quiz.why: Sayyid Ahmed Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875, to give modern education to Muslims. Phule, Vivekananda and Roy led other efforts.
The Prarthana Samaj was established in Bombay in 1867 as a reform society. The other place-year pairs belong to other organisations.
Swami Vivekananda's Ramakrishna Mission stressed social service and selfless action to help the poor. It did not stress rituals or revenue collection.

quiz.q: First Singh Sabha was formed in:
quiz.why: The first Singh Sabha was formed at Amritsar in 1873, and another followed at Lahore in 1879. They worked for Sikh reform and education.

courses.title: History · The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947
courses.summary: The rise of nationalism, the founding of the Indian National Congress, Moderates and Radicals, the Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi, Gandhi's mass movements (Rowlatt, Non-Cooperation, Salt March, Quit India), the growth of communal politics, and Independence and Partition in 1947.
outcomes: Learners can explain why nationalism grew in the late 19th century
Learners can compare Moderate and Radical approaches and the Swadeshi movement
Learners can narrate the main Gandhian movements and their methods
Learners can explain the events leading to Independence and Partition in 1947

lessons.title: The emergence of nationalism and the Congress

scenes.text: December 1885: 72 delegates from across India meet in Bombay.
They form the Indian National Congress.
For the first time, a body claims to speak for all Indians.

steps.title: Why nationalism grew
steps.body: After 1857, a consciousness grew that India belonged to its people — of all classes, colours, castes, creeds, languages and genders — and that the country, its resources and systems were theirs. British control was resented. Political associations formed in the 1870s and 1880s (e.g. the **Poona Sarvajanik Sabha**, the **Indian Association**, the **Madras Mahajan Sabha**, the **Bombay Presidency Association**). Laws increased dissatisfaction: the **Arms Act (1878)** disallowed Indians from possessing arms; the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** allowed confiscation of newspapers that published 'objectionable' material. In **1883** the government tried to introduce the **Ilbert Bill**, allowing Indian judges to try British or European persons; white opposition forced its withdrawal — showing the racial attitudes of the British.

steps.title: Indian National Congress (1885)
steps.body: Established in **December 1885** in **Bombay** with **72 delegates**. Early leaders included **Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji, W.C. Bonnerji, Surendranath Banerji, Romesh Chandra Dutt, S. Subramania Iyer**. A retired British official, **A.O. Hume**, played a part in bringing them together. Dadabhai Naoroji wrote *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*, criticising the economic impact of British rule (drain of wealth).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did the Ilbert Bill controversy strengthen nationalism? → It exposed the racial attitudes of the British, who did not accept Indians as equals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Congress was founded in Delhi or in 1905.
- Thinking only Hindus or only the rich were early leaders — the founders were diverse.

activity.prompt: Order the early events

events.text: Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act
Indian National Congress founded in Bombay

quiz.q: Indian National Congress was founded in:
quiz.why: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, in Bombay. 1857 was the Revolt and 1905 the Partition of Bengal.

quiz.q: Number of delegates at the first Congress session:
quiz.why: The first Congress session in 1885 was attended by 72 delegates from different parts of India. It was a small beginning.

quiz.q: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was written by:
quiz.why: Dadabhai Naoroji wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, explaining the drain of wealth from India. He was a Moderate leader.

options: Allow Indian judges to try Europeans
quiz.why: The Ilbert Bill proposed that Indian judges could try Europeans. Europeans opposed it strongly, and the Bill was withdrawn.

quiz.q: The Vernacular Press Act (1878) allowed the government to:
quiz.why: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 let the government confiscate newspapers that printed material it called objectionable. It was a form of censorship.

lessons.title: Moderates, Radicals and Swadeshi

scenes.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak declares: 'Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!'
In 1905 Lord Curzon partitions Bengal.
People burn foreign cloth and buy swadeshi goods.

steps.title: Moderates
steps.body: Early Congress leaders, called **Moderates**, wanted a greater voice for Indians in government and administration; they demanded more Indians in high posts, separation of the judiciary from the executive, repeal of the Arms Act, freedom of speech. They believed in **petitions, resolutions and speeches** and in British respect for justice, aiming to make the government aware of Indian sentiments.

steps.title: Radicals ('Freedom is our birthright')
steps.body: By the 1890s, leaders like **Bipin Chandra Pal** (Bengal), **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** (Maharashtra) and **Lala Lajpat Rai** (Punjab) — 'Lal Bal Pal' — criticised the Moderates' 'politics of prayers'. They emphasised **self-reliance** and **constructive work**, saying people must fight for swaraj. Tilak raised the slogan **'Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!'**

steps.title: Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi (1905)
steps.body: In **1905** Viceroy **Curzon partitioned Bengal**, claiming administrative convenience; but it was seen as a way to curtail the influence of Bengali politicians and divide Bengali people. Protest led to the **Swadeshi movement**: boycott of British goods and institutions, use of swadeshi goods, national education, and in some cases revolutionary violence. In **1906** the **All India Muslim League** was formed at **Dacca**; it supported the partition. In **1907** the Congress split (at Surat) between Moderates and Radicals. Bengal was reunited in **1911**, and the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did Radicals criticise the Moderates? → They felt petitions to the British were 'politics of prayers'; people themselves had to struggle for swaraj.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Muslim League opposed the 1905 partition (it supported it).
- Mixing up Lal (Lajpat Rai, Punjab), Bal (Tilak, Maharashtra), Pal (Bipin Chandra Pal, Bengal).

activity.prompt: Moderate or Radical approach?

items.text: Petitions and resolutions to the government
Faith in British sense of justice

quiz.why: Lord Curzon, the Viceroy, partitioned Bengal in 1905. Mountbatten, Dalhousie and Canning belong to other times.

quiz.q: 'Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!' was said by:
quiz.why: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, a Radical leader, said 'Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it!'. Moderates like Naoroji and Gokhale preferred petitions.
The Muslim League was formed in 1906 at Dacca. 1885 was the Congress and 1940 the Lahore resolution.

quiz.q: The Swadeshi movement urged people to:
options: Boycott British goods and use Indian goods
quiz.why: The Swadeshi movement urged people to boycott British goods and use Indian-made goods instead. It was a call for self-reliance.
Lal Bal Pal means Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal. They were Radical leaders, not Moderates or British officers.

lessons.title: The growth of mass nationalism under Gandhi

scenes.text: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi starts walking from Sabarmati with 78 volunteers.
On 6 April he reaches Dandi and makes salt from sea water — breaking the salt law.
Millions join; the world watches.

steps.title: Gandhi's arrival and early campaigns
steps.body: **Mahatma Gandhi** returned from South Africa in **1915**, where he had fought racist restrictions with **satyagraha** (non-violent resistance). He travelled across India; his early campaigns were in **Champaran (1917)**, **Kheda** and **Ahmedabad** (1917–18).

steps.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh (1919)
steps.body: The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** curbed fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and strengthened police powers. Gandhi called for a satyagraha. On **13 April 1919**, at **Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar**, General **Dyer** ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering, killing hundreds. **Rabindranath Tagore** renounced his knighthood in protest.

steps.title: Non-Cooperation and Khilafat (1920–22)
steps.body: With the **Khilafat** issue (Indian Muslims' support for the Ottoman Khalifa), Gandhi launched the **Non-Cooperation Movement** in 1920: boycott of British titles, schools, colleges, courts, foreign cloth; and non-payment of taxes in some areas. Thousands joined across India. In **February 1922**, a crowd attacked and set fire to a police station at **Chauri Chaura** (UP), killing policemen; Gandhi called off the movement because he was opposed to violence.

steps.title: Civil Disobedience: Salt March (1930)
steps.body: In **December 1929**, the Congress under **Jawaharlal Nehru** resolved for **'Purna Swaraj'** (complete independence); **26 January 1930** was observed as 'Independence Day'. Gandhi led the **Salt March** (**Dandi March**) from **Sabarmati to Dandi** (about 240 miles), breaking the salt law on **6 April 1930** — salt was something everyone used, so the tax hurt the poor most. Peasants, tribals and women participated in large numbers. The **Government of India Act, 1935** provided for provincial autonomy; elections were held in **1937** and the Congress formed governments in 7 of 11 provinces.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Gandhi called off Non-Cooperation because of Jallianwala Bagh (it was Chauri Chaura, 1922).
- Mixing 1919 (Rowlatt, Jallianwala) with 1929 (Purna Swaraj).

activity.prompt: Order the Gandhian era events

quiz.q: Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on:
quiz.why: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, at Amritsar, took place on 13 April 1919. 8 August 1942 was Quit India and 15 August 1947 independence.
Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922 after violence at Chauri Chaura, as he insisted on non-violence.
The Salt March began at Sabarmati and ended at Dandi on 6 April 1930, where Gandhi broke the salt law.

quiz.q: Purna Swaraj resolution was passed under the presidency of:
quiz.why: The Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution was passed at the Lahore session of 1929, under Jawaharlal Nehru as president.

quiz.q: Tagore renounced his knighthood to protest:
quiz.why: Rabindranath Tagore gave up his knighthood to protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919.
