lessons.title: Quit India, communal politics and 1947

scenes.text: On 8 August 1942, Gandhi tells the British to 'Quit India' and urges Indians to 'Do or Die'.
Leaders are jailed at once, yet people continue the movement.
Five years later, India is free — but divided.

steps.title: Quit India (1942)
steps.body: During the Second World War, the Congress was angry that India was dragged into the war without consulting Indians. In **August 1942**, Gandhi launched **Quit India**, telling the British to leave, and asked people to **'Do or Die'** — but non-violently. Leaders were jailed immediately; still the movement spread, with strikes, demonstrations and sabotage, especially among students, peasants and workers. The British responded with great force; yet it brought the Raj to its knees.

steps.title: Revolutionaries and the INA
steps.body: Some nationalists believed in revolutionary action: **Bhagat Singh**, **Chandra Shekhar Azad**, **Sukhdev** and others formed the **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)** in 1928; Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw a bomb in the Legislative Assembly in 1929 (to make the deaf hear, not to kill). Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were executed in **1931**. **Subhas Chandra Bose** organised the **Indian National Army (INA)** with support from Japan to free India by force; INA prisoners' trials in 1945–46 inspired mass protests.

steps.title: Towards Independence and Partition
steps.body: The **Muslim League** under **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** passed a resolution in **1940** (Lahore) demanding 'Independent States' for Muslims in the north-western and eastern areas. After the 1946 elections, the **Cabinet Mission** (1946) proposed a loose federation; negotiations broke down. The League called for **'Direct Action Day' (16 August 1946)**, followed by large-scale violence. India became independent on **15 August 1947**, and **Pakistan** was created. Partition caused immense violence and displacement — millions were uprooted and many lost their lives. Gandhi worked to restore communal harmony; he was assassinated on **30 January 1948**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was the Quit India Movement significant despite repression? → It showed the depth of mass anti-British feeling and made it clear British rule could not continue for long.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Quit India was launched in 1947.
- Forgetting that freedom came with the trauma of Partition.

activity.prompt: Match the event to its year
pairs: Execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru

quiz.q: 'Do or Die' was Gandhi's call during:
quiz.why: Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die' during the Quit India Movement of August 1942. The Salt March and other movements had different slogans.
Subhas Chandra Bose organised the Indian National Army (INA), with Japan's support, to fight the British. It was not Nehru's or Bhagat Singh's organisation.

quiz.q: Muslim League's Lahore resolution was in:
quiz.why: The Muslim League's Lahore resolution was in 1940. It demanded separate states for Muslims.
Bhagat Singh was executed in 1931, along with Sukhdev and Rajguru. 1947 is independence and 1942 Quit India.
India became independent on 15 August 1947. 26 January 1950 is Republic Day and 26 January 1930 was Purna Swaraj Day.

questions.q: Assertion: Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922. Reason: Violence broke out at Chauri Chaura.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Violence at Chauri Chaura in 1922 made Gandhi, who insisted on non-violence, withdraw the movement.

questions.q: Who among these was a Moderate leader?
questions.why: Dadabhai Naoroji was a Moderate who used petitions and appeals. Lajpat Rai, Pal and Tilak were Radicals.

questions.q: Purna Swaraj was declared in:
questions.why: Purna Swaraj was declared at the Lahore session in 1929. 1919 was the Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh.

questions.q: The Muslim League was founded at:
questions.why: The Muslim League was founded at Dacca in 1906. Bombay 1885 was the Congress and Lahore 1940 the League's resolution.

questions.q: The Rowlatt Act (1919):
options: Curbed fundamental rights and increased police powers
questions.why: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 curbed fundamental rights and gave the police more powers. It did not end the salt tax or create Pakistan.

questions.q: Case: A leader asks Indians to boycott British schools, courts, titles and foreign cloth and to spin khadi, together with the Khilafat cause. Which movement?
questions.why: Boycott of British schools, courts and cloth, together with spinning khadi and the Khilafat cause, marks the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22).

questions.q: Why did Gandhi choose salt for civil disobedience?
options: Everyone used it, and the tax hurt the poor most
questions.why: Salt was used by everyone, rich or poor, and the tax hurt the poor most. So it made a strong symbol for civil disobedience.

questions.q: Assertion: The Ilbert Bill was withdrawn. Reason: White opposition objected to Indian judges trying Europeans.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. White opposition to Indian judges trying Europeans led to the withdrawal of the Ilbert Bill, exposing racial attitudes.

questions.q: Correct order:
options: Jallianwala Bagh → Congress → Partition of Bengal
Congress founded → Partition of Bengal → Jallianwala Bagh → Salt March → Quit India
questions.why: The dates are Congress 1885, Partition of Bengal 1905, Jallianwala Bagh 1919, Salt March 1930 and Quit India 1942. That is the correct order.

questions.q: Elections under the 1935 Act were held in:
questions.why: Elections under the Government of India Act 1935 were held in 1937 for provincial governments. 1946 was another election, and 1950 is later.

questions.q: Direct Action Day was called by:
questions.why: The Muslim League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946. It led to serious riots.

questions.q: Case: A movement in 1942 continued even after all major leaders were jailed, through strikes and protests by students and peasants. This shows:
options: Nationalism had become a mass movement
questions.why: The 1942 movement went on through strikes and protests by students and peasants even when leaders were jailed. This shows nationalism had become a mass movement.

questions.q: Why did Radicals call Moderates' methods 'politics of prayers'?
options: They relied on petitions to the British rather than mass struggle
questions.why: Radicals criticised the Moderates for relying on petitions and prayers to the British instead of mass struggle. That is why they called it the 'politics of prayers'.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

courses.title: Geography Ch 1 · Resources
courses.summary: What makes something a resource, how resources are classified (natural, human-made, human; renewable and non-renewable; actual and potential; ubiquitous and localised), and why sustainable development and conservation matter.
outcomes: Learners can define a resource and explain how value and utility arise
Learners can classify resources in several ways
Learners can explain the role of human resources
Learners can describe principles of sustainable development and conservation

lessons.title: What is a resource?

scenes.text: In Rahul's town, water flows freely from taps.
In a dry village, families walk 3 km for a pot of water.
Anything with utility and value can be a resource.

steps.title: Resource, utility and value
steps.body: Anything that can be used to satisfy a need is a **resource**. **Utility** (usability) gives a thing **value**. Some resources have **economic value** (metals can be bought and sold); some don't but are still important — like a beautiful landscape (it adds to our well-being, aesthetic value). **Time and technology** can change substances into resources: e.g. a medicinal plant becomes a resource when people learn its use; fire, wheels and new technologies turned many things into resources.

steps.title: People make resources
steps.body: People themselves are the most important resource — their ideas, knowledge, inventions and discoveries lead to the creation of more resources. Improving the quality of people's skills (education and health) is **human resource development**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Is a rock a resource? → It becomes a resource when people can use it, e.g. as building stone or as a source of a mineral. Technology and need decide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only things with a price are resources (scenery, clean air, culture have value too).
- Forgetting that humans are a resource.

statements.s: A resource must always have economic value.
statements.why: Some have aesthetic or other value.

statements.s: Utility gives a substance value.
Technology can turn substances into resources.
People are not a resource.
statements.why: Human resources are the most important.

quiz.q: Something that can be used to satisfy a need is a:
quiz.why: Anything that can be used to satisfy a need is a resource. A pollutant or waste has no use in that sense.
A beautiful landscape gives pleasure and well-being, so it has aesthetic value. It is not measured mainly in money.
A substance gets value from its utility, i.e. how useful it is. Age, colour and weight do not make something a resource.

quiz.q: Improving people's skills and health is:
quiz.why: Improving people's skills and health is human resource development. Mining, deforestation and recycling are different activities.

quiz.q: Two factors that can turn substances into resources:
quiz.why: Substances become resources with time and technology, as people learn new uses and ways to extract them. Weather, luck or size do not decide this.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Types of resources

scenes.text: The class sorts items: sunlight, coal, a bridge, a doctor's skill.
'Is coal natural or human-made? Renewable or not?'
Each resource fits in more than one category.

steps.title: Natural, human-made, human
steps.body:
- **Natural resources:** drawn from nature and used without much modification — air, water, soils, minerals, forests, wildlife.
- **Human-made resources:** natural substances become resources when their original form is changed — iron ore → machines; buildings, bridges, roads, technology.
- **Human resources:** people with knowledge, skills and technology.

steps.title: Classifying natural resources
steps.body:
- By **level of development and use**: **actual** resources (quantity known, being used now — e.g. Ruhr coal, Saudi oil) vs **potential** resources (exist but not fully used now — e.g. uranium in Ladakh, possibly usable in future).
- By **origin**: **abiotic** (non-living: soil, rocks, minerals) vs **biotic** (living: plants, animals).
- By **distribution**: **ubiquitous** (found everywhere — air) vs **localised** (only in certain places — copper, iron ore).
- By **renewability**: **renewable** (renewed quickly — solar, wind; though water, soil and forests can be harmed by overuse) vs **non-renewable** (limited stock — coal, petroleum, natural gas; take thousands of years to form).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify coal: natural, abiotic, localised, non-renewable, and (where mined) actual.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling water 'unlimited' — careless use can exhaust usable water.
- Confusing potential (not yet used) with non-renewable.

activity.prompt: Renewable or non-renewable?

quiz.why: Resources found everywhere, like air, are called ubiquitous. Localised resources occur only in certain places.

quiz.q: Uranium in Ladakh is an example of a:
quiz.why: Uranium in Ladakh is known to exist but is not yet used, so it is a potential resource. An actual resource is already being used.
A bridge is built by people, so it is a human-made resource. It is not a natural or biotic resource.
Biotic resources come from the living world, such as plants and animals. Non-living ones are abiotic.

options: It takes very long to form and stock is limited
quiz.why: Coal takes millions of years to form and the stock is limited, so it can run out. That is why it is non-renewable.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Conserving resources and sustainable development

scenes.text: The eco-club starts 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' week.
Students fix a dripping tap — saving thousands of litres a year.
'Use today, but leave enough for tomorrow.'

steps.title: Why conserve?
steps.body: Using resources carefully and giving them time to get renewed is **resource conservation**. Balancing the need to use resources and also conserve them for the future is **sustainable development**.

steps.title: Principles of sustainable development
steps.body:
- Respect and care for all forms of life
- Improve the quality of human life
- Conserve the earth's vitality and diversity
- Minimise the depletion of natural resources
- Change personal attitudes and practices towards the environment
- Enable communities to care for their own environment

steps.title: What each of us can do
steps.body: **Reduce, Reuse, Recycle**: reduce consumption, reuse things instead of throwing them, recycle materials. Switch off lights and fans, save water, use public transport, avoid single-use plastic.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A family switches to LED bulbs and switches off fans when leaving rooms. Which principle? → Minimising depletion of resources (and changing personal practices).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking conservation means not using resources at all — it means wise use.
- Thinking only governments can conserve.

activity.prompt: My sustainable-living week
items: Carry a water bottle and cloth bag
Switch off lights and fans when leaving a room
Use both sides of paper
Repair something instead of replacing it
Segregate wet and dry waste at home

quiz.q: Using resources carefully and allowing renewal is:
quiz.why: Using resources carefully so that they can renew and last is conservation. Mining and deforestation use them up.
Sustainable development balances present needs with the needs of future generations. It is not only profit or only conservation.

quiz.q: Which is a principle of sustainable development?
options: Respect and care for all forms of life
quiz.why: Respect and care for all forms of life is a principle of sustainable development. Cutting forests or using everything now is the opposite.
The 3 Rs stand for Reduce, Reuse and Recycle. They are simple ways to conserve resources.

quiz.q: Fixing a leaking tap helps to:
quiz.why: Fixing a leaking tap stops water from being wasted drop by drop. Small actions like this conserve water.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Applying ideas: case studies

story.title: The village that saved its well

scenes.text: A Rajasthan village builds small check dams and rooftop tanks.
Wells that dried every summer now have water.
The community managed its own resource — sustainably.

steps.title: Case 1: Water in a dry village
steps.body: Rainwater harvesting (rooftop tanks, check dams) recharges groundwater; communities agree rules for use. This turns a scarce resource into a reliable one — technology + cooperation.

steps.title: Case 2: Solar in a remote hamlet
steps.body: Solar panels convert a ubiquitous, renewable resource (sunlight) into electricity where grid lines are costly. Children study after dark; small shops stay open.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is sunlight in a desert both ubiquitous and a resource? → It's available everywhere there, and with solar technology it satisfies energy needs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming technology alone solves problems; people's participation matters.
- Thinking renewable means 'can be wasted'.

activity.prompt: Match the action to the idea

quiz.why: Rainwater harvesting stores rainwater and lets it soak in, which recharges groundwater. It does not increase floods or pollute rivers.
Sunlight is available everywhere and does not run out, so it is renewable and ubiquitous. It is not human-made or non-renewable.
Training people in skills is human resource development. Mining, deforestation and overgrazing damage resources.
Recycling paper means fewer trees need to be cut for new paper, so forests are conserved. Burning wood or clearing land destroys forests.

quiz.q: Community management of a resource reflects which principle?
options: Enable communities to care for their environment
quiz.why: Letting communities manage and care for their own environment reflects the principle of enabling communities to care for their environment. Wasteful use or ignoring the future is not sustainable.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

questions.q: A resource is anything with:
questions.why: A resource is anything that has utility, i.e. is useful to satisfy a need. Weight, age or colour alone do not make it one.

questions.q: Air is a:
questions.why: Air is found everywhere, so it is a ubiquitous resource. Localised resources occur only in some places.

questions.q: Which is human-made?
questions.why: A road is built by people, so it is human-made. Coal, forests and soil are natural.

questions.q: Non-renewable resource:
questions.why: Petroleum took millions of years to form and its stock is limited, so it is non-renewable. Wind and solar energy are renewable.

questions.q: Biotic resources include:
questions.why: Biotic resources come from living things, i.e. plants and animals. Rocks and minerals are abiotic.

questions.q: Assertion: People are the most important resource. Reason: Their knowledge and skills create more resources.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. People's knowledge and skills turn substances into resources and create more of them.

questions.q: Potential resources are:
options: Known to exist but not fully used now
questions.why: Potential resources are known to exist but are not fully used at present, though they may be used in future. They are not exhausted or imaginary.

questions.q: Sustainable development means:
options: Meeting present needs while conserving for the future
questions.why: Sustainable development means meeting present needs while conserving resources for the future. It does not mean stopping all use.

questions.q: Copper and iron ore are examples of:
questions.why: Copper and iron ore are found only in certain places, so they are localised resources. Ubiquitous ones, like air, are found everywhere.

questions.q: Case: A country discovers huge oil reserves but lacks technology to extract them. The oil is currently a:
questions.why: Oil that is known to exist but cannot be used for lack of technology is a potential resource. It becomes an actual resource once it is extracted.

questions.q: Which is NOT a principle of sustainable development?
questions.why: Sustainable development aims to minimise, not maximise, the depletion of resources. Respecting life, conserving diversity and improving quality of life are principles.

questions.q: Why can renewable resources still be exhausted?
options: Overuse and pollution can exceed their renewal
questions.why: Renewable resources renew only at a certain rate. Overuse and pollution can exceed that rate, so they can still be exhausted.

questions.q: Assertion: A medicinal plant becomes a resource only after people learn its use. Reason: Knowledge and technology give substances utility.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. A plant has no use until knowledge of its medicinal value gives it utility.

questions.q: Classify coal correctly:
questions.why: Coal is natural, abiotic (non-living), found only in certain places (localised) and non-renewable. The other options mix the categories wrongly.

questions.q: Case: A town replaces diesel generators with solar panels and trains local youth to maintain them. Which ideas are shown?
options: Renewable resource use and human resource development
questions.why: Solar panels use a renewable resource, and training local youth is human resource development. So both ideas are shown.

courses.title: Geography Ch 2 · Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources
courses.summary: Land use and conservation, landslides and mitigation, soil formation, degradation and conservation methods, water scarcity and conservation, types of natural vegetation, and the conservation of wildlife.
outcomes: Learners can explain land use patterns and land conservation
Learners can describe soil-forming factors and soil conservation methods
Learners can explain water scarcity and conservation methods
Learners can describe types of natural vegetation and ways to conserve wildlife

lessons.title: Land: use and conservation

scenes.text: Rivers' plains are packed with people; high mountains and deserts are almost empty.
Ninety per cent of the world's people live on about thirty per cent of the land.
Why? And how can we protect land?

steps.title: Land and land use
steps.body:
Land covers only about **30%** of the earth's surface, and not all of it is habitable. Uneven distribution of population is due to land and climate: rugged mountains, steep slopes, low-lying areas prone to waterlogging, deserts and thick forests are sparsely populated; plains and river valleys are densely populated. **Ninety per cent of the world population occupies only thirty per cent of land area.**

**Land use:** using land for agriculture, forestry, mining, roads, industries. Determined by physical factors (topography, soil, climate, minerals, water) and human factors (population, technology). Land can be **private** or **community** land (common property used by all — e.g. for fodder, fruits, fuelwood).

steps.title: Degradation and conservation
steps.body: Growing population and demand lead to expansion of agriculture and settlements, deforestation, land degradation, landslides, soil erosion and desertification. **Conservation:** afforestation, land reclamation, regulated use of chemical pesticides and fertilisers, and checks on overgrazing.

steps.title: Landslides
steps.body: Mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope, often with earthquakes, floods and volcanoes; heavy rainfall can cause them, especially in hilly areas. **Mitigation:** hazard mapping, construction of retention walls, increasing vegetation cover, surface drainage control to control water movement.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why are the Ganga plains densely populated? → Fertile soil, flat land and water make farming and settlement easy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all land is usable.
- Confusing landslide mitigation with prevention — some risk always remains.

activity.prompt: Densely or sparsely populated? (generally)

quiz.q: Land covers about what % of the earth's surface?
quiz.why: Land covers about 30 per cent of the earth's surface, and the rest is water. 70 per cent is the share of water.

quiz.q: 90% of the world's people live on about:
quiz.why: About 90 per cent of the world's people live on about 30 per cent of the land. The rest of the land is thinly populated, so the distribution is uneven.

quiz.q: Common property land is used by:
quiz.why: Common property land is used by the whole community, such as village grazing grounds and ponds. It is not owned by one person.
Retention walls hold the slope and reduce landslides. Cutting trees, building on steep slopes and blocking drains make landslides more likely.

quiz.q: Which is a land conservation method?
quiz.why: Afforestation, planting trees, holds the soil and conserves land. Deforestation, overgrazing and overuse of fertilisers damage it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Soil: formation, degradation and conservation

scenes.text: On hill slopes, farmers cut steps — terraces — into the land.
Rain slows down and the soil stays put.
Crops grow where soil would otherwise wash away.

steps.title: Soil and its formation
steps.body: The thin layer of grainy substance covering the earth's surface is **soil**, closely linked to land. **Weathering** (breaking up and decay of exposed rocks by temperature changes, frost action, plants, animals and humans) forms soil. **Factors of soil formation:** **parent rock** (colour, texture, chemical properties, mineral content), **climate** (temperature, rainfall influence weathering and humus), **relief** (altitude and slope determine accumulation), **flora, fauna and micro-organisms** (rate of humus formation), and **time** (thickness of soil profile). Soil formation is very slow.

steps.title: Degradation
steps.body: Factors: deforestation, overgrazing, overuse of chemical fertilisers or pesticides, rain wash, landslides and floods.

steps.title: Conservation methods
steps.body:
- **Mulching:** bare ground between plants covered with organic matter like straw — retains moisture.
- **Contour barriers:** stones, grass, soil used to build barriers along contours; trenches in front collect water.
- **Rock dam:** rocks piled to slow the flow of water, preventing gullies.
- **Terrace farming:** broad flat steps on steep slopes; reduces surface run-off and erosion.
- **Intercropping:** different crops in alternate rows, sown at different times, to protect soil from rain wash.
- **Contour ploughing:** ploughing parallel to the contours of a hill slope forms a natural barrier for water flow.
- **Shelter belts:** rows of trees in coastal and dry regions to check wind movement and protect soil cover.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A desert-edge farm loses topsoil to strong winds. Best method? → Shelter belts of trees.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing contour ploughing (along contours) with ploughing up and down the slope (which increases erosion).
- Thinking soil forms quickly.

activity.prompt: Match the method to how it saves soil
pairs: Flat steps reduce run-off on slopes
Rocks slow water and prevent gullies
Alternate crops protect soil from rain wash

quiz.q: Breaking up of rocks to form soil:
quiz.why: The breaking up of rocks into small particles to form soil is weathering. Erosion is the removal of soil.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a soil-forming factor?
quiz.why: The population of a city does not form soil. Parent rock, climate, time, relief and organic matter are soil-forming factors.
Terrace farming cuts steps in steep slopes, so the soil and water are held. It is not needed on flat deserts, oceans or glaciers.
Shelter belts are rows of trees planted to check the wind and protect soil from erosion. They are not for roads or floods.

quiz.q: Covering bare soil with straw is:
quiz.why: Covering bare soil with straw or dry leaves is mulching. It retains moisture and protects the soil.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Water: scarcity and conservation

scenes.text: Three-fourths of Earth is water — yet many cities face water shortages.
Most fresh water is locked in ice; much of the rest is underground.
Only a very small fraction is easy for us to use.

steps.title: Water availability
steps.body: Fresh water accounts for only about **2.7%** of all water; nearly **70%** of this is in ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland and mountains. Only a tiny portion is available and fit for human use (groundwater, rivers and lakes, water vapour). Water is a renewable resource through the **water cycle** — but it is unevenly distributed, and overuse and pollution create **scarcity**.

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Increasing population, rising demand for food and cash crops, urbanisation and rising standards of living cause shortages. Sewage, agricultural chemicals and industrial effluents **pollute** water. Droughts and floods also matter.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body:
- Forest and vegetation cover slow surface run-off and replenish groundwater.
- **Rainwater harvesting**: collecting rainwater from rooftops and open spaces.
- Canals for irrigation should be **lined** to reduce seepage.
- **Sprinklers** and **drip/trickle irrigation** in dry regions to reduce evaporation.
- Treating industrial effluents before release; cleaning rivers.
- Personal: don't leave taps running; reuse water where safe.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is drip irrigation good for dry regions? → Water reaches roots drop by drop, so less is lost to evaporation and seepage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Water is unlimited because it is renewable.'
- 'Most of Earth's fresh water is in rivers' — most is ice.

activity.prompt: If a dripping tap wastes 1 drop per second and 20 drops = 1 mL, how many litres are wasted in 24 hours?

quiz.q: Share of fresh water in all water (approx.):
quiz.why: About 2.7 per cent of all water on earth is fresh water. The rest, about 97 per cent, is salty.

quiz.q: Most fresh water is found as:
quiz.why: Most fresh water, about 70 per cent, is locked up as ice sheets and glaciers. Lakes and rivers hold only a small share.
Collecting rainwater from rooftops is rainwater harvesting. Mulching and terracing deal with soil.
Lining canals with cement or other material reduces seepage, so less water is lost into the ground. It does not stop evaporation completely.
Untreated industrial waste flowing into water pollutes it. Rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation and afforestation help conserve water.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Natural vegetation and wildlife

scenes.text: Kerala's evergreen forests stay green all year.
In Madhya Pradesh, deciduous trees shed leaves in the dry season.
Both shelter wildlife we must protect.

steps.title: Types of natural vegetation
steps.body:
Vegetation depends mainly on **temperature and moisture** (also slope and soil).

- **Tropical evergreen forests:** heavy rainfall; trees don't shed leaves all at once (e.g. rainforests).
- **Tropical deciduous forests:** trees shed leaves in the dry season to conserve water (e.g. teak, sal).
- **Grasslands:** moderate rainfall; grasses dominate.
- **Thorny bushes/scrubs:** dry areas with low rainfall; plants have thick leaves, waxy stems, thorns.
- **Tundra:** cold polar regions; mosses and lichens.

Forests provide timber, shelter for animals, protect soil, help retain groundwater, give fruits, nuts, rubber, medicines, gum and more.

steps.title: Wildlife and its conservation
steps.body: Wildlife includes animals, birds, insects and aquatic life. Threats: deforestation, poaching, habitat loss, pollution, forest fires. Conservation: **national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves**; awareness programmes like social forestry and **Van Mahotsav** (tree-planting festival) at regional and community level; laws banning **poaching** and trade in animal parts; **CITES** — an international agreement between governments to ensure that trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival. Vultures in India, for example, declined sharply because of a veterinary drug (diclofenac) in cattle carcasses.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why do deciduous trees shed leaves in the dry season? → To reduce water loss through transpiration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking evergreen trees never shed leaves (they shed at different times, not all at once).
- Saying CITES is an Indian law — it's an international agreement.

activity.prompt: Which type of vegetation?

items.text: Heavy rainfall, green throughout the year
Teak and sal shedding leaves in dry season
Cacti-like plants with thorns in dry regions
Mosses and lichens in cold polar areas

quiz.why: Natural vegetation depends mainly on temperature and moisture, that is, climate. Roads, factories and population do not decide it.

quiz.q: Trees shedding leaves in the dry season:
quiz.why: Tropical deciduous trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water. Evergreen trees do not.

options: An international agreement on trade in wild plants and animals
quiz.why: CITES is an international agreement that controls trade in wild plants and animals. It is not a crop, a city or a forest type.
Van Mahotsav is a festival of tree planting held each year. It promotes forest conservation.

quiz.q: Vultures in India declined due to:
quiz.why: Vultures fed on the carcasses of cattle treated with the veterinary drug diclofenac, which poisoned them. Their numbers fell sharply.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

questions.q: Ninety per cent of world population lives on about:
questions.why: About 90 per cent of the world's population lives on about 30 per cent of the land. This shows how unevenly people are spread.

questions.q: Covering soil with straw is:
questions.why: Covering soil with straw is called mulching, and it keeps moisture. Terracing means steps on slopes.

questions.q: Rows of trees to check wind:
questions.why: Shelter belts are rows of trees planted to check the wind and protect the soil. Canals, rock dams and terraces do something else.

questions.q: Most fresh water on Earth is in:
questions.why: About 70 per cent of fresh water is in ice sheets and glaciers. Lakes, rivers and wells hold much less.

questions.q: A soil-forming factor:
questions.why: Parent rock is a soil-forming factor, along with climate, relief, time and living things. Railways, population and markets are not.

questions.q: Assertion: Contour ploughing reduces soil erosion. Reason: Furrows along contours act as barriers to water flow.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Furrows along contours act as barriers that slow down running water and so reduce erosion.

questions.q: Landslide mitigation includes:
questions.why: Hazard mapping and retention walls help reduce landslides. Removing plants, blocking drains or steeper cuts increase the danger.

questions.q: Tundra vegetation consists of:
questions.why: Tundra is very cold, so only mosses and lichens grow there. Cacti, teak and rubber need warmer climates.

questions.q: Drip irrigation is useful because it:
questions.why: Drip irrigation gives water drop by drop at the plant roots, so little is lost to evaporation and seepage. It is a way of saving water.

questions.q: Case: Farmers on a steep hill lose topsoil every monsoon. Best long-term solution:
options: Ploughing up and down the slope
questions.why: On steep hills, terrace farming and contour barriers slow the water and hold the soil. Ploughing up and down the slope or removing plants increases erosion.

questions.q: CITES aims to:
options: Ensure trade does not threaten survival of wild species
questions.why: CITES aims to make sure that trade does not threaten the survival of wild species. It does not promote hunting or mining.

questions.q: Why are rugged mountains sparsely populated?
options: Steep slopes and harsh conditions make farming and transport difficult
questions.why: Rugged mountains have steep slopes and harsh conditions, which make farming and transport difficult. So few people live there.

questions.q: Assertion: Water is renewable, so it can never be scarce. Reason: Overuse and pollution can make usable water scarce.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because water can become scarce even though it is renewable. The reason is true: overuse and pollution can make usable water scarce.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
options: Intercropping — alternate rows of different crops
questions.why: Intercropping means growing different crops in alternate rows. Terraces are steps on slopes, mulching is straw cover and shelter belts are rows of trees against wind.

questions.q: A tap dripping 2 mL per minute wastes how many litres in 30 days?
questions.why: 2 mL × 60 × 24 × 30 = 86,400 mL, which is 86.4 L, since 1000 mL = 1 L. A small drip adds up to a lot.

questions.q: Case: A village shares a grazing ground; overgrazing causes bare, eroding land. Best community action:
options: Rotate grazing, limit animals and plant grass/trees
questions.why: Rotating grazing, limiting the animals and planting grass and trees let the land recover. Burning, selling the land or grazing more would make things worse.

courses.title: Geography · Mineral and Power Resources
courses.summary: Types of minerals, how they are extracted and where they are found, their uses and conservation; conventional and non-conventional sources of power and where India uses them.
outcomes: Learners can classify minerals as metallic (ferrous, non-ferrous) and non-metallic
Learners can describe mining, drilling and quarrying
Learners can name major mineral areas of India and uses of minerals
Learners can compare conventional and non-conventional power sources

lessons.title: Minerals: types and extraction

story.title: What's in your pencil and phone?

scenes.text: Graphite in your pencil, aluminium in the window frame, copper in the charger.
All come from rocks dug or drilled out of the earth.
Minerals are everywhere in daily life.

steps.title: What are minerals?
steps.body: A naturally occurring substance with a definite chemical composition is a **mineral**. Minerals are not evenly distributed; they are formed by natural processes over long periods.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Metallic minerals** (contain metal in raw form): **ferrous** (contain iron — iron ore, manganese, chromite) and **non-ferrous** (no iron — gold, silver, copper, lead, bauxite).
- **Non-metallic minerals:** limestone, mica, gypsum. (Mineral fuels like coal and petroleum are also non-metallic.)

steps.title: Extraction
steps.body:
- **Mining:** taking out minerals from rocks under the earth's surface. **Open-cast mining** for minerals at shallow depths (removing the surface layer); **shaft mining** for deep deposits (deep bores called shafts).
- **Drilling:** deep wells bored to take out petroleum and natural gas.
- **Quarrying:** minerals near the surface are simply dug out.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify bauxite and iron ore. → Both metallic; iron ore is ferrous, bauxite (ore of aluminium) is non-ferrous.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling copper ferrous (it has no iron).
- Mixing quarrying (surface digging) with shaft mining (deep).

activity.prompt: Classify the mineral

quiz.q: A naturally occurring substance with definite chemical composition:
quiz.why: A mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a definite chemical composition. A rock is a mixture of minerals.
Ferrous minerals contain iron, as the Latin ferrum means iron. Gold and aluminium are non-ferrous.
Deposits lying deep are reached by shaft mining. Open-cast mining and quarrying are used for shallow deposits.
Petroleum is a liquid deep underground, so it is taken out by drilling wells. Quarrying and ploughing do not reach it.
Bauxite is the ore from which aluminium is obtained. Aluminium is a non-ferrous metal.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Where minerals are found; uses and conservation

scenes.text: A map of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh glows with iron ore, coal, bauxite and mica.
Steel plants cluster nearby.
But minerals took millions of years to form — we must use them wisely.

steps.title: Distribution
steps.body: Minerals occur in different types of rocks: **metallic minerals** mostly in **igneous and metamorphic** rocks (large plateaus); **non-metallic minerals** and mineral fuels (coal, petroleum) in **sedimentary** rocks. In India: **iron ore** — Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Goa, Maharashtra, Karnataka; **bauxite** — Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu; **mica** — Jharkhand, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan; **copper** — Rajasthan, MP, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh; **manganese** — Maharashtra, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh; **limestone** — many states including Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body: Minerals are used in many industries: copper in coins, pipes and electrical wires; aluminium (from bauxite) in aircraft, automobiles and utensils; silicon (from quartz) in computers; limestone in cement; mica in electrical and electronics industries; gold and silver in jewellery; iron for steel and construction.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body: Minerals are **non-renewable**; formation takes thousands to millions of years. Reduce wastage in mining; **recycle** metals (aluminium, copper, steel).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is recycling aluminium cans important? → Bauxite is non-renewable and extracting aluminium uses a lot of energy; recycling saves both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking minerals are renewable.
- Placing coal in igneous rocks (coal is in sedimentary rocks).

activity.prompt: Match the mineral with a use

quiz.q: Metallic minerals are mostly found in:
quiz.why: Metallic minerals are mostly found in igneous and metamorphic rocks. Fuels like coal and oil are found in sedimentary rocks.
Mica is mainly mined in Jharkhand, and also in Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan. It is not mainly from Goa, Kerala or Punjab.
Cement is made mainly from limestone, together with other materials. Gold, copper and mica are not its raw materials.

quiz.q: Minerals should be conserved because they are:
quiz.why: Minerals take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly, so they are non-renewable. That is why they must be conserved.

quiz.q: Coal and petroleum occur mainly in:
quiz.why: Coal and petroleum formed from remains of plants and animals buried in layers, so they are found in sedimentary rocks.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Conventional sources of power

scenes.text: When Ananya switches on a light, a power station far away may be burning coal.
Or water may be rushing through turbines at a dam.
These are conventional sources.

steps.title: Conventional sources
steps.body:
Commonly used for a long time:

- **Firewood:** cooking and heating in villages (cutting trees has environmental costs).
- **Fossil fuels:** coal (thermal power), petroleum (refined into petrol, diesel, kerosene etc.), natural gas (CNG; cleaner). Coal is mined in Jharia, Dhanbad, Bokaro (Jharkhand) and other places; petroleum in Digboi (Assam), Bombay High (Mumbai), Gujarat and the deltas of the Krishna and Godavari; natural gas in Jaisalmer, Krishna–Godavari delta, Tripura and off-shore Mumbai.
- **Hydel power:** rain water or river water stored in dams turns turbines to make electricity. Bhakra Nangal is one well-known multipurpose project in India. Hydel power is renewable, but dams can displace people and change ecosystems.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is natural gas called a cleaner fuel? → It produces less smoke and harmful pollution than coal or petrol when burnt.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling hydel power non-renewable (water is renewed by the water cycle).
- Forgetting that fossil fuels pollute and are limited.

activity.prompt: Renewable or non-renewable source?

quiz.q: Thermal power is mainly produced by burning:
quiz.why: Thermal power is made by burning coal, a fossil fuel, to produce steam. Wind, water and sunlight do not need burning.
Hydel power uses falling or flowing water to turn turbines. Coal, uranium and sunlight are used in other types of power.
Natural gas burns more cleanly than coal and oil, so it causes less pollution. Firewood and coal produce more smoke.

quiz.q: Petroleum is found in India at:
quiz.why: Petroleum is found in India at Digboi (Assam) and Bombay High, among other places. Delhi and Shimla have no oil fields.
Large dams flood big areas, and the people living there have to be displaced. They produce electricity without smoke and use no coal.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Non-conventional sources of power

scenes.text: A rooftop solar panel powers a village school in Rajasthan.
Giant windmills turn between Nagercoil and Madurai in Tamil Nadu.
Clean energy for a growing India.

steps.title: Sources
steps.body:
- **Solar energy:** solar cells convert sunlight to electricity; solar cookers, heaters, street lights. Very useful in tropical countries like India.
- **Wind energy:** windmills; in India, the largest wind-farm cluster is in **Tamil Nadu, from Nagercoil to Madurai**; also in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra, Lakshadweep.
- **Nuclear power:** energy from atoms of radioactive elements like **uranium and thorium**, which undergo nuclear fission. Uranium deposits occur in **Jharkhand** and the **Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan**; thorium in **monazite sands of Kerala**. Nuclear stations: **Tarapur** (Maharashtra), **Rawatbhata** (Rajasthan), **Kalpakkam** (Tamil Nadu), **Narora** (UP), **Kaiga** (Karnataka), **Kakrapar** (Gujarat). Waste is hazardous and must be handled very carefully.
- **Geothermal energy:** heat from the earth; in India at **Manikaran** (Himachal Pradesh) and **Puga Valley** (Ladakh).
- **Tidal energy:** from tides; suitable sites in India — **Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kachchh** (Gujarat) and the **Sundarbans** (West Bengal).
- **Biogas:** organic waste (dead plants, animal dung, kitchen waste) produces gas for cooking and lighting, and leaves manure.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is biogas good for villages? → Uses locally available cow dung and waste; gives clean fuel and manure; reduces firewood use.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling nuclear power 'pollution-free with no risks' — radioactive waste is dangerous.
- Thinking solar works only in cold countries.

activity.prompt: Match the source to an Indian location

quiz.q: Thorium is found in monazite sands of:
quiz.why: Thorium is found in the monazite sands of the Kerala coast. Assam, Punjab and Delhi are not known for it.
Geothermal energy comes from the heat inside the earth. Tides, sunlight and wind are different sources.

quiz.q: A nuclear power station in Tamil Nadu:
quiz.why: Kalpakkam is the nuclear power station in Tamil Nadu. Tarapur is in Maharashtra, Kaiga in Karnataka and Narora in Uttar Pradesh.
Biogas is made when bacteria decompose organic waste and animal dung. Seawater, uranium and coal are not used.
Solar energy is a non-conventional, renewable source. Coal, petroleum and firewood are conventional sources.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

questions.q: Iron ore is a:
questions.why: Iron ore contains iron, so it is a ferrous mineral. Non-ferrous minerals contain no iron.

questions.q: Extracting minerals near the surface by digging:
questions.why: Taking out minerals near the surface by digging is quarrying (open-cast). Drilling is for oil and shaft mining for deep deposits.

questions.q: Copper is used mainly in:
questions.why: Copper conducts electricity well, so it is used mainly in electrical wires. It is not used in paper, fertiliser or cement.

questions.q: Solar energy is a:
questions.why: Solar energy is a non-conventional, renewable source. Fossil fuels and firewood are conventional.

questions.q: Uranium deposits occur in:
options: Jharkhand and the Aravallis of Rajasthan
questions.why: Uranium deposits occur in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan. The Punjab plains, Kerala backwaters and Goa beaches are not known for it.

questions.q: Assertion: Minerals should be recycled. Reason: Minerals are non-renewable.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Minerals are non-renewable, so recycling them helps them last longer.

questions.q: Open-cast mining is used for minerals at:
questions.why: Open-cast mining is used for minerals lying at shallow depths, near the surface. Deep deposits need shaft mining.

questions.q: A geothermal site in India:
questions.why: The Puga Valley in Ladakh is a geothermal site in India. Jharia is a coalfield, Bombay High an oil field and Tarapur a nuclear plant.

questions.q: Which is non-metallic?
questions.why: Limestone is a non-metallic mineral. Copper, manganese and gold are metallic.

questions.q: Case: A coastal village with large tidal range wants local power. Which source is most suitable?
questions.why: A coastal village with a large tidal range can use the energy of tides. Uranium, coal and geothermal energy are not suited to that setting.

questions.q: Why is hydel power considered renewable?
options: Water is replenished by the water cycle
questions.why: Water in rivers is replenished by the water cycle, so hydel power is renewable. It does not burn water or coal.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: Kaiga is in Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu, so that pair is wrong. Kakrapar (Gujarat), Rawatbhata (Rajasthan) and Narora (Uttar Pradesh) are correct.

questions.q: Assertion: Nuclear energy has no environmental risks. Reason: Nuclear waste is radioactive and must be stored safely.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false, as nuclear energy has risks. The reason is true: nuclear waste is radioactive and has to be stored safely, so risks exist.

questions.q: Why are metallic minerals often found on large plateaus?
options: They occur in igneous and metamorphic rocks that form such plateaus
questions.why: Metallic minerals occur in igneous and metamorphic rocks, and these rocks form large plateaus like the Chotanagpur plateau. So minerals are found there.

questions.q: Case: A village switches from firewood to biogas. Two benefits:
options: Less deforestation and manure as by-product
questions.why: Biogas saves the trees that would be cut for firewood, so there is less deforestation. The leftover slurry is also good manure.

courses.title: Geography · Agriculture
courses.summary: Primary, secondary and tertiary activities; agriculture as a farm system; subsistence and commercial farming types; growing conditions and leading areas of major crops; agricultural development; and comparing farms in India and a developed country.
outcomes: Learners can classify economic activities
Learners can explain the farm system of inputs, processes and outputs
Learners can distinguish types of farming with examples from the world
Learners can describe conditions and regions for rice, wheat, millets, maize, cotton, jute, coffee and tea

lessons.title: Economic activities and the farm system

story.title: From wheat to bread to shop

scenes.text: A farmer grows wheat (primary).
A bakery turns flour into bread (secondary).
A truck and a shop deliver it to you (tertiary).

steps.title: Three types of activities
steps.body:
- **Primary:** extraction and production of natural resources — agriculture, fishing, gathering, mining, forestry.
- **Secondary:** processing these into goods — steel, bread, cloth.
- **Tertiary:** support services — transport, trade, banking, insurance, advertising.

Agriculture is a primary activity; in India about two-thirds of people depend on it (NCERT figure).

steps.title: Agriculture and related terms
steps.body: 'Agriculture' comes from Latin *ager* (field) + *cultura* (cultivation). Growing crops, fruits, vegetables, flowers and rearing livestock. Related: **sericulture** (rearing silkworms), **pisciculture** (fish), **viticulture** (grapes), **horticulture** (vegetables, flowers, fruits). **Arable land** is land on which crops are grown.

steps.title: Farm system
steps.body:
Agriculture is a **system**:

- **Inputs:** seeds, fertilisers, machinery, labour.
- **Operations (processes):** ploughing, sowing, irrigation, weeding, harvesting.
- **Outputs:** crops, wool, dairy and poultry products.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify: a fisherman, a cement factory worker, a bank clerk. → Primary, secondary, tertiary.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a bakery primary.
- Thinking agriculture means only crops (livestock is included).

activity.prompt: Primary, secondary or tertiary?

quiz.why: Agriculture is a primary activity because it uses natural resources like land, soil and water directly. Secondary activities make goods and tertiary ones give services.
Rearing silkworms to make silk is sericulture. Pisciculture is fish, viticulture grapes and horticulture fruits and flowers.

quiz.q: Which is an input in the farm system?
quiz.why: Seeds are put into the farm, so they are inputs. Crops, dairy products and wool are outputs.
Transport and banking give services, so they are tertiary activities. Primary ones use natural resources.
Viticulture is the cultivation of grapes, grown on vines. It is not flowers, fish or silkworms.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Types of farming

scenes.text: In a Vietnamese village, a family grows rice on a tiny plot by hand.
In the US Midwest, one farmer harvests hundreds of hectares by machine.
In Brazil, a coffee estate employs hundreds of workers.

steps.title: Subsistence farming
steps.body:
Practised to meet the needs of the farmer's family; low technology and household labour, small output.

- **Intensive subsistence:** small plot, simple tools, more labour; climate with many sunny days and fertile soil allows more than one crop a year; **rice** is the main crop, with wheat, maize, pulses and oilseeds; common in thickly populated areas of the **monsoon regions** of south, southeast and east Asia.
- **Primitive subsistence:** (a) **shifting cultivation** — a patch of forest is cleared by felling and burning; ashes added to soil; crops grown till fertility declines; then moved. Called **'slash and burn'**. Found in heavy-rainfall areas of the Amazon basin, tropical Africa, parts of southeast Asia and northeast India. Local names: **Milpa** (Mexico and Central America), **Roca** (Brazil), **Ladang** (Malaysia), **Jhum** (NE India). (b) **Nomadic herding** — herdsmen move from place to place with animals for fodder and water along defined routes; sheep, camels, yak, goats; semi-arid and arid regions of Sahara, Central Asia and parts of India like Rajasthan and Jammu & Kashmir.

steps.title: Commercial farming
steps.body:
Crops grown and animals reared for **sale** in the market; large areas and large capital; much machinery.

- **Commercial grain farming:** wheat and maize on vast areas in temperate grasslands of North America, Europe and Asia.
- **Mixed farming:** land used for growing food and fodder crops and rearing livestock — Europe, eastern USA, Argentina, southeast Australia, New Zealand, South Africa.
- **Plantations:** a single crop — tea, coffee, sugarcane, cashew, rubber, banana or cotton; large labour and capital; produce may be processed on the farm itself; transport network essential. Major plantations in tropical regions: rubber in Malaysia, coffee in Brazil, tea in India and Sri Lanka.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all Indian farming is subsistence — plantations (tea in Assam) are commercial.
- Mixing Milpa (Mexico) and Roca (Brazil).

activity.prompt: Match the shifting-cultivation name to the region

quiz.q: Main crop of intensive subsistence farming:
quiz.why: Rice is the main crop of intensive subsistence farming, especially in monsoon Asia. Coffee, tea and rubber are plantation crops.
Slash and burn is another name for shifting cultivation, where land is cleared by burning. It is not plantation or mixed farming.
Nomadic herding is found in dry regions like the Sahara and Central Asia, where herders move with their animals. It is not found in cities or the Ganga delta.
Plantations grow a single crop on a large area, mainly for sale. They are not for family food or many crops.
Mixed farming combines growing crops with rearing livestock. It is not mining or banking.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Major crops: food crops

scenes.text: Rice from Punjab or West Bengal, roti from wheat, ragi dosa, corn on the cob.
Each crop needs its own climate and soil.
Which countries lead in growing them?

steps.title: Rice
steps.body: Major food crop of the world; staple in tropical and subtropical regions. Needs **high temperature, high humidity and rainfall**; grows best in **alluvial clayey soil** that can retain water. **China** leads, followed by **India, Japan, Sri Lanka and Egypt**. In favourable conditions (West Bengal, Bangladesh) two or three crops a year are grown.

steps.title: Wheat
steps.body: Requires **moderate temperature and rainfall** during the growing season and **bright sunshine at harvest**; thrives in **well-drained loamy soil**. Grown extensively in USA, Canada, Argentina, Russia, Ukraine, Australia and India. In India it is grown in **winter**.

steps.title: Millets and maize
steps.body:
- **Millets** (jowar, bajra, ragi) are **coarse grains**; can grow on **less fertile and sandy soils**; hardy, need low rainfall and high to moderate temperature; highly nutritious. Grown in India, Nigeria, China and Niger.
- **Maize** requires **moderate temperature, rainfall and lots of sunshine**; needs well-drained fertile soils; used as food and fodder. Grown in North America, Brazil, China, Russia, Canada, India and Mexico.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why can millets grow in Rajasthan's sandy soils with low rain? → Millets are hardy crops that need little water and tolerate less fertile soils.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying wheat needs heavy rainfall (it needs moderate rain and bright sunshine at harvest).
- Thinking India leads world rice production (China leads).

activity.prompt: Which crop's growing conditions?

items.text: High temperature, humidity and rainfall; clayey alluvial soil
Moderate temperature and rain; bright sunshine at harvest
Sandy, less fertile soil; low rainfall; hardy
Moderate temperature and rainfall with lots of sunshine; fertile well-drained soil

quiz.why: China is the leading producer of rice, followed by India. Canada, the USA and Brazil produce far less.

quiz.q: Wheat in India is grown in:
quiz.why: Wheat in India is a rabi crop, sown in winter and harvested in spring. It is not grown in the monsoon or summer.
Jowar, bajra and ragi are millets, which are coarse grains. They are not beverages, oilseeds or fibre crops.
Rice needs plenty of water, so it grows best in alluvial clayey soil, which holds water. Sandy and rocky soils drain it away.
Maize is used both as food and as fodder for animals. It is not only a fuel, beverage or fibre.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Fibre and beverage crops; agricultural development

scenes.text: Jute sacks carry grain across India.
Coffee from Karnataka's hills, tea from Assam's slopes.
Better seeds, irrigation and machines raise yields — but differently on small and big farms.

steps.title: Fibre crops
steps.body:
- **Cotton:** needs **high temperature, light rainfall, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine**; grows best on **black and alluvial soils**. Leading producers: China, USA, India, Pakistan, Brazil and Egypt. Raw material for cotton textiles.
- **Jute** ('**golden fibre**'): grows on **alluvial soil**, needs **high temperature, heavy rainfall and humid climate**; grown in tropical areas; **India and Bangladesh** are leading producers.

steps.title: Beverage crops
steps.body:
- **Coffee:** needs **warm and wet climate** and **well-drained loamy soil**; hill slopes are suitable. **Brazil** is the leading producer, followed by Colombia and India.
- **Tea:** grown on plantations; needs **cool climate and well-distributed high rainfall**; well-drained loamy soils and **gentle slopes**; lots of labour for picking leaves. Kenya, India, China and Sri Lanka produce the best-quality tea.

steps.title: Agricultural development
steps.body: Efforts to increase farm production to meet growing demand: increasing the cropped area, growing more crops, improving irrigation, using fertilisers and **high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds**, and mechanisation. Developed countries have large, mechanised farms using computers and advanced technology (e.g. a typical farm in the USA is very large, and the farmer may use satellite and computer data). In India, most farmers have small holdings (often around 1–2 hectares), use family labour, and depend on monsoon rains and loans; government schemes, cooperatives and better access to seeds, credit and markets help.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is tea grown on gentle slopes? → Water drains well (tea roots must not be waterlogged) while rainfall is high.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cotton the 'golden fibre' (it's jute).
- Saying tea needs a hot, dry climate.

activity.prompt: Match the crop to its condition or leading producer
pairs: Cool climate, high rainfall, gentle slopes

quiz.why: Jute is called the golden fibre because of its golden colour and its value. Wool, silk and cotton have other names.

quiz.q: Cotton needs about how many frost-free days?
quiz.why: Cotton needs about 210 frost-free days to grow, along with warmth and sunshine. It cannot survive frost.
Brazil is the leading producer of coffee in the world. India, Japan and Kenya produce less.
Tea grows best on gentle slopes with good drainage, so water does not stand around the roots. It does not grow in deserts or flooded plains.

options: Using HYV seeds and better irrigation
quiz.why: Using high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds and better irrigation increases output. Reducing irrigation or fertilisers would lower it.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

questions.q: Agriculture is a ___ activity.
questions.why: Agriculture is a primary activity because it uses natural resources like land and water directly. Tertiary activities are services.

questions.q: Pisciculture means:
questions.why: Pisciculture means breeding fish. Sericulture is silkworms, floriculture flowers and viticulture grapes.

questions.q: Shifting cultivation in Brazil is called:
questions.why: Shifting cultivation in Brazil is called roca. Jhum is the Indian name, milpa is from Central America and ladang from Indonesia.

questions.q: Jute is called the:
questions.why: Jute is called the golden fibre because of its colour and value. It is not called silver fibre or white gold.

questions.q: Which is an output of the farm system?
questions.why: Dairy products come out of the farm system, so they are outputs. Seeds, labour and machinery are inputs.

questions.q: Assertion: Intensive subsistence farming is common in monsoon Asia. Reason: Dense population and fertile soils with many sunny days allow multiple crops on small plots.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Dense population, fertile soils and many sunny days let farmers grow several crops a year on small plots.

questions.q: Plantation crops include:
questions.why: Tea, coffee and rubber are plantation crops, grown as single cash crops over large areas. Millets, rice and wheat are not.

questions.q: Wheat requires at harvest:
questions.why: Wheat needs bright sunshine at harvest time for ripening. Rain or floods would damage the crop.

questions.q: Mixed farming is found in:
questions.why: Mixed farming is found in Europe, eastern USA and Argentina, among other places. It is not typical of the Sahara, the Amazon or Antarctica.

questions.q: Case: A farmer in sandy, dry Rajasthan with little irrigation wants a reliable food crop. Best choice:
questions.why: Millets like bajra are hardy and need little water, so they suit sandy, dry soil. Rice, jute and tea need much more water.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: Coffee needs a warm, wet climate and is damaged by frost, so that pair is wrong. The others are matched correctly.

questions.q: Nomadic herders move to:
options: Find fodder and water for animals
questions.why: Nomadic herders move from place to place to find fodder and water for their animals. They do not move to mine or sell land.

questions.q: Assertion: Commercial farming uses large capital and machinery. Reason: Crops are grown mainly for sale in the market on large areas.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Commercial farming grows crops for sale on large areas, which needs big capital and machines.

questions.q: Why do plantations need a good transport network?
options: They grow food for the family
Produce must reach processing units and markets quickly
questions.why: Plantation produce is sold, and it often needs processing. So a good transport network is needed to move it to processing units and markets fast.

questions.q: Case: A large US farm uses satellite data, computers and machines; a small Indian farm uses family labour and monsoon rain. The key difference is:
questions.why: The US farm has large scale, much capital and advanced technology, while the Indian farm is small and uses family labour and rain. That is the key difference.

questions.q: Which correctly orders the chain from field to customer?
options: Growing cotton (primary) → spinning cloth (secondary) → selling in a shop (tertiary)
questions.why: Cotton is grown in the field (primary), spun into cloth in a mill (secondary) and sold in a shop (tertiary). The other orders do not follow this chain.
