courses.title: Geography · Industries
courses.summary: Classifying industries by raw material, size and ownership; factors that decide where industries locate; the industrial system and industrial regions; industrial disasters and safety; and case studies of iron and steel, cotton textiles and information technology.
outcomes: Learners can classify industries by raw material, size and ownership with examples
Learners can explain factors affecting the location of industries
Learners can describe industrial disasters and safety measures
Learners can compare the iron and steel, cotton textile and IT industries in India and the world

lessons.title: Classifying industries

scenes.text: Thousands of dairy farmers in Gujarat pool their milk.
Their cooperative turns it into butter and cheese sold nationwide.
That's an agro-based, cooperative industry.

steps.title: Industry
steps.body: **Industry** refers to an economic activity concerned with production of goods, extraction of minerals or provision of services (e.g. iron and steel, coal mining, tourism).

steps.title: By raw material
steps.body:
- **Agro-based:** plant and animal products — food processing, vegetable oil, cotton textile, dairy, leather.
- **Mineral-based:** mineral ores — iron and steel, cement, aluminium, machine tools.
- **Marine-based:** products from sea and oceans — processed seafood, fish oil.
- **Forest-based:** forest produce — pulp and paper, pharmaceuticals, furniture, buildings.

steps.title: By size and ownership
steps.body:
- **Size:** **small-scale** (less capital and technology; often manual labour — silk weaving, food processing; **cottage/household** industries like basket weaving, pottery and handicrafts) vs **large-scale** (huge capital, advanced technology — automobiles, heavy machinery).
- **Ownership:** **private sector** (owned by individuals or a group — e.g. Tata Steel, Bajaj Auto Ltd); **public sector** (owned and run by the government — e.g. Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd, Steel Authority of India Ltd); **joint sector** (jointly by the state and individuals — e.g. Maruti Udyog Ltd was jointly owned by the Indian government and Suzuki); **cooperative sector** (owned and operated by producers or suppliers of raw materials, workers or both — e.g. Anand Milk Union Ltd (Amul) and Sudha Dairy).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify a paper mill: forest-based, usually large-scale; ownership may be private or public.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling cotton textile mineral-based (it's agro-based).
- Thinking cooperatives are government-owned.

activity.prompt: Classify by raw material

quiz.why: Amul is owned by milk producers, so it is in the cooperative sector. Public sector is owned by the government.

quiz.q: Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd is in the:
quiz.why: Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd is owned by the government, so it is public sector. Private sector is owned by individuals or companies.

quiz.q: Basket weaving at home is a:
quiz.why: Basket weaving done at home by a family is a cottage industry. It is small-scale and uses simple tools.
The cement industry depends on limestone, a mineral, so it is mineral-based. Agro-based ones use farm products.

quiz.q: Joint sector industries are owned by:
quiz.why: A joint sector industry is owned by the state and private individuals together. Maruti is an example.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Factors of location and the industrial system

scenes.text: In the early 1900s, explorers look for a site with iron ore, coal, water and a railway.
They pick a spot near the Subarnarekha river in Jharkhand.
Jamshedpur grows into a steel city.

steps.title: Factors of location
steps.body:
Raw material, land, water, labour, power, capital, transport and market. Industries are situated where some or all of these are easily available. Sometimes the **government provides incentives** (subsidised power, lower transport cost) to set up industries in backward areas.

Industrialisation often leads to the development of towns and cities.

steps.title: The industrial system
steps.body:
- **Inputs:** raw materials, labour, costs of land, transport, power and other infrastructure.
- **Processes:** activities that convert raw material into finished products.
- **Outputs:** end product and the income earned.

E.g. textile industry: cotton (input) → ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing, printing (processes) → shirt (output).

steps.title: Industrial regions
steps.body: Industrial regions emerge when a number of industries locate close to each other and share benefits. Major regions in the world: **eastern North America, western and central Europe, eastern Europe and eastern Asia** (mostly in temperate areas near sea ports and coal fields). In **India**: Mumbai–Pune cluster, Bangalore–Tamil Nadu region, Hugli region, Ahmedabad–Baroda region, Chottanagpur industrial belt, Vishakhapatnam–Guntur belt, Gurgaon–Delhi–Meerut region and the Kollam–Thiruvananthapuram industrial cluster.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why are many steel plants near coal and iron fields? → Raw materials are heavy and bulky; locating near them reduces transport cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 'market' as a factor.
- Confusing input (cotton) with output (shirt).

activity.prompt: Order the industrial system for a cotton shirt
items: Inputs: cotton, labour, power, transport
Ginning and spinning into yarn
Weaving into cloth
Dyeing and printing
Stitching into a shirt (output)
Selling and earning income

quiz.q: Which is NOT a factor of industrial location?
quiz.why: Raw material, labour, market, power and transport affect where industries are located. The colour of a factory has no effect.

quiz.q: In the industrial system, cotton is an:
quiz.why: Cotton is the raw material put into a textile industry, so it is an input. The cloth is the output.
The Hugli region in West Bengal is an Indian industrial region. The Amazon, Sahara and Siberia are not.

quiz.q: Governments give incentives to industries in:
quiz.why: Governments offer incentives to industries to move to backward areas, to bring jobs and balanced growth. They don't aim only at big cities or deserts.

quiz.q: World industrial regions are mostly in:
options: Temperate areas near ports and coal fields
quiz.why: Most world industrial regions are in temperate areas near ports and coalfields. Deserts, polar areas and rainforests are not suited to industry.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Industrial disasters and safety

scenes.text: A toxic gas leaks from a pesticide factory in Bhopal.
Thousands die; many more suffer lifelong illness.
Industrial safety can be a matter of life and death.

steps.title: Bhopal gas tragedy (1984)
steps.body: On **3 December 1984**, **methyl isocyanate (MIC)**, a highly poisonous gas, along with other gases, leaked from the **Union Carbide** pesticide factory in **Bhopal**. Officially about 3,598 people died (1989 figure); hundreds of thousands were affected, with many still suffering from blindness, impaired immune systems and other illnesses. It is one of the worst industrial disasters in history.

steps.title: Jaipur oil depot fire (2009)
steps.body: On **29 October 2009**, a massive fire broke out at the **Indian Oil Corporation** oil depot in **Jaipur**; people died and many were injured; the fire raged for over a week, and thousands had to be evacuated.

steps.title: Risk reduction measures
steps.body:
- Densely populated residential areas should be separated far from industrial areas.
- People living near industries should be aware of storage of toxic substances and their possible effects.
- Fire warning and fighting systems should be improved.
- Storage capacity of toxic substances should be limited.
- Pollution dispersion qualities should be improved.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why should homes not be built right next to chemical factories? → In an accident, toxic gases or fires affect nearby residents first and most severely.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Misdating Bhopal (it was 1984).
- Thinking disasters can't be prevented — many risks can be reduced with planning.

activity.prompt: Industrial-safety awareness checklist
items: Find out if any factory near your home stores hazardous chemicals
Know the local emergency number 112
Know your nearest open assembly point
Support zoning that keeps homes away from hazardous industries
Learn basic fire safety at school

quiz.q: Bhopal gas tragedy took place in:
quiz.why: The Bhopal gas tragedy took place on 3 December 1984. 1947 was independence and 1857 the Revolt.

quiz.q: The gas that leaked at Bhopal:
quiz.why: The gas that leaked at Bhopal was methyl isocyanate (MIC), a deadly toxic gas. It was not carbon dioxide, oxygen or nitrogen.

quiz.q: The Jaipur oil depot fire was in:
quiz.why: The Jaipur oil depot fire took place on 29 October 2009. 1984 was Bhopal.

options: Separate residential areas from industrial areas
quiz.why: Keeping residential areas apart from industrial areas reduces the risk to people if an accident occurs. Building homes beside factories raises it.
The Bhopal factory of Union Carbide produced pesticides. It did not make steel, textiles or software.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

lessons.title: Case studies: iron and steel, cotton textiles, IT

scenes.text: Jamshedpur makes steel; Pittsburgh in the USA did too.
Ahmedabad weaves cloth — the 'Manchester of India'.
Bengaluru writes software — India's 'Silicon Valley'.

steps.title: Iron and steel
steps.body: Called a **feeder industry** because its products are raw material for other industries. Inputs: **iron ore, coal and limestone**, with labour, capital, site and infrastructure; iron ore is smelted in a **blast furnace**. India: before 1947 there was only one plant — **Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO)**, set up in **1907** at **Jamshedpur** (Jharkhand) near the confluence of the **Subarnarekha** and **Kharkai** rivers; it got coal from **Jharia** coalfields and iron ore from **Noamundi and Badam Pahar** (Odisha/Jharkhand), and Kolkata provided a market. Other plants: Bhilai, Durgapur, Burnpur, Rourkela, Bokaro, Visakhapatnam, Salem, Bhadravati, Vijayanagar. **Pittsburgh** (USA) was an important steel city with local coal and nearby iron ore.

steps.title: Cotton textile
steps.body: Agro-based. India has a long tradition of fine cotton (e.g. Dhaka muslin, Masulipatnam chintz, Calicut calicos, Surat and Vadodara gold-embroidered cotton). The power loom introduced during the Industrial Revolution in England (18th century) changed everything. The first successful mechanised textile mill in India was established in **Mumbai in 1854**. **Ahmedabad** ('Manchester of India') has favourable humid climate, port nearness, cotton-growing hinterland, labour and market. **Osaka** in Japan ('Manchester of Japan') grew with flat land, humid climate, port, labour and imported cotton.

steps.title: Information technology
steps.body: The IT industry deals with storage, processing and distribution of information. Major hubs are near universities, research centres, good infrastructure and skilled labour. **Bengaluru** (on the Deccan Plateau, called the 'Silicon Plateau') has mild climate, institutes, and many IT companies; other hubs: Mumbai, New Delhi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata, Pune, Gurugram, Noida. **Silicon Valley** in California (USA) is a famous global IT hub.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is iron and steel called a feeder industry? → Its products (steel) feed other industries like automobiles, machinery and construction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying TISCO was set up after Independence (it was 1907).
- Calling Ahmedabad the 'Silicon Valley of India'.

activity.prompt: Match the place to its industry/nickname
pairs: IT hub on the Deccan Plateau

quiz.why: Iron and steel need iron ore, coal and limestone as raw materials. Cotton, silk, sand or fish and salt are not used.
TISCO (Tata Iron and Steel Company) was set up in 1907 at Jamshedpur. 1947 is independence.

quiz.q: First successful textile mill in India:
quiz.why: The first successful textile mill in India was set up in Mumbai in 1854. Ahmedabad grew later.

quiz.q: Iron and steel is called a feeder industry because:
options: Its products are raw materials for other industries
quiz.why: Iron and steel is called a feeder industry because its products serve as raw materials for other industries, like machinery. It has nothing to do with food.

quiz.q: Which city is called the Silicon Plateau?
quiz.why: Bengaluru is called the Silicon Plateau because it is an IT hub on the Deccan Plateau. Kolkata, Patna and Jaipur are not.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Geography — Resources and Development (topic)

questions.q: Cotton textile is:
questions.why: Cotton textile uses cotton, a plant product, so it is agro-based. Cement is mineral-based and paper forest-based.

questions.q: Public sector example:
questions.why: The Steel Authority of India Ltd is government-owned, so it is public sector. Amul is cooperative, and Tata Steel and Bajaj are private.

questions.q: The Bhopal gas tragedy happened in:
questions.why: The Bhopal gas tragedy happened on 3 December 1984. It is one of the worst industrial disasters.

questions.q: Inputs for steel include:
questions.why: Steel needs iron ore, coal and limestone. Fish, cotton, jute, wood and paper are not its inputs.

questions.q: Ahmedabad is known as the:
questions.why: Ahmedabad is called the Manchester of India because of its large textile industry. Manchester in England was a cotton textile centre.

questions.q: Assertion: Steel plants are often located near coal and iron ore mines. Reason: Raw materials are heavy and bulky, making transport costly.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Coal and iron ore are heavy and bulky and costly to carry, so plants are placed near them.

questions.q: Cooperative sector industry is owned by:
options: Producers/suppliers of raw materials, workers or both
questions.why: Cooperative sector industries are owned by the producers or suppliers of raw materials, the workers or both. They are not owned by one family or the government alone.

questions.q: TISCO gets coal from:
questions.why: TISCO at Jamshedpur gets its coal from Jharia in Jharkhand. Neyveli has lignite and Digboi oil.

questions.q: Which is a forest-based industry?
questions.why: Paper uses wood pulp from forests, so it is forest-based. Cement is mineral-based and dairy is animal-based.

questions.q: Case: A government offers cheap power and land to set up factories in an underdeveloped district. Why?
options: To encourage industry and jobs in backward areas
questions.why: Cheap power and land attract industry to backward areas. This creates jobs and helps these areas develop.

questions.q: Osaka grew as a textile centre because of:
options: Flat land, humid climate, port and labour
questions.why: Osaka grew as a textile centre because of flat land, a humid climate, a port and labour. It has no iron ore mines or oil wells for this.

questions.q: Which is a risk reduction measure for industrial disasters?
questions.why: Limiting the storage of toxic substances reduces the harm in case of an accident. Removing alarms, hiding information or building houses near factories raises the risk.

questions.q: Assertion: IT hubs develop near universities and research centres. Reason: IT needs skilled labour and knowledge.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. IT needs skilled people and knowledge, so it grows near universities and research centres.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: Maruti Udyog was a joint sector company, not cooperative, so that pair is wrong. Tata Steel is private, Amul cooperative and HAL public.

questions.q: In the industrial system of a steel plant, smelting in a blast furnace is a:
questions.why: Smelting in a blast furnace turns the inputs into iron, so it is the process. The ore and coal are inputs and steel is the output.

questions.q: Case: A city plans a new chemical factory 500 m from a crowded colony. Based on lessons from Bhopal, the best advice is:
options: Locate it far from residential areas with strict safety systems
questions.why: The Bhopal lesson is to place hazardous factories far from residential areas, with strict safety systems. Hiding information or removing fire services makes accidents worse.

questions.q: Why was Jamshedpur a good site for TISCO?
options: Near iron ore, coal, water (rivers), railway and the Kolkata market
questions.why: Jamshedpur had iron ore and coal nearby, rivers for water, rail links and the Kolkata market, all together. These factors made it a good site, not the sea or oil wells.
