courses.title: Civics Ch 1 · The Indian Constitution
courses.summary: Why a country needs a constitution, how India's Constitution was made, and its key features: federalism, parliamentary government, separation of powers, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties and secularism.
outcomes: Learners can explain why democracies need a constitution
Learners can describe the making of the Indian Constitution
Learners can explain federalism, parliamentary government and separation of powers
Learners can list the Fundamental Rights and explain why they matter

lessons.title: Why does a country need a constitution?

scenes.text: Class 8 forms a cricket club. Who decides captains? How are funds spent?
They write a set of rules everyone agrees to — and limits on what the captain can do.
A constitution is that, for a whole nation.

steps.title: What a constitution does
steps.body:
A **constitution** is a set of fundamental rules and principles by which a country is governed.

- It lays out the **ideals** that form the basis of the kind of country citizens want to live in (equality, liberty, justice).
- It defines the **nature of the political system** (e.g. India is a democracy).
- It contains **rules to prevent misuse of authority** by political leaders.
- It protects **minorities** from the **tyranny of the majority** — e.g. guaranteeing that minorities are not excluded from what the majority has access to.
- It saves us **from ourselves** — it protects us from decisions we might take in a moment of anger that harm our larger interests.

steps.title: Nepal as an example
steps.body: Nepal, for a long period, was a monarchy; after a long struggle including a people's movement in 2006, the country moved towards democracy and adopted a new Constitution in **2015**, reflecting the ideals of the struggle.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why must a constitution limit the powers of a majority government? → Otherwise it could pass laws that discriminate against minorities or curb freedoms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a constitution is only a list of laws — it sets ideals and limits power too.
- Thinking only monarchies need constitutions.

statements.s: A constitution lays down the ideals of a society.
Constitutions protect minorities from the tyranny of the majority.
A constitution has no role in limiting leaders' power.
Nepal adopted a new Constitution in 2015.

options: A set of fundamental rules for governing a country
quiz.why: A constitution is a set of fundamental rules by which a country is governed. It is not a timetable, a bank paper or a film rulebook.

options: The majority imposing its will unfairly on minorities
quiz.why: Tyranny of the majority means the majority imposes its will on minorities in an unfair way. A constitution protects against this danger.

quiz.q: A constitution saves us from ourselves by:
options: Preventing hasty decisions that harm long-term interests
quiz.why: A constitution stops us from taking hasty decisions that could harm our long-term interests, so it saves us from ourselves. It does not ban elections or make us rich.

quiz.q: Which is a role of a constitution?
options: Define the nature of the political system
quiz.why: A constitution defines the nature of the political system, i.e. how power is shared and used. It does not name streets or fix daily prices.
Nepal adopted its new Constitution in 2015, after the 2006 people's movement ended monarchy's rule. 1950 and 1947 are Indian dates.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Making the Constitution

scenes.text: From December 1946, about 300 members of the Constituent Assembly meet in Delhi.
They study constitutions of many countries and debate every article.
On 26 January 1950 the Constitution comes into force.

steps.title: The Constituent Assembly
steps.body: By the 1930s the Indian National Congress had demanded a Constituent Assembly. In **December 1946**, about **300** Indians who were members of the **Constituent Assembly** began meeting to write the Constitution; they met till **November 1949**. The Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** (now observed as Constitution Day) and came into effect on **26 January 1950** (Republic Day). Members came from different regions, religions, languages and backgrounds and had very different views; they worked through debate to reach agreement. **Dr B.R. Ambedkar** was the **Chairman of the Drafting Committee**; he is often called the 'Father of the Indian Constitution'.

steps.title: Challenges they faced
steps.body: India was a land of huge diversity, very poor after colonial rule, and was facing the violence of Partition and the integration of princely states. The Constitution had to unite people, protect democracy and work for social and economic justice.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is 26 January celebrated as Republic Day? → The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 (also echoing Purna Swaraj Day, 26 January 1930).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing 26 November 1949 (adopted) with 26 January 1950 (came into force).
- Thinking the Constitution was written by one person — it was a collective effort.

activity.prompt: Order the making of the Constitution

quiz.q: The Constitution came into force on:
quiz.why: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, now celebrated as Republic Day. 26 November 1949 is the day it was adopted.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar was the chairman of the Drafting Committee. Patel, Prasad and Nehru had other roles.

quiz.q: The Constituent Assembly first met in:
quiz.why: The Constituent Assembly first met in December 1946. 15 August 1947 is independence and January 1950 when the Constitution came into force.

quiz.q: About how many members were in the Constituent Assembly?
quiz.why: The Constituent Assembly had about 300 members, as per NCERT. 543 is the number of Lok Sabha seats.
Constitution Day, 26 November, marks the adoption of the Constitution in 1949. It came into force later, on 26 January 1950.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Key features: federalism, parliamentary government, separation of powers

scenes.text: Your panchayat fixes the village well; your state runs the police; the Union runs the army.
You will vote for all of them once you turn 18.
And no single organ holds all the power.

steps.title: Federalism
steps.body: More than one level of government: at the **Centre (Union)**, the **States** and the **Panchayati Raj**/local level. Each level has independent powers; the Constitution has lists of subjects: **Union List**, **State List** and **Concurrent List** (both can make laws). Each state enjoys autonomy on some issues; on matters of national concern, all states follow central laws.

steps.title: Parliamentary form of government
steps.body: Representatives at every level are elected by the people. The Constitution guarantees **universal adult franchise** — every adult citizen (**18 years and above**) has the right to vote, irrespective of caste, religion, gender, education or wealth. Citizens can choose their representatives directly; the government is accountable to the legislature, which is accountable to the people.

steps.title: Separation of powers
steps.body: Three organs of the State: **legislature** (our elected representatives, makes laws), **executive** (a smaller group that implements laws and runs the government), **judiciary** (system of courts). To prevent misuse of power, the Constitution says each organ should exercise different powers and **check** the others, maintaining a balance.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is universal adult franchise a radical feature? → In 1950 many older democracies had only recently given votes to all; India gave every adult equal vote from the start, regardless of wealth, gender or education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the 'executive' means only the President (it includes ministers and the administration).
- Confusing federal (levels) with parliamentary (elected representatives).

activity.prompt: Match the organ to its work
pairs: Implements laws and runs the government
Subjects on which both Union and States can make laws

quiz.why: Voting age in India is 18 years, under universal adult franchise. It was lowered from 21 to 18.
India has three levels of government: the Union, the State and the local (Panchayati Raj) level. Federalism means more than one level.

options: Misuse of power by any one organ
quiz.why: Separation of powers divides power among the legislature, executive and judiciary. It prevents any one organ from misusing power, through checks and balances.
The executive implements the laws and runs the government. The legislature makes laws and the judiciary interprets them.

quiz.q: Subjects for both Union and states are in the:
quiz.why: Subjects on which both the Union and the states can make laws are in the Concurrent List. The Union List and State List are separate.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights, duties and secularism

scenes.text: A 12-year-old is made to work in a factory instead of going to school.
The Constitution says: no child under 14 may work in factories or hazardous jobs; every child 6–14 has the right to education.
Fundamental Rights protect citizens against the arbitrary use of State power.

steps.title: The Fundamental Rights
steps.body:
Called the **'conscience'** of the Constitution, they protect citizens against the arbitrary and absolute exercise of power by the State, and protect minorities. The Constitution guarantees:

- **Right to Equality:** all persons equal before the law; no discrimination on grounds of religion, caste, gender or place of birth; equal access to public places; **untouchability abolished**.
- **Right to Freedom:** of speech and expression, to form associations, to move freely and reside in any part of the country, to practise any profession, occupation or business.
- **Right against Exploitation:** prohibits human trafficking, forced labour and employment of children under 14 years in factories and hazardous work.
- **Right to Freedom of Religion.**
- **Cultural and Educational Rights:** minorities can set up their own educational institutions to preserve their culture.
- **Right to Constitutional Remedies:** citizens can move the court if they believe any Fundamental Right has been violated by the State. Dr Ambedkar called it the **'heart and soul'** of the Constitution.

The **Right to Education** (free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14) was added later as part of the right to life and liberty.

steps.title: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
steps.body: **Directive Principles of State Policy** guide the government to introduce social and economic reforms and reduce poverty (not enforceable in courts, but fundamental to governance). **Fundamental Duties** list citizens' duties, such as respecting the Constitution, national flag and anthem, protecting the environment, and promoting harmony.

steps.title: Secular State
steps.body: India is a **secular** state: it does not officially promote any one religion as the state religion. (Explored in the next chapter.)

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: If a person's freedom of speech is unfairly restricted by a government order, what can they do? → Use the Right to Constitutional Remedies — approach the High Court or Supreme Court.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Directive Principles are enforceable in courts like Fundamental Rights.
- Forgetting that Fundamental Rights are not absolute — reasonable restrictions apply.

activity.prompt: Which Fundamental Right does it relate to?

items.text: Moving to any state to live and work
No child under 14 in hazardous work
Going to the Supreme Court when a right is violated

quiz.q: Which right did Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.why: Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies the heart and soul of the Constitution because it lets citizens go to court to enforce their other rights.

quiz.q: Children under ___ cannot be employed in factories or hazardous work.
quiz.why: Under the Right against Exploitation, children below 14 cannot be employed in factories or hazardous work. This protects them from exploitation.
Untouchability is abolished under the Right to Equality. Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties do not abolish it.

options: Guide the government on social and economic reforms
quiz.why: Directive Principles guide the government in making policies for social and economic reforms. They cannot be enforced by courts, unlike Fundamental Rights.

quiz.q: Minorities' right to set up their own schools is under:
quiz.why: The right of minorities to set up their own schools falls under Cultural and Educational Rights. It protects their language and culture.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: Indian Constitution came into force on:
questions.why: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. 15 August 1947 is independence and 26 November 1949 is the date of adoption.

questions.q: Chairman of the Drafting Committee:
questions.why: B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly. Gandhi was not a member of it.

questions.q: Voting age for universal adult franchise:
questions.why: In universal adult franchise every citizen aged 18 or above can vote. The age is not 21 or 25 now.

questions.q: Which organ makes laws?
questions.why: The legislature (Parliament) makes laws. The executive carries them out and the judiciary interprets them.

questions.q: Federalism means:
options: More than one level of government
questions.why: Federalism means there is more than one level of government, such as the Union and state governments. It is not rule by one king or the army.

questions.q: Assertion: The Constitution protects minorities. Reason: It guards against the tyranny of the majority.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The Constitution guards minorities against the tyranny of the majority, so it protects them.

questions.q: Right against Exploitation prohibits:
questions.why: The Right against Exploitation prohibits forced labour and trafficking, and child labour in hazardous jobs. It does not ban speech, voting or religion.

questions.q: Which is a Fundamental Duty?
questions.why: Protecting the natural environment is a Fundamental Duty of citizens. Avoiding taxes, elections or disrespecting the flag are not duties.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly met from:
questions.why: The Constituent Assembly worked from December 1946 until November 1949, when the Constitution was adopted. It did not meet from 1947 to 1950 only.

questions.q: Case: A state passes a law on a subject in the Concurrent List; Parliament later passes a conflicting law on the same subject. Generally:
questions.why: For subjects in the Concurrent List, if a state law and a Union law conflict, the Union law prevails. Both are not cancelled.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: The judiciary settles disputes, so that pair is correct. The legislature makes laws, not courts, and the executive does more than make laws.

questions.q: Why is separation of powers important?
options: To ensure no single organ misuses power; each checks the others
questions.why: Separation of powers ensures that no single organ misuses power, because each can check the others. It does not remove elections or give the army power.

questions.q: Assertion: Directive Principles can be enforced in courts like Fundamental Rights. Reason: Directive Principles guide the government in making policies.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because Directive Principles cannot be enforced in court like Fundamental Rights. The reason is true: they guide the government in making policy.

questions.q: Case: A school refuses admission to a child because of her caste. Which right is violated?
questions.why: Refusing admission because of caste is discrimination, which violates the Right to Equality. The Constitution bans discrimination on grounds like caste.

questions.q: Why is universal adult franchise significant for democracy?
options: Every adult has an equal say regardless of wealth, caste, gender or education
questions.why: Universal adult franchise gives every adult one equal vote, no matter their wealth, caste, gender or education. This is a basic equality in democracy.

questions.q: A constitution 'saves us from ourselves' means:
options: It makes us vote one way
It prevents decisions taken in passion that might hurt long-term interests
questions.why: A constitution stops us from taking decisions in passion or haste that might hurt our long-term interests. It does not control our votes, opinions or diet.

courses.title: Civics Ch 2 · Understanding Secularism
courses.summary: What secularism means, why separating religion from the State matters, and the strategies the Indian State uses — distance, non-interference and intervention — compared with secularism in other countries.
outcomes: Learners can define secularism and explain why it is important
Learners can explain how religious domination can lead to discrimination
Learners can describe the three strategies of Indian secularism
Learners can compare Indian secularism with that of other countries

lessons.title: What is secularism and why is it important?

scenes.text: Meera's school calendar has Diwali, Eid, Christmas, Guru Purab and Navroz.
The government school does not promote any one religion.
Everyone's faith is respected; no one's is imposed.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Secularism** refers to the **separation of religion from the State**. The State does not promote or favour any one religion, and allows citizens freedom to practise, profess and propagate any religion — or none.

steps.title: Why separate?
steps.body:
- To prevent the **domination** of one religious group over others (which can lead to discrimination, coercion or even violence against minorities).
- To protect the freedom of individuals to **exit** their religion, embrace another, or interpret religious teachings differently.
- History shows dangers: e.g. in Nazi Germany, the persecution and killing of Jews was carried out by the State. When State power is used for one religion, minorities suffer.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is it a problem if a government gives jobs only to followers of one religion? → It discriminates against others and violates equality — the State must treat all equally.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking secularism means being against religion — it means the State stays separate and neutral.
- Thinking only minorities benefit — everyone's freedom is protected.

statements.s: Secularism means separation of religion from the State.
A secular State promotes one official religion.
Secularism protects the freedom to interpret religion differently.
Secularism means citizens cannot follow any religion.

options: Separation of religion from the State
quiz.why: Secularism means religion is kept separate from the State, so the State is not run by any religion. It does not ban religion.

options: Prevent domination by one religious group
quiz.why: Secularism prevents one religious group from dominating others, so everyone has equal freedom. It does not promote one religion or stop festivals.
A secular State does not favour any religion. It does not force conversions, fund only one faith or ban worship.

options: Interpret religion differently or change religion
quiz.why: Secularism protects the freedom to interpret one's religion differently or to change it. It does not allow discrimination or forcing others.

quiz.q: Historical example of State-led religious persecution in NCERT:
quiz.why: Nazi Germany persecuted Jews, which shows how a State can persecute people for their religion. It is the NCERT example.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Indian secularism: three strategies

scenes.text: A law says motorcycle riders must wear helmets.
For Sikhs, wearing a turban (pugri) is central to their faith.
Indian law exempts turbaned Sikhs — respecting religion without favouring it.

steps.title: 1. Distance
steps.body: The State distances itself from religion: e.g. **government spaces** such as law courts, police stations, government schools and offices are not supposed to display or promote any one religion. Government schools cannot promote any religion through morning prayers or celebrations.

steps.title: 2. Non-interference
steps.body: To respect the sentiments of all religions and not interfere with religious practices, the State makes certain exceptions for particular communities: e.g. **Sikhs are exempted from wearing helmets** because the pugri is central to their faith.

steps.title: 3. Intervention
steps.body: To prevent religion-based exclusion and discrimination of 'lower castes', the Constitution **bans untouchability**. The State may intervene in religious practices to ensure equality — e.g. ensuring daughters have a share in family property (in Hindu inheritance laws). Intervention is also seen in State support to communities: the Constitution grants the right to set up their own schools and colleges, and the State may give them financial aid on a non-preferential basis.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify: (a) a government school not holding religious prayers; (b) exemption for Sikhs from helmet rules; (c) the ban on untouchability. → (a) distance, (b) non-interference, (c) intervention.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking intervention means the State promotes a religion — it intervenes to protect rights.
- Thinking secularism means the State never deals with religion.

activity.prompt: Which strategy of Indian secularism?

items.text: No religious display in a police station
Government school doesn't hold religious prayers
Daughters get equal share in family property

quiz.q: Exemption for Sikhs from helmet rules is an example of:
quiz.why: Exempting Sikhs from helmet rules respects their religious practice, so the State does not interfere. It is non-interference.

quiz.q: Banning untouchability is an example of:
quiz.why: Banning untouchability means the State steps in to stop a harmful religious practice. That is intervention to protect equality.

quiz.q: Government offices not displaying one religion is:
quiz.why: Government offices that do not display symbols of one religion keep a distance between State and religion. This is distance, as it shows neutrality.

quiz.q: Minorities can set up their own schools; the State may give aid:
quiz.why: Minorities may set up schools, and the State can give aid on a non-preferential basis, i.e. without favouring any religion. This keeps it fair.

quiz.q: Indian secularism allows the State to:
options: Intervene in religion to ensure equality
quiz.why: Indian secularism allows the State to intervene in religion when needed to ensure equality, for example to end untouchability. It does not ban faiths.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Indian and other secularisms; living secularism

scenes.text: In the USA, the Constitution's First Amendment forbids the legislature from making laws 'respecting an establishment of religion'.
In India, the State can intervene in religion to end injustice.
Both are secular — in different ways.

steps.title: Comparing with the USA
steps.body:
In the **USA**, the State and religion are strictly separate: the State cannot interfere in religion and religion cannot interfere in State affairs (the **First Amendment** prohibits the legislature from making laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise of religion). Most children there study in public schools that do not begin with religious prayers.

In **India**, the State can **intervene** in religious affairs (e.g. to ban untouchability). This is a key difference.

steps.title: Living secularism
steps.body: Secularism is not only for governments. It is practised every day when people celebrate each other's festivals, oppose hateful speech, help neighbours of other faiths and refuse to discriminate. Majority domination can occur in subtle ways — constant vigilance by citizens, media and courts protects secularism.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why can the Indian State intervene in religion but the US State generally cannot? → The Indian Constitution aims to end social inequalities rooted in some religious practices, so it allows intervention; the US model emphasises strict separation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all secular states are identical.
- Thinking secularism is only the job of courts.

a.text: A classmate shares a joke mocking another religion in the class group chat. What do you do?

choices.label: Say calmly that it's hurtful and ask them to delete it

w.text: Forwarding can hurt many people and spread hate. Let's undo that: apologise and delete it.

b.text: The classmate says 'It's just a joke'. Your next step?

choices.label: Explain that jokes that target someone's faith can hurt; suggest a teacher if it continues
choices.feedback: Good — and seek adult help if needed.

w2.text: Responding with hate makes things worse. Choose respect and seek help.

choices.label: Talk respectfully and involve a teacher

e.text: Living secularism means respecting all faiths — in everyday actions.

quiz.q: In the USA, strict separation is guaranteed by the:
quiz.why: In the USA, the First Amendment keeps State and religion strictly separate. India's model differs from it.

quiz.q: A key difference of Indian secularism:
options: The State can intervene in religion to ensure equality
The State has an official religion
quiz.why: Indian secularism allows the State to intervene in religion to ensure equality, which makes it different from the strict US model. It has no official religion.
Living secularism means respecting others and celebrating their festivals together. Discrimination or hateful jokes go against it.
Secularism is protected by citizens, the media and the courts together, who stay watchful. It is not left to the police or leaders alone.

options: Is the same as a state religion
quiz.why: Secularism takes different forms in different countries, depending on their history. It is not identical everywhere, and is not a state religion.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: Secularism means:
options: Separation of religion from the State
questions.why: Secularism means separating religion from the State. It is not rule by priests or a state religion.

questions.q: Indian Constitution bans:
questions.why: The Indian Constitution bans untouchability, which is a discriminatory practice. It does not ban religions, prayers or festivals.

questions.q: Sikhs' exemption from helmets reflects:
questions.why: Exempting Sikhs from helmets respects their practice without interfering, so it shows non-interference. It is not intervention.

questions.q: Government schools in India:
options: Should not promote any one religion
Must hold prayers of one faith
questions.why: Government schools should not promote any one religion, to keep distance between State and religion. They need not close on all festivals.

questions.q: Assertion: Secularism protects minorities. Reason: It prevents domination of one religious group through State power.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. By preventing one religious group from using State power to dominate, secularism protects minorities.

questions.q: Which is an example of intervention?
questions.why: A law ensuring daughters' property rights is intervention in personal practice to promote equality. Holidays, courts without symbols and turban exemptions are other things.

questions.q: The US model of secularism:
options: Allows State intervention to reform religion
questions.why: The US model strictly separates State and religion, under the First Amendment. It does not ban worship or have a state religion.

questions.q: Case: A government office displays symbols of only one religion at its entrance. Which principle is violated?
questions.why: Showing symbols of only one religion at a government office breaks the distance between State and religion. The State should stay neutral.

questions.q: Why do individuals need protection within their own religion?
options: To be free to interpret it differently or leave it
questions.why: People need protection within their religion so they can interpret it differently or even leave it. This is freedom within religion.

questions.q: Assertion: Indian secularism forbids the State from ever dealing with religion. Reason: The State intervenes to end discrimination like untouchability.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because Indian secularism does allow the State to deal with religion when needed. The reason is true: it intervenes, for example, to end untouchability.

questions.q: Minority institutions may receive State aid:
questions.why: Minority institutions may receive State aid on a non-preferential basis, so no faith is favoured. It is not never or only for one faith.

questions.q: Case: Students of all faiths organise a joint festival celebration at school. This shows:
questions.why: Students of all faiths celebrating together is living secularism, respecting each other's festivals. It is not discrimination or State intervention.

questions.q: Which best explains why the State must not be run by one religion?
options: It can use its power to discriminate against others
questions.why: If one religion ran the State, it could use State power to discriminate against others. That is why the State must not be run by any religion.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
options: Minority schools' right — cultural and educational rights
No religious prayers in government schools — distance
questions.why: The turban exemption is non-interference, not intervention, so that pair is wrong. The other pairs are correctly matched.

questions.q: Secularism is mainly concerned with:
options: Relations between religion and the State, and freedom of individuals
questions.why: Secularism deals with the relation between religion and the State, and the freedom of individuals. It is not about sports, foreign policy or growth.

courses.title: Civics Ch 3 · Parliament and the Making of Laws
courses.summary: Why India has a Parliament, how people participate through elections, the two Houses and their roles (selecting and controlling the government, law-making), who our MPs are, how laws are made, and how citizens respond to unpopular or controversial laws.
outcomes: Learners can explain why Parliament is central to democracy
Learners can describe the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha and their roles
Learners can explain how a Bill becomes a law
Learners can describe how citizens influence and question laws

lessons.title: Why do we need a Parliament?

scenes.text: Grandma remembers voting in India's first general election (1951–52).
Her vote counted exactly as much as a factory owner's.
Through their votes, people send representatives to Parliament.

steps.title: Participation and consent
steps.body:
The idea of **consent** — the desire, approval and participation of people — is central to democracy. The decisions of a democratic government are taken by representatives chosen by the people. In India, **universal adult franchise** lets every citizen aged **18 and above** vote. The freedom struggle had demanded this; it was guaranteed by the Constitution.

Individuals elect representatives; through them they participate in decision-making and can **question** the government. The **Parliament** is the final authority for making laws in India — it enables citizens to participate in decision-making and control the government.

steps.title: Elections
steps.body: The country is divided into **constituencies**; each elects one representative to the **Lok Sabha**. The candidate with the most votes wins (Members of Parliament, MPs). Lok Sabha elections are normally held every **five years**. Political parties contest; independent candidates may too.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is universal adult franchise important for consent? → Every adult's approval counts equally, so the government gets its authority from all the people.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only educated or property-owning citizens can vote.
- Confusing constituency (area) with party.

statements.s: Every Indian citizen aged 18 and above can vote.
Parliament is the final authority for making laws.
Lok Sabha elections are held every year.
Each constituency elects one MP to the Lok Sabha.

quiz.why: Consent in a democracy means that people approve of the rulers and take part in decisions. Rule by force or one person goes against it.

quiz.q: Lok Sabha elections are normally held every:
quiz.why: Lok Sabha elections are normally held every 5 years, the term of the House. This lets people change their government.

quiz.q: An area that elects one MP is a:
quiz.why: An area that elects one MP is a constituency. A ward or a panchayat is a local unit.
The voting age is 18 years under universal adult franchise. It is not 21 or 25 now.

options: Participate in decisions and question government
quiz.why: Elected representatives let citizens take part in decisions and question the government. They don't remove laws or elections.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: The two Houses and their roles

scenes.text: At 11 a.m., an MP asks the Railway Minister why trains in her area are always late.
The minister must answer with facts.
That's Parliament controlling and guiding the government.

steps.title: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
steps.body:
Parliament consists of the **President**, the **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States) and the **Lok Sabha** (House of the People).

- **Lok Sabha:** **543** elected members from constituencies (Anglo-Indian nominated seats were discontinued in 2020).
- **Rajya Sabha:** represents the **states**; members (up to **250**) are elected by members of state Legislative Assemblies, and **12** are nominated by the President for their contribution to literature, science, art and social service. It can initiate legislation; a Bill must pass both Houses to become law; it reviews and can alter laws initiated by the Lok Sabha.

steps.title: Roles of Parliament
steps.body:
- **Selecting the national government:** after elections, the party (or coalition) with a **majority** in the Lok Sabha (at least **272** of 543) forms the government. The executive is headed by the **Prime Minister**, who selects ministers.
- **Controlling, guiding and informing the government:** e.g. **Question Hour** — MPs ask questions to elicit information and keep the government accountable. The **Opposition** plays a crucial role in highlighting drawbacks.
- **Law-making:** Parliament makes laws for the country; it also approves the budget (government's spending needs Parliament's approval).

steps.title: Who are our MPs?
steps.body: Parliament today has MPs from varied backgrounds — more from rural areas and many regional parties. Seats are **reserved** in the Lok Sabha for **Scheduled Castes** and **Scheduled Tribes**. In 2023 a constitutional amendment (the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) was passed to reserve **one-third** of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women; it is to take effect after the next census and delimitation.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A coalition of three parties together has 280 seats. Can it form the government? → Yes, it has more than 272, a majority of 543.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Prime Minister is directly elected by all voters (the majority party/coalition in the Lok Sabha chooses the PM).
- Saying Rajya Sabha members are elected directly by people.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: House of the People; directly elected
Council of States; elected by state legislators
Parties not in government that question it
Alliance of parties forming a government
Majority mark in a 543-member Lok Sabha

quiz.q: Majority needed in the Lok Sabha to form government:
quiz.why: A majority needs more than half of the 543 seats, i.e. 272, to form a government in the Lok Sabha. Half plus one makes a majority.

quiz.q: Rajya Sabha members are elected by:
quiz.why: Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by the members of the state Legislative Assemblies. Voters do not elect them directly.

quiz.q: Number of Rajya Sabha members nominated by the President:
quiz.why: The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha, for their contribution to fields like arts, science and literature.
Question Hour lets MPs ask ministers questions, so Parliament can control the government and be informed. It makes the government answerable.

quiz.q: The head of the government (executive) in India:
quiz.why: The Prime Minister heads the government (executive) in India. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice heads the judiciary.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: How a law is made

scenes.text: Women's groups document cases of violence at home.
They campaign for years; a Bill is drafted and debated.
In 2005 Parliament passes the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- A proposed law is called a **Bill**. It may be introduced by a minister or a member.
- It is **debated**, discussed in committees, and **voted on** in both Houses.
- After passing both Houses it goes to the **President** for **assent**; then it becomes an **Act** (law).

Citizens play a role: issues are raised by people, newspapers, organisations; parliamentary committees may invite public opinion.

steps.title: Case: Domestic violence law
steps.body: Domestic violence includes injury or harm (physical, sexual, verbal, emotional, economic abuse) by an adult male, usually the husband, against a woman in the household. Women's groups campaigned through the 1990s; a Bill was introduced in 2002; after public consultation and committee recommendations, the **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act** was passed in **2005** (in force from 2006). It gives women the right to live in their shared household, protection orders, and monetary relief.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is public participation important in law-making? → People affected know the problem best; their views make laws fair and workable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a Bill becomes law after one House passes it.
- Forgetting the President's assent.

activity.prompt: Order the steps for a Bill to become a law
items: An issue is raised by citizens, groups or the media
A Bill is drafted and introduced in Parliament
Debate and committee review
Passed by both Houses
President gives assent
It becomes an Act (law)

quiz.q: A proposed law is called a:
quiz.why: A proposed law is called a Bill. It becomes an Act only after it is passed and assented to.

options: Both Houses pass it and the President assents
quiz.why: A Bill becomes law after both Houses pass it and the President gives assent. Lok Sabha alone or the PM's signature is not enough.

quiz.q: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was passed in 2005 and came into force in 2006. It gives women legal protection at home.

options: Physical, emotional, verbal and economic abuse
quiz.why: Domestic violence covers physical, emotional, verbal and economic abuse, not just physical injury. The Act has a broad definition.
The President gives assent to Bills passed by Parliament, and then they become law. The Speaker or Chief Justice does not.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Unpopular and controversial laws

scenes.text: A city passes a rule restricting street vendors from most areas.
Vendors protest: 'We have a right to earn a livelihood!'
They also approach the courts — laws can be questioned.

steps.title: When laws are questioned
steps.body: Sometimes laws passed by Parliament are **constitutionally valid** but unpopular, or seen as unfair by some groups. People can criticise them, hold public meetings, write in newspapers, report to TV channels, and lobby their MPs. If a law violates the Constitution, citizens can approach the **courts**, which can modify or cancel laws that don't adhere to the Constitution (judicial review).

steps.title: Role of citizens
steps.body: Citizens' role does not end with voting. They can use newspapers, media, peaceful protests and petitions to keep track of the work of MPs and criticise actions. In a democracy, people's voices can lead to laws being reconsidered.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A municipal rule bans street vendors from all public spaces. Which fundamental right might vendors argue is affected? → Right to Freedom to practise any profession, occupation, trade or business (with reasonable restrictions).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking that once a law is passed it can never be changed.
- Thinking protest must be violent — peaceful, democratic methods are effective and lawful.

activity.prompt: Ways I can take part in democracy before I turn 18
items: Read and discuss news about Parliament
Write a polite letter to my MP or local representative about a local problem
Join a school debate on a current Bill
Encourage adults in my family to vote
Learn the name of my Lok Sabha constituency and MP

quiz.q: If a law violates the Constitution, citizens can:
quiz.why: If a law violates the Constitution, citizens can approach the courts, which can set it aside. This is called judicial review.

quiz.q: Peaceful ways to oppose an unpopular law include:
quiz.why: Peaceful ways to oppose a law include petitions, public meetings and using the media. Violence and destroying property are not democratic.

options: Modify or cancel laws that violate the Constitution
quiz.why: Courts can modify or cancel laws that violate the Constitution, through judicial review. They cannot make all laws or elect MPs.

quiz.q: Citizens' role in democracy ends after voting.
options: False — they keep questioning and participating
quiz.why: The statement is false because citizens keep questioning and taking part after voting. Active citizenship continues between elections.

quiz.q: A vendor's right to earn is connected to the right to:
quiz.why: A vendor's right to earn a living is part of the right to practise any profession or occupation, under the Right to Freedom. It does not mean free housing.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: Indian Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and:
questions.why: Parliament consists of the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The Supreme Court and the Election Commission are not part of it.

questions.q: Lok Sabha elected seats:
questions.why: The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats, one from each constituency. 245 is about the elected Rajya Sabha size.

questions.q: A proposed law is called a:
questions.why: A proposed law is a Bill. After it is passed and signed it becomes an Act.

questions.q: Members of Rajya Sabha are elected by:
questions.why: Rajya Sabha members are elected by the state Legislative Assemblies, so it is indirect election. The people vote directly only for the Lok Sabha.

questions.q: Majority to form a government in Lok Sabha:
questions.why: A majority needs 272 of the 543 Lok Sabha seats, which is half plus one. 200 is too few.

questions.q: Assertion: Question Hour strengthens democracy. Reason: It makes the government answerable to elected representatives.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Question Hour makes the government answer to elected representatives, which strengthens democracy.

questions.q: The executive is headed by:
questions.why: The executive is headed by the Prime Minister. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice heads the courts.

questions.q: Domestic Violence Act was passed in:
questions.why: The Domestic Violence Act was passed in 2005. It protects women from violence at home.

questions.q: Case: No single party wins 272 seats; three parties together cross 272 and form the government. This is:
questions.why: When no single party has a majority and several parties join together to cross 272 and form a government, it is a coalition government. It is not a dictatorship.

questions.q: Why do Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes have reserved seats?
options: To ensure representation of groups historically excluded
questions.why: Seats are reserved for SC and ST so groups that were historically excluded get representation. It is not to favour the rich or change Parliament's size.

questions.q: Assertion: A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha alone becomes law. Reason: The Rajya Sabha has no role in law-making.
questions.why: Both are false. A Bill needs the approval of both Houses and the President, and the Rajya Sabha does play a role in law-making.

questions.q: The 2023 women's reservation amendment provides for:
options: One-third seats for women in Lok Sabha and state assemblies, after delimitation following the next census
questions.why: The 2023 amendment reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies. It is to be applied after delimitation following the next census, so not immediately.

questions.q: Role of the Opposition:
options: Highlight drawbacks and question government policies
questions.why: The Opposition points out drawbacks and questions the government's policies. This keeps the government accountable and not above debate.

questions.q: Which order is correct?
options: Bill introduced → debated → passed by both Houses → President's assent → Act
questions.why: A Bill is introduced, debated, passed by both Houses, given the President's assent and becomes an Act. The other orders break this sequence.

questions.q: Case: Citizens believe a new law restricts free speech beyond reasonable limits. The constitutional route is to:
options: File a petition in the High Court or Supreme Court
questions.why: If a law seems to violate a right, citizens can file a petition in the High Court or Supreme Court. Violence or ignoring the law is not constitutional.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition (in older editions this was two chapters: 'Why do we need a Parliament?' and 'Understanding Laws')

courses.title: Civics Ch 4 · Judiciary
courses.summary: The role of the judiciary, why its independence matters, the structure of courts in India, the difference between civil and criminal law, and how ordinary people can access courts (including Public Interest Litigation).
outcomes: Learners can describe the roles of the judiciary including judicial review
Learners can explain the independence of the judiciary
Learners can describe the three levels of courts and the appellate system
Learners can distinguish civil and criminal law and explain PIL
courses.guardianNote: Mentions a real dowry-death court case and crimes such as theft, dowry harassment and murder only in one or two factual lines, to explain criminal and civil law and the court system. No graphic detail. Includes the note that this is general education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: What does the judiciary do?

scenes.text: Two states disagree on sharing a river's water.
They go to the Supreme Court.
The court settles disputes — between citizens, citizens and the government, and between governments.

steps.title: Roles
steps.body:
- **Dispute resolution:** between citizens, between citizens and the government, between two state governments, and between the Centre and states.
- **Judicial review:** as the final interpreter of the Constitution, the judiciary can strike down laws passed by Parliament if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution.
- **Upholding the law and enforcing Fundamental Rights:** every citizen can approach the Supreme Court or High Court if their Fundamental Rights are violated.

steps.title: Independence of the judiciary
steps.body: The judiciary must be independent of the legislature and executive (the **separation of powers**) so that the powerful cannot control courts. Judges of High Courts and the Supreme Court are appointed with very little interference from other branches of government; once appointed, it is very difficult to remove them. Independence lets courts check the misuse of power by the legislature and executive and protect citizens' rights.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why would democracy be at risk if a politician could fire judges who ruled against him? → Courts could no longer act fairly; rights could be violated without remedy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking courts only punish criminals — they also resolve civil disputes and review laws.
- Thinking independence means judges are above the law.

activity.prompt: Which role of the judiciary?

items.text: Settling a river-water dispute between two states
Striking down a law that violates the Constitution
Hearing a citizen whose right to equality was violated
Deciding a land dispute between neighbours

options: Strike down laws violating the Constitution
quiz.why: Judicial review means courts can strike down laws that violate the Constitution. They cannot elect the PM or make all laws.

options: Courts are not controlled by the legislature or executive
quiz.why: Independence of the judiciary means courts are not controlled by the legislature or the executive. It does not mean judges are above the law.

options: Between citizens, citizens and government, and governments
quiz.why: Courts settle disputes between citizens, between citizens and the government, and between governments. They are not limited to citizens only.
The judiciary, with the Supreme Court at the top, interprets the Constitution finally. The Lok Sabha makes laws and the police enforce them.

quiz.q: Judges of higher courts are difficult to:
quiz.why: Judges of higher courts are hard to remove, which protects their independence through security of tenure. They can be removed only by a special process.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Structure of courts

scenes.text: In 1980, Sudha Goel died of burns; her husband and in-laws were accused.
The trial court convicted them; the High Court acquitted them on appeal.
The Supreme Court finally convicted her husband and mother-in-law in 1985.

steps.title: Three levels
steps.body:
- **Subordinate/District courts** (at the lowest level; most people approach these first): district courts, Sessions courts, courts of the Magistrate, civil judges.
- **High Courts** at the state level: the first were set up in **1862** in **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** (the three Presidencies). Today there are **25** High Courts; some serve more than one state or Union Territory; several have benches in other places.
- **Supreme Court** at the apex, located in **New Delhi**, headed by the **Chief Justice of India**; established on **26 January 1950**. Its decisions are binding on all other courts.

steps.title: Integrated judicial system and appeals
steps.body: India has an **integrated judicial system** — decisions of higher courts are binding on lower courts. A person dissatisfied with a lower court's verdict can **appeal** to a higher court. The Sudha Goel case shows the appellate system at work: trial court (conviction, 1983) → High Court (acquittal) → Supreme Court (conviction of husband and mother-in-law, 1985; her brother-in-law acquitted for lack of evidence).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is an integrated system useful? → It ensures consistency: lower courts follow higher courts' interpretations; mistakes can be corrected on appeal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Supreme Court is the first court to approach in every case.
- Saying the Supreme Court was established in 1947 (it was 26 January 1950).

activity.prompt: Arrange the courts from lowest to highest
items: District / subordinate courts
High Court
Supreme Court

quiz.q: The Supreme Court was established on:
quiz.why: The Supreme Court was established on 26 January 1950, when the Constitution came into force. 1862 was the setting up of the first High Courts.

quiz.q: The first High Courts (1862) were in:
quiz.why: The first High Courts were set up in 1862 in the three Presidencies: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court is headed by the:
quiz.why: The Supreme Court is headed by the Chief Justice of India. The PM, President and Attorney General are not its head.

quiz.q: Going to a higher court against a verdict is:
quiz.why: Going to a higher court against a verdict is an appeal. An FIR starts a criminal case, and a Bill is a proposed law.

options: Each court is independent with no link
Higher courts' decisions bind lower courts
quiz.why: An integrated judicial system means decisions of higher courts are binding on lower courts. The courts are linked in a hierarchy.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Civil and criminal law

scenes.text: A tenant is forced out of a flat without notice — he files a suit in court.
A woman is harassed for dowry — her family files an FIR with the police.
The first is civil; the second criminal.

steps.title: Criminal law
steps.body: Deals with conduct or acts the law defines as **offences**: theft, harassing a woman to bring more dowry, murder. It usually begins with lodging a **First Information Report (FIR)** with the police, who investigate; a case is then filed in court. If found guilty, the accused can be sent to jail and fined. In India, offences are now defined mainly in the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)**, and criminal procedure in the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** — in force from **1 July 2024**, replacing the Indian Penal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure.

steps.title: Civil law
steps.body: Deals with any **harm or injury to the rights** of individuals: disputes relating to sale of land, purchase of goods, rent matters, divorce cases. A **petition** is filed before the relevant court by the **affected party only** (e.g. a tenant could file against a landlord). The court gives **specific relief** (e.g. the tenant cannot be evicted; pending rent must be paid).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Classify: (a) a landlord refusing to return a security deposit; (b) a chain snatching. → (a) civil, (b) criminal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the IPC is still the current criminal code (it was replaced by the BNS from 1 July 2024).
- Thinking civil cases begin with an FIR.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Civil or criminal case?

quiz.q: A criminal case usually begins with:
options: An FIR at the police station
quiz.why: A criminal case usually begins with an FIR (First Information Report) at the police station. Civil matters begin with a petition.

quiz.q: A civil case is filed by:
quiz.why: In a civil case, the affected party files a petition in the court concerned. It is not filed by the police.

quiz.q: Which law replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024?
quiz.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024. The Evidence Act and the other laws are different.

quiz.q: Punishment in criminal law can include:
quiz.why: Criminal law punishments can include jail and fines. Civil matters like rent are settled differently, and divorce is not a punishment.

quiz.q: A dispute over the purchase of goods is:
quiz.why: A dispute over buying goods is a civil matter. It concerns rights between parties, not an offence against the State.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Access to courts and Public Interest Litigation

story.title: A letter that became a case

scenes.text: In the 1980s, the Supreme Court begins treating letters and telegrams about injustice as petitions.
Later, a petition leads the Court to order cooked mid-day meals in government schools (2001).
Millions of children benefit.

steps.title: Access to justice
steps.body: All citizens can access courts, and every citizen has a right to justice. But for the poor, court procedures involve a lot of money, paperwork and time; justice delayed is justice denied. **Free legal aid** is available through Legal Services Authorities.

steps.title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
steps.body:
In the early **1980s**, the Supreme Court devised **PIL** to increase access to justice: any individual or organisation could file a PIL in the **High Court or Supreme Court** on behalf of those whose rights were being violated; the legal process was simplified, and even a **letter or telegram** addressed to the Court could be treated as a PIL. PIL has been used to free bonded labourers, and to secure the release of undertrial prisoners kept in jail longer than their possible sentences.

**Mid-day meal case:** after drought in Rajasthan and Odisha in 2001, when food stocks lay in government godowns while people went hungry, the **People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL)** filed a PIL; the Supreme Court said the right to life (Article 21) includes the right to food and ordered, among other things, **cooked mid-day meals** in government and government-aided schools.

steps.title: Olga Tellis case (1985)
steps.body: Pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay argued that eviction would take away their **livelihood**. The Supreme Court held that the **right to livelihood is part of the right to life**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How did PIL make courts accessible to the poor? → It allowed others to file on their behalf, simplified procedure, and even accepted letters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking PIL can only be filed by the victim.
- Thinking the mid-day meal order came from Parliament (it came from the Supreme Court in a PIL).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Match the case/idea to its outcome
pairs: Letters and telegrams treated as petitions
Cooked mid-day meals ordered in schools
Right to livelihood is part of right to life
Supreme Court convicted husband and mother-in-law (1985)
Help for those who can't afford lawyers

quiz.q: PIL was devised by the Supreme Court in the:
quiz.why: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) was devised by the Supreme Court in the early 1980s, to give people easier access to justice.

quiz.q: A PIL can be filed in:
options: High Courts or the Supreme Court
quiz.why: A PIL can be filed in the High Courts or the Supreme Court. It is not filed in police stations or Parliament.

options: Pavement dwellers and right to livelihood
quiz.why: The Olga Tellis case (1985) dealt with pavement dwellers and the right to livelihood. It is not about taxes or dowry.

quiz.q: Mid-day meal order was linked to the right to:
quiz.why: The mid-day meal order was linked to the right to life, which includes the right to food, under Article 21. It was not linked to property or voting.

options: Long delays defeat the purpose of justice
quiz.why: 'Justice delayed is justice denied' means long delays defeat the purpose of justice. It does not mean courts should close or that quick trials are bad.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: The apex court of India:
questions.why: The Supreme Court is the apex (highest) court in India. The High Court and District Court are below it.

questions.q: Supreme Court is located in:
questions.why: The Supreme Court is located in New Delhi, the capital. It is not in Mumbai, Chennai or Kolkata.

questions.q: An FIR is filed in a:
questions.why: An FIR is filed at a police station in a criminal case. A civil case starts with a petition.

questions.q: A rent dispute is a:
questions.why: A rent dispute is a civil case, between a landlord and tenant. It is not a criminal case.

questions.q: First High Courts were set up in:
questions.why: The first High Courts were set up in 1862 in the three Presidencies. 1947 and 1950 are later.

questions.q: Assertion: The judiciary must be independent. Reason: It must be able to check misuse of power by the legislature and executive.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. An independent judiciary can check misuse of power by the legislature and executive.

questions.q: India's current criminal code (from 1 July 2024):
questions.why: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is the criminal code from 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code. The Rowlatt Act was a colonial law.

questions.q: Judicial review allows courts to:
questions.why: Judicial review lets courts strike down laws that are unconstitutional. They do not appoint ministers or run elections.

questions.q: In the Sudha Goel case, the High Court:
questions.why: In the Sudha Goel case, the High Court acquitted the accused, and the Supreme Court later convicted them. This shows the appeal system.

questions.q: Case: A newspaper reports bonded labour in a quarry. A social worker writes a letter to the Supreme Court. This could be treated as:
questions.why: A letter from a social worker about a public wrong can be treated by the court as a Public Interest Litigation. PIL lets others act for those who cannot.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: The Olga Tellis case was about the right to livelihood, so that pair is correct. The other pairs are mismatched.

questions.q: Integrated judicial system means:
options: Decisions of higher courts are binding on lower courts
questions.why: In an integrated system, decisions of higher courts are binding on lower courts. It does not mean all courts are equal or that appeals are absent.

questions.q: Assertion: In a civil case, any citizen can file a petition on behalf of anyone. Reason: In civil cases the affected party files the petition.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because in civil cases only the affected party files the petition, not any citizen. The reason is true; PIL is a separate exception.

questions.q: Why was PIL important for the poor?
options: It was only for the rich
It removed barriers of cost and procedure; others could file for them
questions.why: PIL removed barriers of cost and procedure, as others could file on behalf of the poor. So it opened the courts to them.

questions.q: Order of appeal:
options: District court → High Court → Supreme Court
questions.why: An appeal goes from the district court to the High Court and then to the Supreme Court, going up the hierarchy. The other orders are wrong.

questions.q: Case: A woman is harassed for dowry. Best first legal step and type of law:
options: File a rent petition — civil law
questions.why: Dowry harassment is a criminal offence, so the first step is to file an FIR with the police. It is criminal law, not a rent or civil matter.

questions.q: The Supreme Court held that the right to life includes the right to food in:
questions.why: In the PUCL mid-day meal case (from 2001) the Supreme Court held that the right to life includes the right to food. Olga Tellis was about livelihood.

courses.title: Civics Ch 5 · Understanding Marginalisation
courses.summary: What it means to be socially marginalised; the experiences of Adivasis — their lives, stereotypes, loss of forests and displacement; and of minorities, with Muslims as an example, including safeguards in the Constitution and the Sachar Committee findings.

Learners can describe Adivasi lives and the impact of displacement and stereotyping
Learners can explain why minorities need safeguards

lessons.title: What is marginalisation?

story.title: At the edge of the playground

scenes.text: Every day, the same few children are left out of games because of where they come from.
Slowly, they stop trying to join.
When whole communities are pushed to the edges of society, it's called marginalisation.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: To be **marginalised** is to be forced to occupy the sides or fringes, and thus not be at the centre of things. Marginalised groups often do not have the same access to resources and opportunities, and do not get to assert their rights. They experience a sense of disadvantage and powerlessness vis-à-vis more powerful and dominant sections of society who own land, are wealthy, better educated and politically powerful.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Marginalisation can occur because of speaking a different language, following different customs, belonging to a different religious group from the majority; being poor or considered 'low' social status; or being seen as less human than others. It is linked to economic, social, cultural and political factors that work together.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A family is denied a rented home because of their religion. How is this marginalisation? → They are excluded from a basic resource (housing) because of identity, pushing them to the margins.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking marginalisation is only about money (it is also social, cultural, political).
- Blaming marginalised people for their situation.

activity.prompt: Have you ever felt left out because of something about who you are? How did it feel, and what helped?
activity.hint: There's no right answer. Notice how small acts of inclusion make a big difference.

quiz.q: To be marginalised means to be:
options: Forced to the fringes of society
quiz.why: To be marginalised is to be pushed to the fringes, away from power and benefits. It is the opposite of being at the centre.

options: Language, religion, poverty or social status
quiz.why: Marginalisation can arise from language, religion, poverty or social status. It is not caused by food, hair colour or height.
Marginalised groups often lack access to resources and opportunities. They still have culture, feelings and families.

options: Economic, social, cultural and political factors
quiz.why: Marginalisation involves economic, social, cultural and political factors working together. It is not just one cause.

quiz.q: Which is an act of inclusion?
options: Inviting a left-out classmate to join a group
quiz.why: Inviting a left-out classmate to join is inclusion. Ignoring, mocking and spreading rumours exclude people.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Adivasis: lives, stereotypes and displacement

story.title: The hill of the Dongarria Konds

scenes.text: In Odisha, the Dongarria Kond community considers the Niyamgiri hill sacred.
A mining project threatens it.
The community protests; the case reaches the courts.

steps.title: Who are Adivasis?
steps.body: **Adivasis** — the term literally means 'original inhabitants' — are communities who lived, and often continue to live, in close association with forests. Around **8%** of India's population is Adivasi, with over **500 different Adivasi groups**. They are particularly numerous in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal and the north-eastern states. Adivasi societies are distinctive: often little hierarchy, practise a range of tribal religions (worship of ancestors, village and nature spirits), and have their own languages (e.g. Santhali).

steps.title: Stereotypes
steps.body: Adivasis are often portrayed in very stereotypical ways — in colourful costumes, headgear and dancing — and wrongly seen as exotic, primitive and backward. This leads to discrimination and blames them for their lack of 'progress'.

steps.title: Forests and displacement
steps.body: Forests were crucial to the development of all empires and civilisations; Adivasis had deep knowledge of forests. Over the past 200 years, economic changes, forest policies and political force applied by the State and private industry have pushed Adivasis to migrate to work as labourers in plantations, at construction sites, in industries and as domestic workers. Huge tracts of their land have been lost to **mining, dams, factories and national parks**. Many were displaced from their lands; this loss means losing livelihoods, food sources and a way of life. In cities, many face poverty; health and education indicators (literacy, nutrition) are often worse than for other groups.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is displacement more than losing land for Adivasis? → Forests provide food, medicine, livelihood, culture and identity — all lost together.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming all Adivasis live the same way.
- Repeating stereotypes like 'primitive' — they have rich knowledge systems.

statements.s: 'Adivasi' means 'original inhabitants'.
There is only one Adivasi group in India.
Adivasis have lost land to mining, dams and national parks.
Showing Adivasis only in costumes is an accurate picture of their lives.
Around 8% of India's population is Adivasi.

quiz.q: Approximately what share of India's population is Adivasi?
quiz.why: Adivasis make up about 8 per cent of India's population, as per NCERT. They are not half or just 1 per cent.
Niyamgiri hill in Odisha is sacred to the Dongarria Konds. They worship it and depend on it.

quiz.q: A major cause of Adivasi displacement:
quiz.why: Adivasis have been displaced mainly by mining and dam projects, which take over forests and land. Festivals and schools do not displace them.
Labelling Adivasis 'primitive' is a stereotype that leads to discrimination. It does not bring respect or health.

quiz.q: States with large Adivasi populations include:
quiz.why: Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh have large Adivasi populations. Delhi and Goa do not.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Minorities and marginalisation

scenes.text: The Constitution guarantees minorities the right to preserve their culture and set up their own schools.
In 2005 a committee studies the social, economic and educational status of Muslims.
Safeguards protect diversity and promote equality.

steps.title: Why safeguards?
steps.body: The term **minority** most commonly refers to communities that are numerically small in relation to the rest of the population. It is about power, access to resources and social and cultural dimensions. In a society where one community is in a majority, its culture may dominate; the Constitution provides safeguards (cultural and educational rights) to protect minority communities against the possibility of being culturally dominated by the majority and to protect them against discrimination.

steps.title: Muslims and marginalisation
steps.body: As per the **2011 Census**, Muslims are about **14.2%** of India's population. The government set up a high-level committee in **2005**, chaired by **Justice Rajindar Sachar**, to examine the social, economic and educational status of the Muslim community. The **Sachar Committee** report found that on a range of indicators the community lagged behind — e.g. in years of schooling and access to basic amenities — and that Muslims sometimes faced discrimination (e.g. in renting houses). Customs and practices (such as wearing a burqa, sporting a long beard or fez) are sometimes used to stereotype the community, leading to ghettoisation — living in segregated areas.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why does data matter for policy? → Data like the Sachar Committee's shows where gaps exist, so governments can design schemes in education, credit and basic amenities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'minority' is only about numbers — it's about power and access too.
- Using stereotypes to judge a whole community.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Numerically small community, often with less power
Studied status of Muslims in India
Living in segregated areas, often due to discrimination
Fixed, unfair image of a group

quiz.why: The Sachar Committee was chaired by Justice Rajindar Sachar. It studied the condition of Muslims in India in 2005.

quiz.q: As per Census 2011, Muslims are about ___ of India's population.
quiz.why: According to Census 2011, Muslims are about 14.2 per cent of India's population. They are not 30 or 50 per cent.

quiz.q: Minorities need safeguards to protect against:
options: Cultural domination and discrimination by the majority
quiz.why: Minorities need safeguards to protect them from cultural domination and discrimination by the majority. This protects their identity.
Ghettoisation is people living in segregated areas, often because of discrimination or fear. It does not mean owning land or moving abroad.

options: Numbers, power and access to resources
quiz.why: Minority status depends on numbers, power and access to resources, not just population size. A group can be a minority in several ways.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Thinking about marginalisation

scenes.text: Ravi walks 8 km to the nearest school; his friend in the city has three schools nearby.
Ravi's village also lacks a clinic and electricity.
Marginalisation compounds — one disadvantage leads to another.

steps.title: Inter-linked disadvantage
steps.body: Groups may be marginalised for different reasons and experience it differently. Disadvantages reinforce each other: poor access to schools affects jobs; poor jobs affect health and housing; discrimination affects confidence and participation in politics.

steps.title: Responses
steps.body: Marginalised groups seek to maintain their cultural identity while having access to rights, development and opportunities. The Constitution, laws and government schemes (in the next chapter) and people's movements are ways to confront marginalisation.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why does lack of a road in a village affect education? → Children can't reach schools easily, especially girls; teachers may not come regularly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating marginalisation as a single problem with a single fix.
- Ignoring what communities themselves want.

activity.prompt: Being an ally — things I can do
items: Learn about communities different from mine from their own voices
Call out stereotypes politely
Include classmates who are often left out
Support school drives for books and supplies in under-served areas
Respect others' languages, food and dress

quiz.why: Disadvantages often reinforce each other, so poor people face more and more problems. They don't cancel out or vanish on their own.

options: Their cultural identity and access to rights and opportunities
quiz.why: Marginalised groups want to keep their cultural identity and also have access to rights and opportunities. They want both.
Lack of roads cuts off people from schools and clinics. Such facilities are linked to basic access.

options: Calls out stereotypes and includes others
quiz.why: A good ally calls out stereotypes and includes others. Excluding or mocking others is the opposite.

quiz.q: Which is a way to confront marginalisation?
quiz.why: Constitutional rights and people's movements are ways to confront marginalisation. Ignoring inequality or ending schools makes it worse.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.why: The Sachar Committee studied the social, economic and educational status of the Muslim community. It was set up in 2005.

questions.q: Assertion: Stereotyping Adivasis as primitive leads to discrimination. Reason: Stereotypes create unfair and fixed images of groups.

questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Stereotypes create fixed, unfair images of groups, which leads to discrimination.

questions.q: Adivasis have lost land mainly to:

questions.why: Adivasis lost land mainly to mining, dams, industries and national parks. They did not lose it to festivals or schools.

questions.q: Muslims as per Census 2011:

questions.q: Safeguards for minorities include:

questions.q: Assertion: Minority means only a small number of people. Reason: Minority status also involves power and access to resources.

questions.why: The assertion is false because minority status is not only about small numbers. The reason is true: it also involves power and access to resources.

questions.q: Which best describes Adivasi societies?

questions.q: Data like the Sachar report help governments to:

options: How displacement pushes Adivasis into insecure urban work
