questions.why: Marginalisation has economic, social, cultural and political dimensions that reinforce each other. It is not only about money, and it can be addressed.

courses.title: Civics Ch 6 · Confronting Marginalisation
courses.summary: How marginalised groups use Fundamental Rights and specific laws to fight discrimination: the abolition of untouchability, reservations and schemes, the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989, the fight against manual scavenging, and the Forest Rights Act 2006.
outcomes: Learners can explain how Fundamental Rights help marginalised groups
Learners can describe government policies like reservations and scholarships
Learners can explain the purpose of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989
Learners can describe the struggle against manual scavenging and the Forest Rights Act 2006
courses.guardianNote: Explains, in calm factual language, caste discrimination, atrocities law and the injustice of manual scavenging, as covered in the Class 8 civics syllabus. No graphic descriptions; focuses on rights, laws and dignity. Includes the note that this is general education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Invoking Fundamental Rights

scenes.text: Article 17 of the Constitution says: untouchability is abolished.
Dalit groups use it to demand equal access to temples, water and schools.
Rights on paper become power when people use them.

steps.title: Rights as tools
steps.body:
The Constitution's Fundamental Rights are available to all Indians equally. Marginalised groups have drawn on them to insist that the government recognise injustice and enforce the law.

- **Article 17:** **untouchability has been abolished** — no one can now prevent Dalits from educating themselves, entering temples or using public facilities. Practising untouchability is a punishable crime.
- **Article 15:** no citizen shall be discriminated against on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
- **Cultural and educational rights** help minorities (religious and linguistic) preserve their culture.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A village tea stall keeps separate cups for Dalit customers. Which constitutional provision does this violate? → Article 17 (abolition of untouchability) and Article 15 (non-discrimination).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking rights work automatically — people often have to demand them, sometimes through courts.
- Thinking untouchability is legal in private spaces — it's an offence everywhere.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

statements.s: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
Fundamental Rights are only for the majority.
Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, sex.
Marginalised groups have used rights to demand justice.

quiz.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, under the Right to Equality. It makes practising it an offence.

quiz.q: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of:
options: Religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
quiz.why: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Height, marks or clothing are not listed.
Rights become effective when people demand and use them. If they are forgotten, they remain on paper.
Practising untouchability is a punishable crime under the law. It is not a tradition to protect.
Minorities can preserve their culture through cultural and educational rights, which let them run their own institutions.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Laws and policies for the marginalised

scenes.text: Priya, from a Scheduled Tribe family, gets a hostel place and scholarship.
She becomes the first doctor in her village.
Policies can open doors that were closed for generations.

steps.title: Promoting social justice
steps.body: Governments make specific policies for marginalised groups — e.g. free or subsidised **hostels** for Dalit and Adivasi students; **scholarships**; and **reservations** — the policy of reserving seats in education and government jobs for **Scheduled Castes (SC)**, **Scheduled Tribes (ST)** and **Other Backward Classes (OBC)** (and for economically weaker sections). Governments maintain lists of SCs, STs and backward classes. Candidates use caste and tribe certificates to apply.

steps.title: Why reservations?
steps.body: Society has been unfair to Dalits and Adivasis for centuries; reservations help ensure they get access to opportunities they were denied, so that equality becomes real and not just on paper.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How does a hostel scheme help Adivasi students? → It removes the barrier of distance and cost, allowing them to study in towns with better schools.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking reservations are charity — they address historical injustice and promote equality.
- Thinking only education is covered — government jobs too.

activity.prompt: Match the policy to its purpose
pairs: Seats in education and government jobs for disadvantaged groups
Accommodation for students from far-off areas

quiz.why: Reservations apply to education and government jobs, to give opportunities to disadvantaged groups. They don't apply to homes, films or sports clubs.
SC stands for Scheduled Castes, a constitutional category of communities listed for special protection. It is not the Supreme Court here.

options: To correct historical injustice and promote equality
quiz.why: Reservations aim to correct historical injustice and promote equality by giving opportunity to groups long excluded. They are not meant to exclude or reduce education.

quiz.q: To apply for reserved seats, candidates need:
quiz.why: To use reserved seats, candidates need a caste or tribe certificate to prove eligibility. Passports and licences are not needed.

quiz.q: Which is a social justice measure?
quiz.why: Scholarships for disadvantaged students are a social justice measure, as they help them study. Higher fees or closed hostels hurt them.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: The SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, 1989

scenes.text: In some villages, Dalits have been humiliated or attacked for asserting rights.
Dalit groups campaign for a strong law.
In 1989 Parliament passes the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

steps.title: The Act
steps.body: The **Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989** was framed in response to demands by Dalits and others that the government take seriously the ill-treatment and humiliation they face in everyday life. The Act distinguishes several levels of crimes: it lists modes of humiliation that are both physically horrific and morally reprehensible, and seeks to punish those who (i) force a member of an SC or ST to drink or eat an inedible or obnoxious substance, (ii) forcibly remove clothes or parade them, (iii) do anything to insult or humiliate. It also covers dispossessing Dalits and Adivasis of their few resources (land) or forcing them into slave labour, and crimes against Dalit and tribal women. Adivasi activists also refer to it to defend their right to occupy land that was traditionally theirs.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was a special Act needed beyond ordinary criminal law? → Many atrocities targeted people because of caste; a specific law recognises this, sets stricter punishment and special procedures.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Act only covers physical violence (it covers humiliation and land dispossession too).
- Thinking it covers only Dalits (it covers Scheduled Tribes as well).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Covered by the 1989 Act?

items.text: Forcibly removing land from an SC/ST person
Publicly humiliating someone for their caste
Forcing an SC/ST person into bonded labour
A normal disagreement about a cricket score

quiz.q: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was passed in 1989. 1950 is the Constitution and 2006 the Forest Rights Act.
The Act protects Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from atrocities and discrimination. It is not for politicians or businesses.

options: Humiliation, violence and dispossession of land based on caste/tribe
quiz.why: The Act punishes humiliation, violence and dispossession of land that happen because of caste or tribe. It is not about theft or traffic.

quiz.q: Adivasi activists use the Act to:
options: Defend their right to traditional land
quiz.why: Adivasi activists use the Act to defend their right to their traditional land. They use it against land grabbing.

quiz.q: The Act was a response to:
options: Demands by Dalits and others for protection
quiz.why: The Act came in response to demands by Dalits and others for protection from atrocities. It was won through their struggle.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Ending manual scavenging; Forest Rights Act

scenes.text: For generations, some people were forced to clean dry latrines by hand — a deeply degrading practice.
The Safai Karmachari Andolan fights to end it; in 2003 it files a PIL.
Laws ban manual scavenging and promise rehabilitation.

steps.title: Manual scavenging
steps.body: **Manual scavenging** refers to removing human and animal waste/excreta using brooms, tin plates and baskets from dry latrines and carrying it on the head to disposal grounds. It is mostly done by Dalit women and girls. It is a degrading practice and a serious health hazard. The **Safai Karmachari Andolan (SKA)**, formed in **1993**, campaigned against it; in **2003** it and others filed a PIL in the Supreme Court. Parliament passed the **Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993**, and later the **Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013**, which bans the practice and provides for rehabilitation. Enforcement remains a challenge; dangerous cleaning of sewers without protective equipment must stop.

steps.title: Forest Rights Act, 2006
steps.body: The **Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006** acknowledges that Adivasis and forest dwellers suffered **historical injustice** when their lands were taken. It recognises their right to homestead, cultivable and grazing land and to non-timber forest produce, and the right to conserve forests and biodiversity.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why did SKA approach the Supreme Court? → Despite the 1993 law, manual scavenging continued; a PIL could push governments to enforce the law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the 1993 law ended the practice immediately.
- Confusing the Forest Rights Act (2006) with the Forest Conservation Act.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Order the milestones

events.text: Law prohibiting employment of manual scavengers; Safai Karmachari Andolan formed
SKA files PIL in the Supreme Court
New Act banning manual scavenging with rehabilitation

quiz.q: Safai Karmachari Andolan works to end:
quiz.why: The Safai Karmachari Andolan works to end manual scavenging, so as to restore dignity to the people forced into it.

quiz.q: Forest Rights Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Forest Rights Act was passed in 2006. It recognises the rights of forest dwellers and Adivasis.

options: A degrading practice and health hazard, now banned
quiz.why: Manual scavenging is a degrading practice and a health hazard, and it is now banned by law. It is not a respected job.

options: Ban on manual scavenging and rehabilitation
quiz.why: The 2013 Act bans manual scavenging and provides for rehabilitation of those who did this work. It does not allow dry latrines.

quiz.q: Forest Rights Act recognises Adivasis' right to:
options: Land, forest produce and conserving forests
quiz.why: The Forest Rights Act recognises Adivasis' rights to land, forest produce and conserving forests. It does not let them sell forests or allow mining.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: Untouchability is abolished by:
questions.why: Untouchability is abolished by Article 17 of the Constitution. Article 370 and Article 51 deal with other things.

questions.q: Reservations are for:
options: SC, ST and OBC (and EWS) in education and government jobs
questions.why: Reservations are made for SC, ST and OBC (and EWS) in education and government jobs. They are not for the rich, athletes or foreigners.

questions.q: SC/ST Atrocities Act year:
questions.why: The SC/ST Atrocities Act dates from 1989. 2006 is the Forest Rights Act and 2013 the law on manual scavenging.

questions.q: Forest Rights Act year:
questions.why: The Forest Rights Act was passed in 2006. 1989 is the Atrocities Act and 2013 the manual scavenging law.

questions.q: Assertion: Marginalised groups use Fundamental Rights to seek justice. Reason: Fundamental Rights are available to all citizens equally.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Fundamental Rights are available to all citizens equally, so marginalised groups can use them to seek justice.

questions.q: Manual scavenging is mostly done by:
questions.why: Manual scavenging is mostly forced on Dalit women and girls, which makes it a serious injustice. It is not done by machines.

questions.q: Safai Karmachari Andolan was formed in:
questions.why: The Safai Karmachari Andolan was formed in 1993, to fight manual scavenging. 1989 and 2013 are different laws.

questions.q: Why are scholarships and hostels given to Dalit and Adivasi students?
questions.why: Scholarships and hostels remove barriers to education for Dalit and Adivasi students. They are not meant to punish or separate them.

questions.q: Case: An upper-caste group forcibly occupies land belonging to a Dalit family. Which law specifically applies?
questions.why: Forcibly taking a Dalit family's land is dispossession on the basis of caste, covered by the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The other laws do not apply here.

questions.q: The 2003 PIL by SKA asked the Supreme Court to:
options: Enforce the ban on manual scavenging
questions.why: The 2003 PIL by the SKA asked the Supreme Court to enforce the ban on manual scavenging, as it was still practised. It did not seek to ban reservations.

questions.q: Assertion: Laws alone have completely ended manual scavenging. Reason: Enforcement and rehabilitation remain challenges.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because laws alone have not ended manual scavenging. The reason is true: enforcement and rehabilitation remain challenges.

questions.q: The Forest Rights Act acknowledges:
options: That forests belong only to companies
questions.why: The Forest Rights Act acknowledges the historical injustice done to forest dwellers by denying their rights. It does not give forests to companies.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: Article 15 deals with non-discrimination, so that pair is correct. Article 17 is untouchability and the 1989 and 2006 Acts deal with other matters.

questions.q: Why might a Dalit community approach a court even though untouchability is illegal?
options: To get the law enforced when it is violated in practice
questions.why: Untouchability is illegal, but when it is still practised, a community can go to court to get the law enforced. The law needs enforcement.

questions.q: Case: A tribal community seeks legal recognition of grazing land it has used for generations. The best legal basis:
questions.why: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises forest dwellers' rights over land and resources they have used for generations. The other laws deal with other things.

questions.q: What links all these measures (Article 17, reservations, 1989 Act, 2006 Act)?
options: They aim to confront marginalisation and promote equality and dignity
questions.why: Article 17, reservations, the 1989 Act and the 2006 Act all aim to confront marginalisation and promote equality and dignity. They are not only symbolic.

courses.title: Civics Ch 7 · Public Facilities
courses.summary: What public facilities are and why the government must provide them; water as part of the right to life; unequal access in cities (the Chennai example); sanitation; and lessons from Porto Alegre and Cochabamba on public versus private supply.
outcomes: Learners can define public facilities and give examples
Learners can explain why water is part of the right to life
Learners can describe unequal access to water and sanitation
Learners can evaluate the role of government vs private companies in providing facilities

lessons.title: What are public facilities?

scenes.text: In one Chennai neighbourhood, taps run 24 hours.
A few kilometres away, families wait for a water tanker every other day.
Shouldn't everyone have water?

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body:
**Public facilities** are essential services whose benefits can be shared by many people: **water, healthcare, sanitation, electricity, public transport, schools and colleges**. The government has a responsibility to provide them, because private companies work for profit and may not provide them to the poor at affordable rates.

An important characteristic: once a public facility is provided, its benefits can be shared by many (e.g. a school in a village serves all children).

steps.title: Water and the right to life
steps.body: Water is essential for life and good health. Water-borne diseases like diarrhoea, dysentery and cholera are a major cause of illness and death; many could be prevented by safe drinking water. The **Constitution recognises the right to water as part of the Right to Life** (Article 21) — universal access to sufficient and safe water for drinking and other uses is a government responsibility; courts have upheld this in several cases.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is a public bus service a public facility? → Its benefits are shared by many people who use it, and it should be affordable to all.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking public facilities are only for the poor — they are for everyone.
- Thinking the right to water is not a constitutional matter.

activity.prompt: Public facility or private good?

quiz.why: Water supply is a public facility, as many people share its benefits. A private car, jewellery and a laptop are personal.

quiz.q: The right to water is part of the:
quiz.why: The right to water is part of the Right to Life, under Article 21 of the Constitution. Life needs water.

quiz.q: Why must the government provide public facilities?
options: Private companies seek profit and may exclude the poor
quiz.why: Private companies work for profit, so they may leave out the poor. So the government must provide essential public facilities for all.
Cholera is a water-borne disease, spread by unsafe water. Asthma, goitre and diabetes are not.

quiz.q: A key feature of public facilities:
options: They are always free of cost
Benefits can be shared by many
quiz.why: A key feature of public facilities is that their benefits can be shared by many people. They are not for one person alone.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Unequal access: water and sanitation in cities

scenes.text: In some areas, families pay a lot for tanker water or bottled water.
In crowded settlements, dozens of families share one toilet.
Access to basic services is very unequal.

steps.title: The Chennai example
steps.body: In Chennai, some wealthier neighbourhoods get regular municipal water and can afford bottled water and private borewells; middle-class areas get water a few times a week; in poorer settlements, people depend on public taps or tankers and spend hours collecting water. Municipal supply is often insufficient, and private water tankers buy water from wells in nearby villages, depleting farmers' groundwater. This shows how public facilities are **unequally distributed**.

steps.title: Sanitation
steps.body: Safe **sanitation** (toilets, drainage, sewage treatment) is essential to prevent disease. Large numbers of people in India have lacked safe toilets; organisations like **Sulabh International** (founded **1970**) built low-cost public toilets. The government's **Swachh Bharat Mission** (launched **2014**) aimed to make India open-defecation-free through toilet construction and behaviour change. Proper drainage and sewage treatment remain challenges in many cities.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why does tanker water harm farmers near cities? → Tankers pump groundwater from village wells; the water table falls, affecting irrigation and drinking water there.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the problem is only total quantity — distribution and affordability matter.
- Thinking sanitation is a private matter — it affects public health.

statements.s: Access to water in Indian cities is very unequal.
Private tankers never affect village groundwater.
Sulabh International built low-cost public toilets.
Swachh Bharat Mission was launched in 2014.
Poor sanitation has no effect on health.

quiz.q: Which organisation pioneered low-cost public toilets?
quiz.why: Sulabh International pioneered low-cost public toilets, founded in 1970. The RBI, BCCI and ISRO do other work.
The Swachh Bharat Mission began in 2014 to improve sanitation and cleanliness. It is not from 2004 or 2020.
Poorer settlements often depend on public taps or water tankers, while richer areas get regular supply. This shows inequality.

quiz.q: Unsafe water and poor sanitation spread:
quiz.why: Unsafe water and poor sanitation spread diseases like diarrhoea and cholera. They do not bring wealth or education.

options: Some areas get much better services than others
quiz.why: Unequal access means some areas get much better services than others. It is not equal for all.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Public or private? Lessons from around the world

scenes.text: In 2000, a city in Bolivia hands water supply to a private company; prices shoot up.
Massive protests follow; the contract is cancelled.
In Porto Alegre, Brazil, a public water department supplies safe, affordable water to almost everyone.

steps.title: Cochabamba (Bolivia)
steps.body: In **2000**, the government of Bolivia sold the city of **Cochabamba**'s municipal water supply to a multinational company, which **quadrupled** water prices. Many people's water bills were a big share of their income. Protests by citizens (a 'water war') forced the government to cancel the contract and return supply to the municipality.

steps.title: Porto Alegre (Brazil)
steps.body: In **Porto Alegre**, the city's public water department achieved near-universal access to safe water, with low prices for the poor; the department's surplus was used to improve services; people participated in decisions about budget priorities. This shows that public supply can be efficient and fair.

steps.title: Public facilities and the government
steps.body: Private companies operate for profit; they may provide services at higher prices only to those who can pay. Many argue the government must play the key role in providing public facilities, with adequate funding (from taxes) and accountability, while involving citizens. Sometimes the government contracts private firms for parts of the work, but it remains responsible for universal, affordable access.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: What lesson does Cochabamba teach? → Handing an essential service to a profit-seeking company without safeguards can make it unaffordable for many.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking private supply is always better or always worse — the key is universal, affordable access and accountability.
- Mixing Porto Alegre (Brazil) with Cochabamba (Bolivia).

activity.prompt: Match the place or idea
pairs: Privatised water; prices quadrupled; protests reversed it
Public water department with near-universal access
Why private firms may exclude the poor

quiz.q: Water privatisation protests in 2000 took place in:
quiz.why: The 2000 protests against water privatisation took place in Cochabamba, Bolivia. It is known as the water war.
Porto Alegre in Brazil is known for a successful public water supply, run with citizen participation. It was not privatised.

quiz.q: Public facilities are funded mainly by:
quiz.why: Public facilities are mainly paid for from taxes collected by the government. Donations and loans alone cannot fund them.

quiz.q: A risk of privatising essential services:
options: Prices may become unaffordable for the poor
quiz.why: When essential services are privatised, prices may become unaffordable for the poor, as companies aim at profit. Quality does not always improve.
In Cochabamba the private company raised water prices four times (quadrupled), which people could not afford. This led to protests.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: Making public facilities work for all

scenes.text: Residents of a ward survey which streets have broken taps and no streetlights.
They present the data to the municipal corporation.
Repairs begin — citizens' participation works.

steps.title: What can be done?
steps.body:
- Governments must increase coverage and quality, prioritising areas with poor access.
- Fair pricing so the poor can afford essentials.
- **Citizen participation**: ward committees, surveys, complaints, RTI (Right to Information) requests, social audits.
- Use of public transport (like the Mumbai suburban railways and city metros) reduces congestion and pollution.

steps.title: Your role
steps.body: Use water carefully, report leaks, keep public toilets clean, support neighbours who lack access, and raise issues with local representatives.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How can a school make sure every child has safe drinking water? → Water filters, regular cleaning and testing, enough taps, and reporting problems to authorities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only engineers can fix public services — community pressure and monitoring matter.
- Wasting water because 'it's free' in some areas.

activity.prompt: Public-facility audit of my neighbourhood
items: Is there safe drinking water at school?
Are there clean toilets for girls and boys at school?
Are streetlights working?
Is public transport within walking distance?
Is there a nearby government health centre?

quiz.q: A tool for citizens to get information from government:
quiz.why: The Right to Information (RTI) lets citizens ask the government for information, which brings transparency. A Bill, census or FIR does not serve this purpose.
Public transport carries many people together, so it reduces congestion and pollution. It is not only for the rich.

quiz.q: Citizen participation in public services includes:
quiz.why: Citizens take part in public services through surveys, complaints and ward committees. Violence or stealing water is not participation.

options: Water is always free for industries
The poor can afford essential water
quiz.why: Fair pricing means the poor can afford essential water. Only the rich being able to buy it is unfair.

quiz.q: Reporting a leaking public tap is:
quiz.why: Reporting a leaking public tap prevents waste and shows responsible citizenship. It is not illegal or useless.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: Which is a public facility?
questions.why: Public healthcare is a public facility, shared by many. A yacht, jewellery and a phone are private.

questions.q: Right to water is part of:
questions.why: The right to water is part of the Right to Life under Article 21. Life cannot be lived without water.

questions.q: Sulabh International is known for:
questions.why: Sulabh International is known for low-cost public toilets and sanitation work. It has nothing to do with cricket, banking or satellites.

questions.q: Cochabamba water privatisation was in:
questions.why: The Cochabamba water privatisation was in Bolivia in 2000. It led to the famous water war protests.

questions.q: Assertion: The government must ensure public facilities for all. Reason: Private companies operate mainly for profit.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Private companies mainly seek profit and may exclude the poor, so the government must ensure facilities for all.

questions.q: Swachh Bharat Mission began in:
questions.why: The Swachh Bharat Mission began in 2014. It is aimed at sanitation.

questions.q: Porto Alegre shows that:
options: Public water supply can be efficient and fair
questions.why: Porto Alegre shows that public water supply can be efficient and fair when people participate. It disproves the claim that only private firms succeed.

questions.q: Diseases caused by unsafe water:
questions.why: Unsafe water causes diseases like cholera and diarrhoea. Diabetes, asthma, goitre and scurvy come from other causes.

questions.q: Case: In a city, rich areas have 24-hour water while slums get water once a week. This illustrates:
questions.why: Some areas getting regular supply and others getting water once a week is unequal distribution of a public facility. It is not good planning for all.

questions.q: Why do private tankers near cities cause problems for villages?
options: They provide free water to farmers
They pump village groundwater, lowering the water table
questions.why: Private tankers pump groundwater from villages to sell in cities, which lowers the water table. This leaves villages with less water.

questions.q: Assertion: Privatisation always makes services cheaper. Reason: In Cochabamba, prices quadrupled after privatisation.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because privatisation does not always make services cheaper. The reason is true: in Cochabamba prices quadrupled after privatisation, which is a counter-example.

questions.q: Public facilities are funded largely through:
questions.why: Public facilities are mostly funded by taxes collected by the government. Charity and lotteries cannot fund them.

questions.q: Which best ensures accountability of public services?
questions.why: Citizen participation, RTI and audits keep public services answerable. Secrecy or no complaints make them less accountable.

questions.q: Case: A town's public bus service is cancelled and replaced by expensive private cabs. Who is most affected?
options: Poor commuters who can't afford cabs
questions.why: Poor commuters, who cannot afford costly private cabs, are hurt most when public buses stop. Rich car owners are not much affected.

questions.q: Why is water called both a public facility and a right?
options: It's essential for life and must be accessible to all, and courts link it to Article 21
questions.why: Water is essential for life and must be accessible to all, so it is a public facility. Courts link it to the right to life under Article 21.

courses.title: Civics Ch 8 · Law and Social Justice
courses.summary: Why laws are needed to protect workers, consumers and the environment; the Bhopal gas tragedy and its lessons; enforcing safety laws; the environment as a public resource; child labour laws; and new laws and responsibilities.
outcomes: Learners can explain why markets need laws to protect people
Learners can describe the Bhopal tragedy and the failures behind it
Learners can explain worker safety, minimum wages and child labour laws
Learners can explain the right to a clean environment and the role of courts and citizens
courses.guardianNote: Discusses the 1984 Bhopal gas disaster (deaths and illness, stated factually without graphic detail), worker safety and child labour, as in the Class 8 civics syllabus. Includes the Childline number 1098 and a note that this is general education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: Why do we need laws for markets?

scenes.text: A construction worker is paid far less than promised and has no safety helmet.
Laws on minimum wages and safety exist to stop exactly this.
Markets need rules to be fair.

steps.title: Protecting people
steps.body:
In markets, people with less power — workers, consumers, small producers — can be exploited. Laws protect them:

- **Minimum wages law**: workers must be paid not less than a minimum wage, revised periodically.
- **Worker safety laws**: e.g. safety equipment and safe working conditions in factories.
- **Consumer protection**: e.g. laws ensuring the quality of goods and services (the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019** replaced the 1986 Act).
- **Environmental laws**: preventing pollution.

It is the government's role to make laws **and** to **enforce** them (enforcement means ensuring laws are followed).

steps.title: Why enforcement matters
steps.body: Laws on paper don't help if they are not implemented. Workers who are poor or unorganised are often unable to demand their rights; inspections, penalties and awareness are needed. Enforcement is even more important when the law protects the weak from the strong.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why might a worker accept less than the minimum wage? → Many workers compete for few jobs and fear losing work; weak enforcement allows exploitation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking making a law automatically solves the problem — enforcement is essential.
- Thinking markets are always fair on their own.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Which group does the law mainly protect?

items.text: Rules against dumping toxic waste in rivers
Ban on child labour in hazardous work

quiz.q: Minimum wages law ensures workers are paid:
options: Not less than a set minimum
quiz.why: The minimum wages law makes sure workers are paid not less than a set minimum. Employers cannot pay whatever they wish.
Enforcement means ensuring that laws are actually followed. Writing or repealing laws is something else.

quiz.q: The Consumer Protection Act now in force is from:
quiz.why: The Consumer Protection Act now in force is from 2019, which replaced the 1986 Act. It gives consumers stronger protection.

quiz.q: Laws are especially needed to protect:
quiz.why: Laws are especially needed to protect the weak from the strong. Without them, powerful people could misuse their position.

quiz.q: Why might workers not demand rights?
options: Poverty, fear of job loss and lack of organisation
quiz.why: Workers often don't demand their rights because of poverty, fear of losing their job and lack of organisation. They are vulnerable.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

lessons.title: The Bhopal gas tragedy

scenes.text: The Union Carbide factory in Bhopal makes pesticides.
On the night of 2–3 December 1984, a toxic gas leaks.
Thousands die; tens of thousands suffer for decades. What went wrong?

steps.title: What happened
steps.body: **Union Carbide (UC)**, an American company, had a factory in Bhopal producing pesticides. At midnight on **2 December 1984**, **methyl isocyanate (MIC)** — a highly poisonous gas — started leaking. Within three days, more than **8,000** people were dead (as NCERT reports); hundreds of thousands were maimed. Most exposed were from poor working-class families; many survivors developed serious respiratory disorders, eye problems and other illnesses; children developed abnormalities.

steps.title: Why it was not an accident
steps.body: UC had deliberately ignored essential safety measures to cut costs. Safety systems were faulty or switched off; staff had been reduced; long before 1984 there had been warnings of gas leaks. The disaster showed that companies, especially multinationals, may cut safety costs in countries where laws are weak or poorly enforced.

steps.title: The fight for justice
steps.body: Victims and activists fought for decades for justice, medical care and compensation. In **1989**, UC paid **US$470 million** in a settlement (against a demand of US$3 billion). Survivors continue to demand clean drinking water, health care and jobs; the site is still contaminated.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why was safety cut at the plant? → To reduce costs; weak enforcement and low value placed on workers' lives made this possible.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling it simply an 'accident' — it resulted from negligence.
- Confusing UC (the company) with a government agency.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

statements.s: The Bhopal disaster occurred in December 1984.
The gas that leaked was methyl isocyanate.
Union Carbide was an Indian public sector company.
The disaster was caused partly by ignoring safety measures.
Victims received full and fair compensation quickly.
statements.why: Settlement was much lower than demanded; struggle continued.

quiz.why: The Union Carbide plant in Bhopal made pesticides. The deadly gas used in that process leaked in 1984.
The gas that leaked at Bhopal was methyl isocyanate (MIC), a very toxic chemical used in making pesticides. It was not carbon dioxide, oxygen or nitrogen.
In 1989 Union Carbide paid US$470 million in compensation, as a settlement with the Government of India. It was far less than victims had hoped for.

quiz.q: A key reason for the disaster:
options: Safety measures ignored to cut costs
quiz.why: A key reason for the disaster was that safety measures were ignored to cut costs. It was not caused by floods, lightning or an earthquake.
Those most affected were poor working-class families living near the plant. They were the most vulnerable to the gas.

lessons.title: Worker safety, child labour and enforcement

scenes.text: At Alang in Gujarat, old ships from around the world are broken up on the beach.
Workers face toxic materials and accidents.
Strong, enforced laws can protect them.

steps.title: Why safety is often ignored
steps.body: Foreign companies may come to India because of cheap labour; wages are lower and workers may accept longer hours and less safety. Enforcement of safety laws is often weak. Example: old ships are sent for breaking to places like **Alang (Gujarat)**, where labour is cheaper and safety and environmental protections weaker than in developed countries.

steps.title: Child labour laws
steps.body: The Constitution prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories and hazardous work (Right against Exploitation). The **Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986** was amended in **2016**: it now prohibits employing children **below 14 in all occupations** (with limited exceptions like helping in family enterprises after school hours, without hazard) and adolescents **14–18 in hazardous occupations**. Free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 is a right.

steps.title: Strengthening enforcement
steps.body: Inspections, penalties, trade unions, awareness among workers, and courts' orders all help enforce laws. Citizens can report child labour by calling **1098** (Childline).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A 12-year-old is working all day in a roadside eatery. What does the law say, and what can you do? → Employing children under 14 in such work is prohibited; you can inform an adult or call 1098.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking child labour is allowed if the family needs money — the law prohibits it in most work; schemes exist to support families.
- Ignoring adolescent (14–18) protection in hazardous jobs.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

a.text: On a trip, you notice a boy of about 11 working long hours at a factory gate stall during school time.

choices.label: Tell a trusted adult and help them call 1098 (Childline)
choices.feedback: That's the right step — trained people can help him safely.

choices.label: Ignore it — it's normal
choices.feedback: Child labour is not normal or legal.

choices.label: Confront the owner angrily yourself
choices.feedback: That may be unsafe for you and the boy.

w.text: Children under 14 have the right to education and must not be employed in such work. What now?

w2.text: Safety first: let trained authorities handle it.

e.text: Childline connects children with protection, education and support. You helped enforce the law.

quiz.q: Since 2016, children below 14 are prohibited from:
options: Employment in all occupations (with limited family exceptions)
quiz.why: Since the 2016 amendment, children below 14 are prohibited from working in all occupations, with limited exceptions such as helping the family after school. It does not stop them from school or play.
Adolescents aged 14 to 18 are not allowed to work in hazardous occupations, to protect their health and safety. Light work is not covered by this ban.
Childline is the helpline for children in need, and its number is 1098. 100 is the police and 108 an ambulance.

quiz.q: Old ships are broken up at:
quiz.why: Old ships are broken up at Alang in Gujarat, one of the world's largest ship-breaking yards. Bhopal, Jaipur and Shimla are not coastal.

quiz.q: Why do some companies prefer countries with weak laws?
options: Lower costs on wages and safety
quiz.why: Some companies prefer countries with weak laws because they can cut costs on wages and safety. Strong laws would make this more expensive.

lessons.title: A clean environment as a right

scenes.text: A factory dumps untreated waste into a river.
Fish die; villagers fall ill.
Courts say: the right to life includes the right to a pollution-free environment.

steps.title: Environment as a public resource
steps.body: At the time of the Bhopal disaster there were few laws protecting the environment. Since then, the government has introduced new laws on the environment, and polluters are held accountable. The **Supreme Court** has held that the **right to life** (Article 21) includes the **right to enjoy pollution-free water and air** (e.g. the Subhash Kumar vs State of Bihar case, 1991). Courts have ordered polluting industries to close or relocate.

steps.title: Shared responsibility
steps.body: The environment is a **public resource**: no individual or company can damage it for private profit. Governments must set and enforce standards; companies must adopt cleaner technologies; citizens can raise complaints, join campaigns and change habits.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why is relocating polluting factories not a complete solution? → Pollution may simply shift to areas where poor people live; standards must be enforced everywhere and cleaner technologies adopted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking environmental laws are only for forests — they cover air, water and soil.
- Thinking pollution is only the government's problem.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. For a real legal problem, consult a lawyer or a free legal-aid service (District Legal Services Authority). In an emergency, call 112.

activity.prompt: Match the idea to its example
pairs: Part of the right to life (Article 21)
Air and rivers shared by all
Factories made to pay for or stop pollution

quiz.q: The right to a pollution-free environment is part of the:
quiz.why: The right to a pollution-free environment comes from the Right to Life under Article 21, as the courts have held. A polluted place threatens life and health.
The environment is a public resource that belongs to everyone. It is not the private property of factories.

quiz.q: Courts have ordered polluting industries to:
quiz.why: Courts have ordered polluting industries to close or move away from populated areas, to protect people's health. They did not allow them to ignore laws.

quiz.q: A citizen action for the environment:
quiz.why: Filing complaints about pollution is an action citizens can take to protect the environment. Dumping waste or burning plastic harms it.

quiz.q: After Bhopal, environmental laws in India:
quiz.why: After Bhopal, India's environmental laws were strengthened, with new rules to protect people and the environment. They were not removed.

sources: NCERT Class 8 Social and Political Life III (topic)

questions.q: The Bhopal gas tragedy happened in:
questions.why: The Bhopal gas tragedy took place in December 1984. It remains one of the worst industrial disasters.

questions.q: Union Carbide was:
questions.why: Union Carbide was an American company, a multinational corporation (MNC). It owned the Bhopal pesticide plant.

questions.q: Minimum wages law protects:
questions.why: The minimum wages law protects workers by guaranteeing that they are paid at least a fixed amount. It is not meant for employers or tourists.

questions.q: Childline helpline:
questions.why: Childline is the helpline for children and its number is 1098. 101 is the fire service number.

questions.q: Assertion: Laws need to be enforced to protect workers. Reason: Poor, unorganised workers often cannot demand their rights themselves.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Poor, unorganised workers often cannot demand their rights, so laws must be enforced for them.

questions.q: The 2016 amendment to the Child Labour Act prohibits employment of children below 14 in:
questions.why: The 2016 amendment prohibits employment of children below 14 in all occupations, with limited exceptions such as family work after school. It is not limited to factories or mines.

questions.q: Settlement paid by UC in 1989:
questions.why: In 1989 Union Carbide paid US$470 million in a settlement with the Indian government. It was not 47 million or 3 billion.

questions.q: The right to clean environment comes from:
options: Supreme Court's interpretation of the right to life
questions.why: The right to a clean environment comes from the Supreme Court's interpretation of the right to life under Article 21. It is not only a municipal rule.

questions.q: Why are ships often broken at Alang rather than in developed countries?
options: Lower labour costs and weaker safety enforcement
questions.why: Ships are broken at Alang because labour is cheap and safety rules are weakly enforced. It is not because ships are built there.

questions.q: Case: A factory saves money by switching off safety alarms; a leak injures workers. This shows:
options: How weak enforcement and cost-cutting endanger lives
questions.why: Switching off safety alarms to save money, resulting in a leak, shows how weak enforcement and cost-cutting put lives at risk. It is not unavoidable or just worker carelessness.

questions.q: Assertion: The Bhopal disaster was purely an accident. Reason: Safety systems had been neglected to cut costs.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: The assertion is false because Bhopal was not a pure accident. The reason is true: safety systems were neglected to cut costs, which means negligence caused it.

questions.q: Which law protects buyers of faulty goods?
questions.why: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 protects buyers of faulty goods and services. The Forest Rights Act, Arms Act and Child Labour Act deal with other matters.

questions.q: Relocating polluting industries may:
options: Shift pollution to poorer areas if standards aren't enforced
questions.why: Moving polluting industries may only shift the pollution to poorer areas if standards are not enforced. It does not solve all pollution.

questions.q: Case: An adolescent of 16 is employed in a fireworks factory. Under the amended law, this is:
questions.why: A 16-year-old is an adolescent, and the amended law prohibits adolescents from working in hazardous occupations such as fireworks. Being over 14 does not make it allowed.

questions.q: Which best summarises this chapter?
options: Laws protect people from exploitation in markets, but only if enforced
questions.why: The chapter shows that laws protect people from exploitation in markets, but only if they are enforced. Markets need laws, and workers and consumers all need protection.

lessons.title: History timeline sheet

scenes.text: Arjun makes a timeline strip from 1600 to 1950 and sticks it on his wall.
Next to each date he writes one cause and one effect.
Now dates tell a story.

steps.title: Company to Crown
steps.body:
- 1600 EIC charter · 1651 first factory on the Hugli · 1707 Aurangzeb dies · 1757 Plassey · 1764 Buxar · 1765 Diwani · 1770 Bengal famine · 1773 Regulating Act; Warren Hastings first Governor-General · 1793 Permanent Settlement · 1799 Tipu killed at Seringapatam · 1817–19 Third Anglo-Maratha War · 1822 Mahalwari · 1848–56 Doctrine of Lapse (Jhansi 1854) · 1856 Awadh annexed
- 1857: 29 Mar Mangal Pandey; 10 May Meerut; 11 May Delhi · 1858 Government of India Act, Queen's proclamation · 1859 Blue Rebellion · 1862 Bahadur Shah dies in Rangoon

steps.title: Tribals, education, reform
steps.body:
- Birsa Munda (mid-1870s–1900); Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908; revolts: Kol 1831–32, Santhal 1855, Bastar 1910, Warli 1940
- Calcutta Madrasa 1781 · Asiatic Society 1784 · Benaras Hindu College 1791 · Macaulay's Minute & English Education Act 1835 · Wood's Despatch 1854 · universities 1857 · Santiniketan 1901
- Sati banned 1829 · Widow remarriage 1856 · Phules' girls' school c.1848 · Gulamgiri 1873 · Arya Samaj 1875 · MAO College 1875 · Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 · Ambedkar's temple entry movement 1927

steps.title: National movement
steps.body: - INC 1885 · Partition of Bengal 1905 · Muslim League 1906 · Gandhi returns 1915 · Champaran 1917 · Jallianwala Bagh 13 Apr 1919 · Non-Cooperation 1920–22 (Chauri Chaura Feb 1922) · Purna Swaraj 1929 · Salt March 1930 · 1935 Act; 1937 elections · Lahore resolution 1940 · Quit India 1942 · Direct Action Day 16 Aug 1946 · Independence 15 Aug 1947 · Gandhi assassinated 30 Jan 1948

steps.title: Source-based tip
steps.body: Read the source twice. Underline who wrote it, when, and for whom. Answer in your own words, quoting a short phrase as evidence.

activity.prompt: Quick order check

quiz.why: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793. Munro devised ryotwari and Dalhousie the Doctrine of Lapse.
Jyotirao Phule wrote Gulamgiri in 1873, comparing caste oppression with slavery. Ambedkar and Periyar did not write it.
Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854 by Charles Wood. 1835 is Macaulay's Minute and 1857 the Revolt.
Birsa Munda died in 1900 in jail. 1895 was when his movement began.
The Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942. 1930 is the Salt March and 1920 Non-Cooperation.

lessons.title: Geography and Civics fact sheets

scenes.text: Sana draws a mini India map with mineral belts and industrial regions.
On the back she lists the Fundamental Rights and three courts.
Visual + list = strong memory.

steps.title: Geography
steps.body:
- Resources: natural/human-made/human; renewable/non-renewable; actual/potential; ubiquitous/localised; sustainable development; 3 Rs.
- Land 30% of Earth; 90% of people on 30% of land. Soil factors: parent rock, climate, relief, flora/fauna, time. Conservation: mulching, contour barriers, rock dam, terracing, intercropping, contour ploughing, shelter belts. Fresh water ≈ 2.7%. Vegetation: evergreen, deciduous, grassland, scrub, tundra. CITES; Van Mahotsav.
- Minerals: ferrous/non-ferrous/non-metallic; open-cast, shaft, drilling, quarrying. Power: conventional (coal, petroleum, gas, hydel) vs non-conventional (solar, wind, nuclear, geothermal, tidal, biogas).
- Agriculture: primary/secondary/tertiary; farm system; intensive & primitive subsistence (jhum = Milpa/Roca/Ladang), nomadic herding; commercial grain, mixed, plantation; crop conditions (rice, wheat, millets, maize, cotton 210 frost-free days, jute 'golden fibre', coffee Brazil, tea gentle slopes).
- Industries: agro/mineral/marine/forest; small/large; private/public/joint/cooperative; location factors; Bhopal 1984 (MIC); TISCO Jamshedpur 1907; first textile mill Mumbai 1854; Ahmedabad 'Manchester of India'; Bengaluru IT.

steps.title: Civics
steps.body:
- Constitution: in force 26 Jan 1950; Ambedkar chaired Drafting Committee; federalism (Union/State/Concurrent Lists); parliamentary govt; separation of powers; six Fundamental Rights; Right to Constitutional Remedies = 'heart and soul'.
- Secularism: distance, non-interference (turban exemption), intervention (untouchability ban). US First Amendment.
- Parliament: Lok Sabha 543, majority 272; Rajya Sabha (12 nominated); Bill → both Houses → President's assent → Act; Question Hour; Domestic Violence Act 2005.
- Judiciary: SC (26 Jan 1950), High Courts (first 1862), district courts; civil vs criminal (FIR); BNS/BNSS from 1 July 2024; PIL (1980s); Olga Tellis; PUCL mid-day meals.
- Marginalisation: Adivasis ≈ 8%, 500+ groups; Sachar Committee 2005; Article 17, Article 15; SC/ST Atrocities Act 1989; manual scavenging laws 1993 & 2013; Forest Rights Act 2006.
- Public facilities: right to water (Art. 21); Cochabamba vs Porto Alegre. Law & social justice: Bhopal settlement US$470 m (1989); child labour (2016 amendment); right to clean environment.

steps.title: Map tip
steps.body: Practise marking: iron-ore and coal states, the Pachmarhi region, major industrial regions, Jamshedpur, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, nuclear plants (Tarapur, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kaiga, Kakrapar, Rawatbhata).

activity.prompt: Quick match

quiz.why: A Lok Sabha majority needs more than half of 543, i.e. 272 seats. This is half plus one.

quiz.q: Which is a non-conventional power source?
quiz.why: Geothermal energy is a non-conventional source, because it is renewable and newer. Firewood, coal and diesel are conventional.
Exempting Sikhs from helmet rules shows the State respecting their religion and not interfering. That is non-interference.
TISCO was set up in 1907 at Jamshedpur. 1947 is independence and 1984 the Bhopal tragedy.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) is India's criminal code from 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code. The Evidence Act and CrPC are other laws.

lessons.title: Mock paper A (mixed)

scenes.text: 15 minutes, 8 questions, no notes.
Mixed History, Geography, Civics.
7+ correct = ready.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: Attempt all eight. Then read each explanation and redo any you missed tomorrow.

steps.title: Model 3-mark answer (History)
steps.body: *Why did the Blue Rebellion break out in 1859?* → (1) Ryots were forced into indigo contracts (satta) with low prices and endless debt; (2) indigo exhausted the soil and took the best land; (3) they felt supported by local zamindars and by news after the Queen's proclamation; so they refused to grow indigo and attacked factories.

steps.title: Model 3-mark answer (Civics)
steps.body: *Why is an independent judiciary important?* → It can check misuse of power by the legislature and executive, protect Fundamental Rights, and decide disputes fairly without pressure from the powerful.

activity.prompt: Which subject — History, Geography or Civics — feels weakest after Mock A? Write two topics you'll revise first.
activity.hint: Be specific: e.g. 'Mahalwari vs Ryotwari' or 'soil conservation methods'.

options: Outsiders seen as exploiters by tribals
quiz.why: Dikus were outsiders, like moneylenders and traders, whom tribals saw as exploiters. They were not crops or tribal chiefs.

quiz.q: A2. The Subsidiary Alliance was devised by:
quiz.why: Lord Wellesley devised the Subsidiary Alliance (1798-1805). Cornwallis, Dalhousie and Hastings are linked to other policies.
Mulching means covering the soil with organic matter like straw, which keeps moisture. Terraces, contour ploughing and tree rows are different methods.
Fish oil comes from the sea, so it is marine-based. Paper is forest-based, cement is mineral-based and cotton textile is agro-based.

quiz.q: A5. Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens:
options: Approach courts if Fundamental Rights are violated
quiz.why: The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens go to the courts when their Fundamental Rights are violated. It does not allow double voting or tax avoidance.

quiz.q: A6. A rent dispute is a ___ case.
quiz.why: A rent dispute is between private parties over their rights, so it is a civil case. A criminal case involves an offence.

quiz.q: A7. Case: A city privatises water and prices quadruple, sparking protests that reverse the deal. This happened in:
quiz.why: In Cochabamba, Bolivia in 2000, privatised water prices quadrupled and protests forced the deal to be reversed. Porto Alegre had successful public water supply.

quiz.q: A8. Assertion: Gandhi called off Non-Cooperation in 1922. Reason: Violence at Chauri Chaura.
options: A and R true; R explains A
quiz.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Gandhi called off Non-Cooperation in 1922 after the violence at Chauri Chaura, as he held firmly to non-violence.

lessons.title: Mock paper B (mixed)

scenes.text: A day later, Mock B.
More case-based questions.
Read each case slowly; underline key words.

steps.title: Instructions
steps.body: 15 minutes. For case-based questions, identify the concept being described before looking at the options.

steps.title: Model case answer (Geography)
steps.body: *A dry district wants to save water for farming. Suggest three measures.* → Drip/sprinkler irrigation; rainwater harvesting and check dams; lining canals to reduce seepage; growing hardy crops like millets.

steps.title: Assertion–reason method
steps.body: Check A, then R, then whether R explains A. Only then pick.

activity.prompt: Final-week plan
items: Day 1: History timeline + Mock A
Day 2: Geography sheet + map practice
Day 3: Civics sheet + Mock B
Day 4: Redo every wrong answer
Day 5: Light revision and 8+ hours of sleep

quiz.why: Tipu Sultan ruled Mysore and died defending Seringapatam in 1799. He did not rule Awadh, Bengal or Hyderabad.
Rabindranath Tagore founded Santiniketan in 1901. Gandhi, Jones and Macaulay did not.

quiz.q: B3. Case: A farmer's plot is part of a village whose total revenue is fixed and revised periodically, collected by the headman. This is:
quiz.why: When revenue is fixed for the whole village (mahal), revised periodically and collected by the headman, the system is Mahalwari. Permanent Settlement was fixed forever and ryotwari was with the cultivator.

quiz.q: B4. Thorium is found in monazite sands of:
quiz.why: Thorium is found in the monazite sands along the Kerala coast. Rajasthan, Assam and Punjab are not known for it.

quiz.q: B5. Amul is an example of the:
quiz.why: Amul is owned by milk producers, so it is in the cooperative sector. Public sector belongs to the government.
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha, chosen for their contribution to areas like arts and science.

quiz.q: B7. The Forest Rights Act was passed in:
quiz.why: The Forest Rights Act was passed in 2006. 1989 is the SC/ST Atrocities Act and 2013 the manual scavenging law.

quiz.q: B8. Assertion: Secularism in India allows State intervention in religion. Reason: The Constitution bans untouchability.
options: A and R true; R explains A
quiz.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Indian secularism allows the State to intervene in religion, as in banning untouchability, to ensure equality.

sources: NCERT Class 8 (topic)

questions.q: Battle of Plassey:
questions.why: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757, when Robert Clive defeated Sirajuddaulah. 1857 was the Revolt.

questions.q: Ryotwari settlement was with:
questions.why: The ryotwari settlement was made directly with the cultivators (ryots). Zamindars were the base of the Permanent Settlement.

questions.q: Indian Constitution came into force on:
questions.why: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. 15 August 1947 is independence and 26 November 1949 the adoption.

questions.q: A biotic resource:
questions.why: Forests are living, so they are a biotic resource. Soil, minerals and rocks are non-living (abiotic).

questions.q: The Supreme Court was established on:
questions.why: The Supreme Court was established on 26 January 1950, when the Constitution came into force. 1862 was the first High Courts.

questions.q: Jallianwala Bagh massacre:
questions.why: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place at Amritsar in 1919. 1942 is Quit India and 1930 the Salt March.

questions.q: Wheat requires at harvest time:
questions.why: Wheat needs bright sunshine at harvest time to ripen. Rain, floods or snow would harm the crop.

questions.q: Assertion: The Permanent Settlement failed to raise Company income when prices rose. Reason: The revenue demand was permanently fixed.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Because the revenue demand was fixed permanently, the Company could not raise its income when prices rose.

questions.q: Which is a forest-based industry?
questions.why: Paper uses wood pulp from forests, so it is forest-based. Fish oil is marine-based, cement mineral-based and dairy animal-based.

questions.q: Mangal Pandey's protest was at:
questions.why: Mangal Pandey attacked his officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857. The Meerut revolt followed on 10 May.

questions.q: Case: A tribal community clears forest, burns it, sows in ash, and shifts later. In Mexico this is called:
questions.why: Shifting cultivation is called milpa in Mexico. It is roca in Brazil, ladang in Indonesia and jhum in India.

questions.q: Who founded the Self-Respect Movement?
questions.why: Periyar (E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker) founded the Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu. Phule, Ambedkar and Narayana Guru worked in other movements.

questions.q: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of:
options: Religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
questions.why: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Height or only wealth are not grounds listed.

questions.q: Which pair is WRONG?
questions.why: The Asiatic lion lives in Gir, not Kaziranga, so that pair is wrong. Kaziranga is known for the one-horned rhino.

questions.q: Assertion: PIL increased access to justice for the poor. Reason: Any individual or organisation could file on behalf of those whose rights were violated.
options: A and R true; R explains A
questions.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. PIL lets any individual or organisation file on behalf of those whose rights were violated, which opened the courts to the poor.

questions.q: Correct order:
options: Wood's Despatch → Revolt of 1857 → INC founded → Partition of Bengal
questions.why: The dates are Wood's Despatch 1854, Revolt 1857, Congress founded 1885 and Partition of Bengal 1905. That gives the correct order.

questions.q: Case: An MNC cuts safety costs in a pesticide plant near a crowded colony; a gas leak follows. Which lessons apply?
options: Strict enforcement of safety laws and separating homes from hazardous industry
questions.why: The Bhopal lessons are to enforce safety laws strictly and keep homes away from hazardous industry. More cost-cutting or scrapping laws would invite another disaster.

questions.q: Why is iron and steel a 'feeder industry'?
options: Its products are raw materials for many other industries
questions.why: Iron and steel is a feeder industry because its products are raw materials for many other industries, like machines and construction. It has nothing to do with food.

questions.q: Assertion: After 1858 the British increased the proportion of Indian soldiers. Reason: They wanted to reward Indian loyalty.
questions.why: Both are false. After 1858 the British reduced the proportion of Indian soldiers in the army because they no longer trusted the sepoys fully.

questions.q: Which best describes Indian secularism?
options: Principled distance: the State keeps away from religion but may intervene to ensure equality
questions.why: Indian secularism is principled distance: the State keeps away from religion but may intervene to ensure equality. It does not ban religion, nor does it keep a strict wall like the USA.
